In the spring of 2013, just before the midterm elections, the Pew Research Institute conducted a survey to understand how Americans perceive the US political system. They asked a simple question: "How often do you visit the Capitol building to vote?"

It was striking that many respondents, around 14 times a year among Republicans, 15 among Democrats, and 12 among independents, reported not having visited the Capitol at all. This was a significant increase from the 6 times a year reported in the previous Congress.

Interestingly, the Capitol building saw a surge in visitors, with over 1.3 million people visiting in the most recent quarter, the highest number in four years, according to the Office of Personnel Management.

One possible reason for the increased visits could be the approaching election, as the chamber prepares to debate and consider various amendments and policy measures. Many of these measures may benefit incumbent representatives.

However, this trend may not necessarily be beneficial for members of Congress. Public approval of the House has traditionally been low, but it has recently increased to the mid-40s. Nonetheless, it remains a challenging year for representatives.

In particular, the approval rating of House Majority Leader John Boehner has plummeted. His personal approval rating dropped 5 points from the previous year, with only 38 percent of Americans approving of his job performance.

The Pew Research Institute's poll also found that majorities disapproved of the job the House and Senate are doing, with 46 percent disapproving of both. This is worse than the previous year, when only 2 points separated the House and Senate on these measures. The Senate's approval ratings have actually improved over the past year, with 52 percent approving of the job done by Senators Richard Burr, Pat Roberts, and John McCain.

The data was collected between April 13 and 19, 2013, and included 1,010 randomly selected adults from all 50 states and US residents aged 18 or older. The margin of error is plus or minus 3 percentage points, except for the question about visits to the Capitol, which has a margin of error of plus or minus 6 percentage points.

The notion of a "Second American Revolution" is often associated with a pivotal moment in history. This declaration led to the development of new states and cities across the northeastern region.

The roots of this revolution can be traced back to the 1770s, a time of great militancy and political debate in Massachusetts. A group of forty-three individuals gathered at Lexington to discuss their grievances with the British government. Although they were ordered to disperse, they refused and were eventually stopped by British soldiers led by General George Washington. The ensuing skirmish led to the death of four rebels, and the remainder fled into the woods, where they regrouped and began organizing their own army, the Continental Army.

The Continental Army, led by General John Sullivan, fought against the British on two fronts: the northern and southern regions. The war raged across the eastern United States and the western territories of Canada. The Continental Congress officially declared the independence of the United States by passing the Articles of Confederation in 1777. The war was not declared in the colonies until June 1776, after the British declaration of independence.

The Venezuelan opposition coalition accused President Nicolas Maduro of "excessive wrongdoing" during a march to commemorate late President Hugo Chavez's 43-year rule.

The opposition rallied behind its most popular leader, Henrique Capriles Radonski, and sought to use the vigil to highlight government abuses of power.

"We don't want to live under the rule of a regime that doesn't respect the legacy we've handed to those who have given up their lives to defend our freedom," said Capriles, who had a recent encounter with police.

"We won't live under the rule of oppressive regimes in our countries."

Chavez ruled Venezuela for 14 years, and some opposition members and supporters are wary of Maduro's administration. Capriles has clashed with the government before, most notably in January over the nationalization of oil company PDVSA, which the government accuses his team of hoarding.

During the three-day march, Capriles took the lead as opposition rallies broke out in some cities. A senior opposition leader, Capriles took the microphone to denounce Maduro's government and the "unjust" use of force by his security detail during a protest in his home city of Barinas on Friday night.


"Today the Venezuelan people have shown that we will not give up, and this is the beginning of the end of the regime that has committed wrongdoing that surpasses all norms of humanity," Capriles said.

The Venezuelan opposition coalition said some 3 million people had attended and more than 150,000 people were on the streets, including opposition activists and protesters.

Opposition leaders have held vigils for Chavez in every Venezuelan state except for Orinoco, where there was no sign of the revered Chavez who ruled with an iron fist before passing away in March 2013 from cancer.


Supporters of Venezuela's President Hugo Chavez participate in a march to commemorate the 43rd birthday of the late president in the eastern city of Barinas, Venezuela, Sunday, March 6, 2015. (Nicolas Garcia/AP)

Capriles described those who had taken part in past pro-Chavez vigils as "a very small minority," saying that "the majority of Venezuelans are happy with the transition to freedom of Chavez."

In the face of Capriles's popularity, Maduro has accused him of stoking "chaos and provocations," and he has condemned rallies aimed at toppling him.

Opposition leaders have called for a national strike early March 8, when Maduro is scheduled to arrive in New York this weekend for the United Nations General Assembly, and for a day of strikes on Tuesday as part of a one-week strike of state workers.

"These people in the streets, they don't deserve to speak or be heard," Maduro said Sunday afternoon during a speech in Barinas.

While Capriles and others in the opposition acknowledge Maduro's power base is behind him, they say the government has failed to deliver a stable democracy.

"The Chavista regime's only priority is to remain in power by maintaining a constant terror campaign against all forms of opposition," said Alex Lopez, a Caracas-based political analyst. "All of that has worked. But it is going to fail."

Maduro calls his government the political wing of the Venezuelan people and has sought the support of Brazil and Argentina, where Chavez enjoyed a more vibrant movement.

Chavez's rule was marked by a deep sense of national pride and pride in the role Chavez played in fighting for Chavez's ideals.


Chavez supporters gather Sunday outside the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas before a march to commemorate the 63rd anniversary of president Hugo Chavez's birth in Caracas, Venezuela. (Carlos Garcia Rawlins/Reuters)

Calls for more opposition to take part in the marches were muted as the anti-establishment movements that rose up in 2009 against Chavez's rule continued to shrink.

"The march will be huge and the people will rally. I don't know what will happen, but they are going to have a huge turnout. I don't know what's about to happen, but we have to take part, to make sure the government gives a good image to Maduro and this government," said Luis Manuel Rondon, a member of the board of the National Assembly.

As his opposition allies protested across the country Sunday, Maduro was in a hotel in New York.

"They're trying to turn the Caracas demonstrations into a coup against the Venezuelan people. They have failed," Capriles said.

A recent report by Consumer Reports revealed that most health plans with the lowest premiums have annual deductibles exceeding $600. The deductible is the amount individuals must pay before insurance coverage kicks in. The median deductible was $637, with about half of the plans featuring annual out-of-pocket maximums exceeding $2,000.

"The high cost of deductibles, coupled with copays and high out-of-pocket maximums, has become a pressing concern among consumers," said Thomas Mann, Consumer Reports' consumer program director. "Although there is no one-size-fits-all solution, we discovered some strategies to reduce deductibles and maximize benefits on the most affordable health plans."

Consumer Reports analyzed over 3,600 health plans and found that the following characteristics are common among the plans with the lowest premiums:

For a plan with a $99 annual deductible, the average annual cost is approximately $8,560, meaning it would take around 11 years and $8,560 worth of expenses before reimbursement.

For a plan with a $1,000 annual deductible, the annual cost is about $3,760, requiring patients to pay around six years' worth of expenses before reimbursement.

For a plan with a $5,000 annual deductible, the annual cost is $11,660, necessitating patients to pay $15,000 worth of expenses before receiving medical care.

On average, patients eligible for tax credits would owe $500 or less for their deductible. However, this means they would not be eligible for federal subsidies.

The study examined plans for adults 21 and older. A recent study by the Health Care Cost Institute estimated that the average out-of-pocket costs for individuals purchasing their own insurance after receiving tax credits was $1,813 (before tax credits).

The study's lead author, Katherine Hempstead, noted that "cost-sharing reductions – the caps on insurance deductibles – can help keep deductibles down. However, deductibles can only increase, and the law does not set the maximum out-of-pocket limits, so the next consideration will be the maximum costs."

The story was reported first by The Washington Post on Tuesday. It is true that the Russian government paid Facebook to amplify stories of Russian influence. But it is not true that Facebook, which is now under pressure to answer for fake news it hosted as part of its political ad program, "injected news articles" about Ukraine into people's news feeds.

Facebook said in a statement this morning it would not discuss specific clients because of privacy concerns. On Tuesday the Wall Street Journal reported a former Facebook executive had disclosed that in at least one election in 2018, the company may have been involved in a coordinated effort to manipulate Facebook users in that country to vote. Facebook has repeatedly said it has no evidence of that.

Facebook has always been upfront about the fact it was influenced by human beings, from advertisers and other sources. In a blog post last May, the company wrote that "news feeds are not designed to be independent of one another, and there are limits to what stories show up in people's news feeds" — though those limits are not written all those words, it seems clear.

The most important of those limits is "not more" — and Facebook clearly was not looking at a single election at all.

For this year's U.S. general election, Facebook says it "saw and may have influenced more than 12 million pieces of content with a very small amount of advertising dollars." That's roughly 3.67 billion impressions. But it added that the "news feeds of our millions of publishers are not in any way shaped by the election as a whole, not in any way shape or form."

A spokesman for Russia Today, the Kremlin TV channel and propaganda outlet Russia Today (not to be confused with Russia Today Broadcasting Group, which has an ownership stake in The Post), defended its role and the role of Facebook in a tweet this morning. "Facebook is playing an important role in providing information, views, opinion and all other information to the entire world," he wrote.

The ordinance includes such restrictions to ensure that large plastic bags, typically associated with larger grocery store purchases, will not be distributed freely in the city.

In response, the Jacksonville LGBT rights group Florida Gays & Lesbians Anti-Defamation Commission (FGLAC) has filed a lawsuit in federal court challenging the city's ban on plastic bags. On May 5, FGLAC filed an amicus brief in the case — along with dozens of individuals and local organizations, including the American Medical Association (AMA), American Association for Justice, Lambda Legal, NAACP Legal Defense Fund, National Center for Lesbian Rights, and the Center for Science in the Public Interest — in support of the plaintiffs.

According to FGLAC, the ordinance infringes upon the First Amendment and the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment, as well as Florida's Unfair Trade Practices Act, which prohibits discrimination in any industry, including food. The lawsuit cites the example of a Florida doctor who owns a clinic that operates out of a warehouse, but does not want to pay for bags to transport medical waste.

"Plastic bags are a natural product and natural products can include garbage," FGLAC Legal Director, Andrew Schneider said in a press release. "The government cannot treat a natural product differently than other public goods."

According to a press release from FGLAC, this is only the second time in recent history a case has been filed against a city over its plastic bag ban. When the Austin, TX ordinance was first passed in May, the legal challenge was filed on May 14. However, because it was still under review and could possibly be repealed, the appeal was dismissed by the Texas Supreme Court in September.

The case is now being brought to the U.S. Supreme Court in an attempt to overturn Jacksonville's ordinance for the second time in less than three years. Since the ordinance was first passed, the city's legal team has stated that they "are confident that the evidence will show that the [City of Jacksonville] illegally discriminated against its citizens for political reasons."

"The FGLAC Legal Director and we were disappointed to learn that the City of Jacksonville has challenged this ordinance," FGLAC Executive Director, Matt McTighe, said. "Although a number of city leaders have been very supportive of FGLAC and our work to protect the rights of the LGBTQ community, it is disappointing that the City would file a legal challenge that can only have the effect of undermining our work. By protecting business interests and ignoring the concerns of the LGBTQ community, the City has once again shown its deep disrespect for the rights of its citizens."

In April, a similar lawsuit was also filed against Jackson, MS, over its ban on plastic bags and small paper bags in grocery stores, as it argued that the City's ordinance would violate the First Amendment, because it singles out one group of people for its discriminatory policies. A recent investigation has led a diverse group of experts to produce a comprehensive report that may lead to a new method of creating microscopic devices with a specific purpose.

A novel technique that utilizes a polymer to attach a biological cell to a biological material will enable scientists to develop new and potentially more sensitive detection tools. The research was recently published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Scientists have long been intrigued by the possibility of using biological materials in a molecular manufacturing process. Biomimicry has long been viewed as a powerful potential solution because cells and biological materials can work together to create complex new materials. However, researchers have faced a challenge in producing functional bioplastics of any size, with a specific purpose.

The research team at the University of Michigan studied a protein called pectin, a protein that serves as a binding agent that holds the protein building blocks, nucleic acids, together. When an RNA molecule is packaged in the pectin, it is able to carry its genetic code.

"We needed a way to make biological cells attach to each other, so that a cell that has been grown in a lab would bind to another cell that was also grown in a lab," said study co-author Mark Lutz, chair of the U-M department of chemistry and co-director of the Molecular and Bioengineering Institute at the U-M Medical School.

Lutz collaborated with scientists from Rice University and the University of California at Berkeley. Lutz's team applied a polymer to a pectin coating. They found that the adhesive held on to a polymer, and the polymer, when separated, could stick to itself and then to a cell or a drug. The researchers then used the method to create a cell, and it attached to a small, protein-filled vessel filled with a virus. The cells were then injected into a patient and the virus was used to deliver DNA for research.

"The polymer is much easier to manufacture in bulk than natural pectin," he said. "We hope this work opens up new opportunities in manufacturing large biological constructs."

"Using a synthetic polymer made from our polymerized pectin with an additional polymer-reacting agent, we were able to develop a three-state pectin surface to which cells could attach and then that could bind to and release their own RNA into the bloodstream," said Rice University chemical engineers John Gentry, Ph.D., and Junyi Zhang, M.S., the paper's co-authors. "We believe this method is useful for a variety of applications, including molecular manufacturing of functional synthetic cells capable of sensing in vivo the concentration of specific molecules."

The researchers plan to apply this hybrid approach to other types of biology.

"We believe that this work could have a wide range of useful applications, not only in nanotechnology but also in the field of biomedical research," he said.

The research was supported by a National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship, a U-M Postdoctoral Fellowship, a National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship in the Bioengineering program, and National Institutes of Health awards.

Plato suggests that simply uttering "I apologize" or "I give up" is imperfect, as it does not convey genuine contemplation. Instead, it is a hasty admission.

Theophrastus of Tyana proposes that saying "I apologize" or "I forgive" is perfect, as it must be accompanied by a gesture of great charity and generosity.

Confucius emphasizes the importance of apologizing for specific actions or ignorance, rather than one's inherent nature. He believes it is more effective to show compassion than mercy.

A recent study by the University of Queensland unveiled the most beloved Australian creature online, which surprisingly is not a reptile, crustacean, or mammal, but a mammal.

The University of Queensland's research analyzed the most popular animal names globally and discovered that the pig in Australian online culture ranks second only to the feline.

The top 10 most popular animals on the internet, ranked by their popularity among Australians, are:

1. Feline (12.1 million internet users)

2. Equine (10.9 million)

3. Canine (7.2 million)

4. Marsupial (6.5 million)

5. Porcine (6.4 million)

6. Equine, feline, and ursine (6.3 million)

7. Canine, vulpine, and ursine (5.7 million)

8. Canine, vulpine, and canine (5.3 million)

9. Porcine, porcine, porcine (4.7 million)

10. Porcine (4.5 million)

The most common animal used to describe oneself online was the feline, surpassing the equine. On the other hand, the porcine was the least common name in online Australia, accounting for only 1.9 percent of online Australians.

Although some of the most popular animals and words in Australian online culture are familiar to Australians, the results demonstrate that the online Australian community still experiences new phenomena, with the porcine at the forefront of online animal language.

"Australians and people worldwide are constantly innovating, and as they do, we discover new ways to communicate," said Associate Professor Joanne Webster of the university's school of media and communication. "The porcine has played a significant role in Australian online culture and has been a favorite among Australians for a long time."

The study also revealed that Australian internet users are highly aware of Australia's unique animal language.

"Surprisingly, the most common animal name used by non-Australians is not a reptile, crustacean, or mammal but a porcine," said Associate Professor Webster. "This suggests we have a long way to go before we are able to communicate using more familiar animal language, especially if this is something we would want to say to another person."

The results of the survey came as a surprise to several of the researchers who took part, even though it was something that had been predicted by the survey's authors.

"We were not expecting this to be such a big deal, considering that pigs are so popular worldwide," said associate professor Julia Halliday-Smith, who conducted the survey. "One of us is a big pig fan and has the privilege of knowing a few of Australia's pig mascots, so maybe there's this connection."

Despite the strong presence of the porcine on the Australian internet, the researchers found that Australians are actually more likely to be offended than the global public.

"Australians are a bit more sensitive to other cultures' cultural appropriation of their particular cultural heritage," said Ms Halliday-Smith. "One of the researchers thought the reaction of the porcine might even make Australians angry or upset, but he wasn't sure."

Of the 3,600 Australians who took part in the survey, 1,600 answered the "usual name" question, but only 479 gave a response to the "different names" poll. In the online community, the difference in responses to these two polls was explained as a result of the Australian internet culture being "primarily online, rather than face-to-face", the researchers said.

The researchers of the survey hope their report will spark an interest among Australian Internet users to engage in the same kinds of discussions which occurred globally over the past year when the United States began banning the words "Mexican", "Muslim" and "gays" from internet chatrooms.

"People in Australia are really proud of their unique language, so it was interesting to see that it has its own quirks," said Ms Halliday-Smith.

The findings are published in the International Journal of Communication.

Some have questioned the accuracy and authenticity of these accounts, while others have expressed concerns about the potential errors and misconceptions that may be present. In this article, I aim to explore both of these topics and delve deeper into the nature of the Bible.

A friend recently shared with me their thoughts on the matter, having just finished reading a book titled "The Bible Doesn't Know It All: Why Your Favorite Version is Wrong." The author, Kevin DeYoung, is a professor of philosophy and theology at Southern Baptist Theological Seminary and is well-known for his articulate and informed perspectives on the Bible. While he does not believe the New Testament is an exact word of God, he does believe it is the most accurate written work produced by men at the time of Jesus. This book also critiques various parts of the Bible, and I suggest we begin by discussing the basics before moving on to more nuanced topics.

The Basics

When we consider the concept of inerrancy, we often associate it with six specific doctrines: the historicity of biblical stories, the inspiration of literary works, the exact meaning of God's commandments, historical facts, the historicity of Jesus Christ, the nature and date of Jesus' death and resurrection, and the authority of the New Testament. Additionally, the scriptures are generally assumed to be the word of God as delivered to the original audience.

The term "inerrancy" has also been used to deny or minimize certain historical and theological claims of the Bible. For instance, it is often used to explain the lack of historical authenticity of the "gospels," which supposedly record only part of Jesus' life and/or other aspects and events of Christianity. The word "inerrancy" is also used to deny various theological statements attributed to Jesus, which are clearly and decisively in his words.

Determining the infallibility of the Bible can be a complex task. Most Christians would argue that the biblical stories speak for themselves and are therefore without error. However, what does it mean to say the Bible does not speak for itself? Does it mean only that a person speaks for himself, or does it refer to all people in a culture speaking for themselves? Perhaps "speak for itself" means only speaking for oneself or one's own culture. The Bible is considered inerrant when it speaks for that culture, meaning the biblical stories do not vary from culture to culture or from time to time.

In reality, Christians have always been concerned with understanding the Bible's words and evaluating them in light of Christian truth. The Bible cannot speak for itself because it is the Word of God, given by God to prophets and apostles as revelation of God. When God told the prophets and apostles what to write, they would write what God told them, using the divinely given authority that God gave them.

However, not all language makes it into a book of Scripture. When people say "It doesn't matter," they mean "what they don't say doesn't matter." But what if a book or an entire language does not make it into the Bible? If we do not accept that the book or language does not belong in the canon of Holy Scripture, and only a portion (or none at all) of that language should be there, then it would follow that the books which the Bible does contain should likewise be understood according to Christian truth. The books of the Bible are not inerrant just because the entire Bible does not say everything or nothing.

The Quest for Understanding

Many individuals consider Jesus to be a personal and unconditional teacher, providing answers to their daily queries. While this may be true for some, it is crucial to acknowledge that the Bible does not contain all the answers. In fact, the Bible is more of a narrative, a story that has been passed down through generations.

The idea that the Bible is a comprehensive guide to understanding Jesus and his teachings is a misconception. The book "The Bible is Not What it Seems" by Christopher Hitchens highlights this point, stating that the Bible is a collection of historical accounts that span over a thousand years. These accounts are not necessarily accurate or reliable, and they often lack concrete evidence to support their claims.

The story of Jesus, as told in the four Gospels, is a narrative that has been passed down through centuries. It is a story about the Jewish rejection of Jesus and his subsequent conversion to Christianity, as well as his death and resurrection. While this story has been widely accepted as the truth, it is essential to recognize that it is a narrative, not a factual account.

The Christian faith has undergone significant changes over the centuries, and this is reflected in the discrepancies found in Christian teachings today. Many Christians claim to follow Jesus, but they often disagree on fundamental aspects of his teachings. This is because there was no single authority to settle these disputes in the early days of Christianity, and people often created their own stories and interpretations.

A crucial aspect of understanding Jesus and his teachings is recognizing the importance of the Q documents. These documents, which are recognized as part of the New Testament, provide valuable insights into the early Christian community and its understanding of Jesus. However, it is essential to note that the Q documents are not part of the New Testament canon.

The Bible is not a single, authoritative text, but rather a collection of stories and accounts that have been passed down through generations. While it contains valuable insights into Jesus and his teachings, it is essential to approach it with a critical eye and recognize its limitations.

This can save a lot of time and effort.

Performs all the necessary networking, management, and administrative tasks.

Installs, configures, and runs application frameworks.

Installs, adds, or deletes applications and databases.

Handles requests from clients.

The impact of mental health issues on daily life cannot be overstated. Fortunately, most people who experience mental health problems are able to recover. Here are some common mental health issues and how to recognize them:

1. Emotional Imbalance: This condition can cause physical symptoms such as changes in appetite, increased sleep needs, and irritability. With the right treatment, it's possible to manage symptoms and improve overall well-being.

2. Sensory Overload: Some individuals may experience overwhelming feelings of fullness or discomfort, leading to changes in body composition and overall health. Treatment can help alleviate these symptoms and promote a sense of balance.

3. Compulsive Behavior: Addiction can manifest in many forms, including substance abuse, compulsive behaviors, and other self-destructive patterns. Recognizing the signs of addiction and seeking help is crucial for recovery.

4. Nutritional Imbalance: This condition can cause rapid weight loss, fatigue, and other physical symptoms. Treatment typically involves a comprehensive approach that addresses nutritional and emotional needs.

5. Mood Swings: Bipolar disorder is characterized by rapid shifts in mood, from euphoria to depression. Treatment often involves a combination of therapy and medication to stabilize mood and promote emotional well-being.

6. Traumatic Brain Injury: This condition can cause a range of physical and cognitive symptoms, including headaches, memory loss, and difficulty concentrating. Treatment typically involves a multidisciplinary approach that addresses physical, emotional, and cognitive needs.

7. Toxic Relationships: Substance abuse and abusive relationships can have far-reaching consequences for mental and physical health. Recognizing the signs of toxic relationships and seeking help is essential for recovery and well-being.

Remember, mental health issues can have a significant impact on daily life, but with the right treatment and support, it's possible to recover and thrive.

The sun was shining brightly on November 10th when a jury delivered a verdict. Jeffrey Sterling, a former CIA contractor, was found guilty of three counts related to a 2010 Senate Intelligence Committee meeting. The jury's decision came after a lengthy trial, with Sterling's lawyer filing a motion for acquittal just days later.

The motion argued that the evidence presented did not support Sterling's intent to disclose classified information. It also highlighted the risks to national security posed by media coverage of the leaks. The government's legal theory, if proven, would allow them to convict Sterling for reporting information he believed was protected by the First Amendment.

The legal implications of this theory are far-reaching. It could be used to silence whistleblowers who act in good faith, fearing accusations of leaking classified information. The government's approach is akin to claiming a car is safe after an explosion, as long as the explosion occurred within the vehicle.

A federal jury would likely be sympathetic to Sterling's position, given the media's focus on him rather than the actual conduct. Even if Sterling took steps to protect classified information, he could still be convicted if the government can convince jurors he acted with malicious intent.

The government's theory assumes Sterling was motivated by a desire to harm national security, rather than a legitimate interest in the publication of the information. However, the US government frequently publishes operational details and intelligence assessments related to counterterrorism operations.

On November 10, Sterling was sentenced to two years in prison. A new sentencing hearing has been scheduled for January 14, 2015. If a new hearing is not scheduled, Sterling could still be released on bail. If he is convicted on all counts, he faces a 40-year sentence.

The case raises another important question: Does what Sterling did constitute "treason" under the Constitution? The government has charged Sterling with leaking information in a "treasonous" fashion, but the definition of treason under US law is unclear. One way to test the charge is to compare it with the standard language used to support the charges.

In United States v. Miller, Justice Kennedy suggested that the standard language on the conspiracy charge should be compared to the standard language of treason. The Miller holding suggested that the criminal violation of treason requires the defendant to intend to effect their conspiracy by "intentionally and materially assisting and abetting" others.

If the government's theory is that Sterling committed the crime of treason by communicating with the public press or publishing classified information, then it cannot prove that Sterling had "specific intent" to disclose the information. If Sterling acted in good faith, thinking that publication of information might cause significant harm to national security, then he could theoretically justify his leak.

In recent years, there has been a growing trend towards investing in alternative assets, such as real estate and commodities, as investors seek to diversify their portfolios and reduce their reliance on traditional stocks and bonds. However, this trend has also been driven by a growing sense of uncertainty and volatility in the market, as investors become increasingly risk-averse.

Ultimately, the accuracy of predictions is always uncertain, and the best approach is often to focus on developing a long-term strategy that takes into account a range of possible outcomes. By doing so, investors can better prepare themselves for the unexpected and minimize their exposure to potential losses.

In an attempt to strike a balance in determining whether a "tax" on Bitcoin can be considered a successful and viable system, let's examine a few alternative financial systems.

Before World War I, there was no concept of taxes. Every country in the world was governed by a single national tax law, except for the two superpowers engaged in the war.

The British Empire was a significant force and had the power to impose taxation. The empire was also the only one of the superpowers to have a substantial global trading and military relationship (in contrast to its two minor trading partners, France and Spain).

However, if you wanted to transfer funds between countries, you had to go through an intermediary, a bank. Many banks worldwide are currently under investigation for money laundering related to the illegal drug trade. Authorities in many countries are likely to prosecute, convict, or imprison the bank holding your private information.

The US is a popular trading partner for many countries, and therefore, we can assume Bitcoin will generate revenue for some of them, perhaps even more. If the US implements laws similar to those applied to other currencies, it will likely reduce the volume of Bitcoin. Bitcoin will continue to appreciate in value but at a slower rate.

The fact is that Bitcoin is already being considered one of the most efficient and secure financial systems. It has more liquidity than national central banks and is growing exponentially in value.

It is not surprising that a country might decide to implement a tax on Bitcoin in certain circumstances, even if this is an extreme case. However, a better system to implement a "tax" would be an actual tax or a sales tax.

It is possible to tax Bitcoin under all these systems, though it will require compromises. This involves either creating a currency backed by commodities, establishing tax havens, or setting up a system with extremely strict compliance (similar to Switzerland). This is not impossible to implement. The countries that have attempted this (Netherlands, Belgium, Israel) are not considered success stories or economic powerhouses.

Regardless, it is essential for developing countries to have a legitimate, effective, and stable financial system to compete with Western capitalism. However, it would be beneficial if governments, especially emerging ones, recognized Bitcoin as a legitimate form of money or supported a legal and effective industry that will build and support Bitcoin.

The art of job searching is often misunderstood. People assume that being a "good" candidate is something innate, but I've learned that it's a skill that can be developed. After a decade of working in technical recruiting for start-ups and companies in the technology landscape, I've come to realize that it's all about the process.

When I first started, I thought that having strong back-office skills and the ability to deliver results quickly was the key to getting hired as a software engineer. But this approach ignored the underlying process. To get hired, you need to define who you're working with, understand what the company values, and be a good fit for the specific work you'll be doing.

If you don't agree with this, you might be in the wrong company. When you don't agree, you should be willing to adapt or find a new company that aligns with your values. If we don't have an explicit process, we can rely on what we see and read around us. The best examples of who gets hired are those who come with "good" interview skills - the ability to come up with answers, ask excellent questions, and suggest improvements.

As a recruiter, I look for certain traits in candidates. Does the company value the candidate's technical fit with the culture, product, and business? Can the candidate deliver results? Do they have a solid understanding of the product? Do they have strong leadership skills? Are they marketable and passionate about their work?

When I look for traits that go against this, I see two problems to work on. First, I need to be a good listener to understand the value the candidate sees in the company. Second, I need to be a great interviewer to ask the right questions and get to the heart of the candidate's qualifications.

Getting the process right is key. If you get the first part right, the conversation can go in a positive direction. I believe that showing up, working hard, and getting things done is the best way to succeed in a job search.

A recent case study by researchers at MIT showcases the capabilities of deep neural networks: It successfully predicts the next card in a Shogi deck based solely on the current position of the cards. The researchers' algorithm achieved an average error of less than 10%.

The system's deep neural network, comprising interconnected "neurons," learns to predict the next card by analyzing and comparing card positions. The algorithm assesses cards and assigns weights based on the number of cards in each pack. If a pack contains multiple cards with distinct characteristics, the algorithm focuses on that pack. As more cards from the pack become available, the weight of individual cards increases. In a deck containing 32 cards, a pack may contain 28 cards, and 16 of them will be unique. A weight of 1 indicates that the player is likely to receive that card. The weights in some pack pairs will be stronger than others, aiding in predicting whether a particular card will be played or not. However, this weighting is not perfect, as players may hold cards that do not match any card in the deck.

However, if a player's cards are in the ideal position to be played, the weight of the cards increases, and the algorithm performs better in predicting the card's probability.

The algorithm struggled in high-dimensional situations with a large number of cards and the current positions of more than two cards in the deck. It also performed poorly when a player had to choose between two cards with the same number of spots in the deck, and the algorithm was overly sensitive to the positions of cards already played.

How Deep Neural Networks Function

The neural network operates by examining the probabilities of each card—for instance, whether a card is currently out or not, or whether any cards in a pack will be out. The neural network then decides whether to retain this card.

This decision-making process involves taking a large matrix, referred to as the "training data," and dividing it into thousands of randomly selected small subsets and multiplying by a matrix factor. If the small subsets contain high-dimensional situations, the neural network adds the current cards in the deck and multiplies by the size and current position of the cards.

The algorithm then predicts the next card based on the results of the algorithm's analysis of the training data, which is divided into subsets based on the number of cards in the deck at each time. For example, if a deck contains 10 cards, the algorithm will divide it into five training subsets and four subsets for each deck, with each set containing one card out. The algorithm also determines the weights in individual subsets within each set so that the weight factors for each set sum to 1, and then multiplies the two matrices to produce a single matrix of weights for each subset within that set, based solely on the current cards in the set.

The Weight Matrix and the Decision Layer

The algorithm also decides, based on the current cards in the deck, the weight factor for each subset of the deck. When the weights factor equals 1, a subset is chosen; otherwise, a random choice is made. The algorithm then multiplies the weights matrix with the current cards in each subset, calculating the average result between the weighted subsets.

The algorithm takes the difference between the average weights across all subsets, multiplied by that average, and the sum of those squared weights, which determines the final weight for that subset. The result is a matrix and vector, and this is what the neural network uses to make the decision about whether to keep or skip a card. This matrix is used to determine the algorithm's decision.

The problem with "fuzzy" weight matrices is that if the inputs are not well connected, this may result in the weight matrix being too small to be useful for choosing between options. With such a small weight, some possible combinations of cards may be lost or ignored, which can result in poor performance. However, with a large enough weight to distinguish between options, a small number of combinations will be considered more likely than others. With enough computation power and data available, the weight matrix can be made sufficiently detailed to discriminate between options well enough to make an accurate decision.

There are other, more sophisticated, approaches to weighting with data for decision-making problems, but the technique proposed by the MIT researchers seems to work fairly well.

"By leveraging the matrix factor used by the neural network, the resulting weight matrix can be much bigger and more detailed than those used in other methods, making it more useful for decision making," says Raghavendra Saha, assistant professor of electrical engineering and computer science, and senior author of the paper.

The sun shines brightly on the American landscape, illuminating the vast expanse of our great nation. As we gaze out upon this breathtaking vista, we find ourselves pondering the mysteries of energy production. It is a topic that has fascinated us for centuries, and one that continues to shape our world today.

In the United States, a significant proportion of our energy is derived from the earth's rich deposits of coal and natural gas. But how do these two energy sources compare? It is a question that has sparked debate and discussion among experts and laymen alike.

According to the US Energy Information Administration, coal has long been the most common energy source in the United States. In fact, a staggering 78% of the country's energy was derived from coal between 2006 and 2010. Furthermore, during that same period, the US produced a whopping 7 billion tonnes of coal.

In contrast, the United Kingdom and Australia each produced a mere 3.9 billion tonnes of coal during the same year. Meanwhile, Japan derived less than 1% of its energy from coal.

As we delve deeper into the world of energy production, we find that natural gas is a viable alternative to coal. In fact, many experts believe that the growth of natural gas will continue to slow the decline of coal in the coming years.

"Natural gas is more versatile and less costly than coal," remarks Andy Lipow, a senior fellow at the think-tank Resources for the Future. It is a sentiment that is echoed by many in the energy industry.

However, fossil fuels, including coal and natural gas, have a significant drawback. While they do reduce carbon dioxide emissions, they are not particularly efficient. In fact, coal is the least efficient of the two, emitting more carbon dioxide and having a lower life-cycle efficiency than natural gas.

Furthermore, coal is not a cheap energy source. It is more expensive than alternative energy sources such as nuclear, wind, hydro-power, and solar.

Despite these drawbacks, the US coal industry continues to grow. In fact, the US Department of Energy recently reported that the number of new coal-fired power plants approved for construction has reached a record high of 38.

If the coal boom does not turn around soon, the world could be facing a future of rising electricity prices. It is a prospect that has many experts worried.

A coalition of organizations advocating for undocumented immigrants has submitted a brief to the Supreme Court, urging the justices to reconsider a 2014 ruling that affected the "Dream Act," a landmark immigration bill passed in 2013. The brief, filed on behalf of the Dream Action Coalition, the ACLU of Louisiana, the Center for American Progress Action Fund, the National Immigration Law Center, and ImmigrationWorks, argues that the decision was incorrect and that federal immigration law as it applies to families is unconstitutional.

The brief claims that the 2014 decision by the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, written by Chief Judge Roger Gregory, was flawed and that the law unconstitutionally allows for "chain migration," which is the granting of automatic citizenship to the parents of American citizens through their children. The team notes that the new species is a direct descendant of Homo erectus and is believed to have come into existence after the early branch of the human family tree diverged from the branch that eventually resulted in present-day hominids. The researchers also note that the new species appears to have had a different morphological pattern of the spine and a different position of its pelvic bones compared to present-day humans.

The study also suggests that the human ancestors were most closely related to the early ancestors of humans living today in China. The researchers believe that the early ancestors of humans living today in China may have descended from those ancestors.

The findings raise questions about how long ago humanity diversified into the variety of species now known today. The researchers believe that the answers to this question may help to answer a different question, which is, how did Homo sapiens evolve from an even more primitive species to one with the capability of creating the industrial revolutions?

The study also reveals a host of new details about the evolution of human life. The researchers believe that the first human ancestors had a very narrow range of behavior and adaptations and evolved very slowly. They also believe that those changes that occurred in the past were just as important from the point of view of evolution as their current evolutionary implications.

The findings are significant because they provide an important link between hominids in Africa and the hominid fossils and specimens found elsewhere. The discovery is also raising questions about the origins of farming.

His words have resonated with many, but have also sparked criticism from those who feel he is trying to shame them into changing their approach.

The response to his blog post has been mixed, with some praising his efforts to promote data transparency and others dismissing him as an elitist. Despite the criticism, Ioannidis remains committed to his cause, advocating for a more nuanced understanding of data analysis and its limitations.

In a recent Facebook post, Ioannidis asked data scientists for their input on how to best analyze the vast amounts of data being generated. He acknowledged the importance of collaboration and the need for a more comprehensive approach to data analysis.

The debate surrounding Ioannidis' work serves as a reminder of the importance of critical thinking and skepticism in the scientific community. As the world of science continues to evolve, it is essential that we remain vigilant in our pursuit of knowledge and truth.

We've updated our story to reflect the latest information from Roscosmos, the Russian state space corporation, which announced that the Rosetta spacecraft will enter its final orbit around the comet in early August.

Rosetta, which arrived at Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko in 2004, will finally come to rest inside the comet's frozen core on August 27 when it crashes down close to the surface, scientists said.

The spacecraft will begin slowing its descent next week as it heads for the nucleus on March 6 to prepare for its destruction, mission controllers confirmed.

The European Space Agency, Rosetta's prime contractor, plans to release the spacecraft on Thursday from its mothership in Germany to begin a three-and-a-half-year journey to comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko.

Rosetta will then begin a series of maneuvers designed to slow its speed and bring it into the right altitude, orientation, and angle to approach and land on the comet.

The spacecraft will be kept alive by a battery power source called the Philae lander, which will fire harpoons at the comet to bring it down near the surface.

Mission manager Sylvain Lodiot told a news conference that this is a very difficult operation and they are doing everything they can to prevent it from going astray.

On a normal descent, Rosetta will send commands to the lander to "wake up" the spacecraft. However, at a closer approach to the comet, the lander will fire a harpoon into the comet to bring it down closer to the nucleus to study the comet's composition and activity.

In a follow-up television news conference, a Rosetta team member confirmed that the final sequence of the spacecraft's descent will see it begin to slingshot to the comet surface at 5 mph before slowing its velocity down to 1 mph before landing.

A controlled landing near the comet's surface will take place early on August 27, team members announced. Once there, scientists will be able to collect a sampling, analyze the landing site, and attempt to make measurements of the comet's composition and activity.

Rosetta started orbiting the comet in March 2004, more than seven years after launch. The craft has traveled more than 4 billion miles in search of 67P.

"That's quite an achievement, and we are proud in many aspects of the work we have done," said Sylvain Bonacina, Rosetta project manager. "But it also brings into question how we are going to continue doing these [landing] missions in the future."

A few years ago, I had a conversation with my mother and sister about my son's recent diagnosis with a certain condition. My mother shared something that wasn't entirely unexpected. The conversation was interrupted, but I'll never forget her words. She said, "It would be wonderful if we could recognize the unique talents of people with this condition in an open and respectful way."

I responded with a mix of emotions, and my sister was equally stunned. Her response was... unusual. For me, this was the first time I realized two important things.

The first point is that our understanding of this condition is still evolving. While many experts agree on the underlying causes, there's ongoing debate about the best treatment approaches. The goal is to support people with this condition to achieve their best possible quality of life.

Unfortunately, a significant part of the scientific community still views people with this condition as having a specific cognitive impairment. This bias is not limited to this condition; it's also present in other developmental disorders. There's a significant imbalance in the amount of research devoted to this condition compared to other diseases.

The second point is that without a deep understanding of the condition, we can't develop effective treatments. My mother said, "We need to do something. We need to understand this condition and then find a cure."

I knew what she meant, but it didn't sink in. This condition is not limited to a specific individual, and our treatment decisions should be guided by the goal of minimizing the impact on the person's life.

The third point is that most research has focused on specific skills, like language and social communication. While these are important, we should also consider other areas that could be improved. The goal is to help people achieve their full potential in life, not just to address specific symptoms.

We can't achieve this goal by focusing solely on symptoms we're familiar with.

In the past, someone posed the question about the best way to make a woman feel good about herself. Some responders suggested starting by making her feel empowered over her life, but noted that there's more to truly feeling loved. I've been thinking about this statement a lot lately.

Why do people need to feel like they're in control of their lives? There are many reasons, and I'll only touch on a few. For me, the main reason is to feel secure. And security is precisely why the idea of having power over one's life has become a problem for many men. Why do women need to make everything feel like their own if they're already making it their own?

When we have the power to make our lives feel like our own, it's a gift. Many of us struggle to comprehend the amount of power we already possess. But a woman who lacks security has little to live for. We need a reason to do and feel the things we need to do and feel. The fact that we need to consider the opinions of others can be an obstacle to feeling and doing what we want. How do we make others feel useful? How do we make ourselves feel useful? How do we make a woman feel useful? How do we make a boy feel loved and useful? How do we make the world feel useful?

There's nothing else we can ask or do besides putting in the work. But the truth is, when we're trying to please others, we always need to work hard to please ourselves. We need to feel good about ourselves. Men need friendship and love, women need to feel good about themselves, and children need to feel wanted. It's simple. What's the point of anything if we don't enjoy the experience? It's not like doing math or writing or working out: the more time we put in, the better. So don't we need to make sure our work doesn't feel like work if we don't enjoy it? Don't we need to set an example of how much we love people to make sure they will love and love us back?

But there's another factor at play here, too. Many of us are afraid to look outside ourselves and see someone else doing something we like and doing it well. Maybe your sister or dad does a great job, and you respect them for it, or maybe you didn't try to find a job you liked because you were afraid of what others would think. So we look at ourselves and only see what we don't want to see. And for a young person, there's always something they don't want to see. You can't turn back the clock, but you can make up for it by working hard to make others see something you want to see.

As I've previously mentioned, our nation is faced with two distinct paths forward. One option is to succumb to permanent financial ruin, while the other is a less-than-ideal scenario of economic stagnation.

However, there exists a third, often overlooked alternative: the U.S. government can address its outstanding debts in a responsible and sustainable manner.

In reality, the debt has already been settled. A permanent solution to the world's problems has been achieved, but the world is now grappling with a new crisis, and instead of seeking support from taxpayers, Washington is attempting to deceive the debt-burdened public.

It's essential to recognize that the U.S. government has not been paying its debts for nearly half a century. In fact, the U.S. government, along with other governments, defaulted on its debt in 1937 and again from 1941 to 1955.

Despite this, debt continues to grow, becoming increasingly crippling and intrusive. As we've seen, debt cannot be ignored; it only grows larger, faster, and more burdensome.

We are now operating in a new mode of spending that cannot be reversed by paying off debt, but rather requires continued growth and a continuous stream of new borrowing.

Debt does not magically increase without being addressed. This is why we cannot afford debt, as it serves as a ticking time bomb that will continue to grow as American taxpayers continue to pour more money into it.

This is not only true of the debt owed to foreign countries. According to a recent report by the New York Times, the combined total of America's outstanding debt over the next 12 years – $17 trillion – dwarfs our Gross Domestic Product, which is roughly $16 trillion.

Regardless of how many times our country has been saved from bankruptcy, the debt continues to accumulate. If we continue on this path, we won't only be paying for past policies, we're paying for them right now through higher interest rates.

This is why we must reduce spending and, especially, increase taxation.

The issue here is that tax revenue as a percentage of GDP is much lower than at any time in our history (except for the Reagan years when tax rates were up considerably).

Worse still, we must implement these changes simultaneously. If you cut taxes on the very wealthy, you will force companies to relocate facilities offshore and hire fewer workers. If you don't slash tax rates on corporations, you'll force corporations to lay off tens of thousands of jobs.

And if we don't alter our tax system before it affects American workers and families, we'll be adding another $300 trillion to the national debt. This is not a viable solution for saving America.

One of the things that makes America exceptional is that we've never run a huge trade deficit. That is, we have never, as a country, bought more from other countries than we've sold to them, thereby creating more jobs for our citizens. And we won't want to start now if we're forced to make that change.

The student governing body is facing a backlash from a group of students who claim the group should be reclassified as a "negative influence."

The president of UW-Madison's governing body stated the group has already faced intense criticism from students, faculty members, the university administration, and the national media.

"People are saying, 'What am I going to do? My friends already told me to stop my chapter to avoid any controversy so I haven't done anything,'" said Brandon White, president of the governing body.

The group, UW-Madison College Republicans, was founded by freshman Ben Abraham, who said he wanted to foster a college Republican culture that does not tolerate discrimination.

"I mean, I think it was a reaction to what was going on," Abraham said of the group's inception.

"I think it was pretty clear it would not be a welcoming environment," said Abraham, noting that many students in the group complained.

In September, the group hosted a social activity at the campus Republican society meeting, during which one of its members, Brandon Clark, was elected the group's president.

While Abraham said the group has not excluded anyone, several students have expressed their concern that the group continues to discriminate against people based on their gender, race, socioeconomic status, and religion.

"This group is very much focused on inclusivity and I can't tell you how many students have contacted me saying 'I want to meet, I want to talk but I don't want to be on the floor with them,'" said Abraham.

"It's a group that is very much against hate and intolerance. They are very much for equality and understanding. I wouldn't be surprised if they made a mockery of inequality," said sophomore Rachel Beers.

After an internal investigation, the governing body said it became aware that White, Clark and another student member created a social media profile and posted neutral comments.

On Saturday, the group held a meeting to discuss the new social media policy for all governing body groups.

Clark, who recently resigned as president of the group, said a policy change to make all governing body chapters more transparent about their social media status would be an important first step towards rebuilding their public image.

"I think we need to continue to work on being more open and transparent to show our true values and show what we stand for," Clark said of the meeting.

The group will hold another meeting on Monday to discuss another policy change, namely banning the use of a school email account and university-issued computer when social media is used.

University of Wisconsin-Madison police Sgt. Steve Johnson said he has been following the issue of the group's social media policies closely with members of the governing body and the dean of the College Republicans. The university also made public statements about the group's social media policies.

For now, White said he is confident that UW-Madison's governing body has taken appropriate steps to correct its past errors or be sued in court. The group's new social media policy goes into effect on Sept. 6.

After the group's meeting, some students spoke out in an email to the student newspaper, The Argus Review.

"There is a lot of stuff in this letter that is unclear and there is very little substance in it. It seems more like an attempt by [Clark]'s fellow senators to make him look like a bad guy than a sincere effort to work against negativity," said senior Samantha Beardsley, a member of the governing body's College Republicans.

The Argus Review reached out to the UW-Madison chapter of Unity. They did not respond to the story in time for publication.

The following is the third installment in a series of posts that will outline a simple model I utilize in my app development workflow to determine the optimal time for releasing apps. I've noticed a significant amount of discussion regarding the "best time" for each release, but I wanted to clarify the differences and offer my own insights on the matter.

I've endeavored to keep this post concise and straightforward. Feel free to leave comments and ask questions via the comment section!

The Approach

When designing a release schedule for a new app, I prefer to first consider the following factors:

1. Does the app possess a stable user base that requires engagement and usage?

2. Does the user base exhibit staleness as users transition to new devices? This is particularly relevant for iOS.

3. Is the app in a stable enough state for release?

If the answers to these questions are affirmative, and you're confident in the app's long-term viability, then the release date should reflect this certainty.

For instance, let's assume you're certain the app will only have a one-year lifespan. If this is the case, you'll have approximately 30 days to prepare for the next release. By the time you've completed testing, you'll have only a few months remaining.

To illustrate this example, let's consider the context of the iPhone X:

If your app has a one-year lifespan, you should release it three years after the iPhone X launch.

If your app has a shorter lifespan, you can choose a release window between 7 weeks and 2 months, depending on your experience with the app.

If you're aware of the app's lifecycle, including iOS 10 (as it does for iOS 9), 2 months is a more suitable choice.

So, what do we think is appropriate for our model – 4 weeks, or 2 months?

One aspect that frustrates me about some app users is the proliferation of "what ifs?" and "maybe ifs?" I've witnessed numerous instances of these over the past 12 months, particularly during the launch period. When users discover I didn't have sufficient time to conduct certain tests, they become frustrated and send me angry messages. This is not the type of experience I desire for my app.

So, when is the right time to release?

My model for determining the optimal release time begins with these three points:

Does the app possess a stable user base that requires engagement and usage? Once the app has a stable user base, it's easier to understand how you might need to adjust your schedule. Does the user base exhibit staleness as users transition to new devices? When users see the apps you've designed but don't have them, they'll perceive your app as buggy, slow, or broken. In some cases, these issues may be accurate. (For example, iPhone users typically have an average of two devices to purchase apps for – not necessarily in any order.) Does the app in a stable enough state for release? This is a challenging aspect, as it's not solely about knowing the features required for a smooth user experience. Your users have likely heard about your new feature in the news, so it's essential to put your app through the test of how it functions.

As I mentioned, some apps don't require re-testing for every release, but I've found it's always beneficial to have a backup in case there are any bugs or issues hiding on the iOS 10 beta.

The Release Schedule

I've utilized the following schedule for the past seven years:

Each Monday morning, I review the app on iOS and iOS Simulator, identify any issues that need to be addressed, and then submit the fix by 10 am. This schedule provides me with 3.5 days to test. If I complete the fixes by 11 am, I'm done. However, if I make additional fixes after my third pull-request from my development cycle, I have an extra two days to test again.

This process seems obvious and is likely a significant factor in why many of us (including myself) end up following the same routine every day. There's also a notable benefit for your business, as a release schedule helps your average users gain a better understanding of how the app will function. It enables you to focus your development efforts on making things perfect or fast.

If this doesn't make sense, you may have a different perspective – I've seen numerous companies with no release schedules that have achieved remarkable releases. But if you do have a release schedule, I hope I've provided some valuable insights and helped clarify your reasoning behind implementing your own.

"The new development project is a fantastic chance for our company to create a unique path in the downtown area and for the region," says Tom D'Agostino, president and CEO of the Downtown Denver Partnership. "It's a significant investment to complete our vision."

"We had an expectation that they would take a close look at what this project would do," he says. "We were hopeful that their assessment was that the impact would be small or moderate and that it would be cost-effective."

In April 2001, The Broadmoor hotel, also located near South Broadway and Colfax, moved to a higher elevation and installed a bike and pedestrian bridge over the I-70 overpass that crosses Broadway as the new hotel is built. "The city was able to deal with the situation and the highway was still open. But that is a concern," he says. "There was a significant impact to the daily traffic on South Broadway. Other details of the project are still being finalized. For example, how the path would connect to existing paths on South Broadway will depend on how and when the new Uptown high-rises are built.

The B.C. Liberal government's plan to build the Site C dam is having the opposite effect on the environment, environmentalists claim.

They say a recent flood of sediment upstream from Site C has brought contaminants and pollution to local rivers that are directly connected to water supplies for more than 500,000 people in the region.

In a Facebook post, Vancouver Aquarium director of science David Hui said some contaminants have been spotted in the Fraser River, while others have been "clearly identified" in the Peace River.

"There's absolutely no indication that any of the substances are naturally occurring or in any other part of the environment in British Columbia," he said.

Hui's post is the latest in a series of Facebook posts documenting the effects of the dam on waterways in the region.

In an interview, Dr. Paul Daffern, an environmental scientist with Fraser Health, said the B.C. government is misleading people by insisting there is no evidence of a health-risk from drinking the water.

He said he has met with residents impacted by the river contamination and they have no concerns about food or water supply.

Daffern said contaminated sediment upstream of Site C is a concern, because the province says an environmental approval for the project was given in 2011.

"What really is being missed is a lot of the things that could be affecting us downstream," Daffern said. "There are going to be impacts, especially for fish, that can be found in the Peace River."

The Peace River, which originates in Alberta, flows north into the Gulf of Georgia before joining the Fraser River on what's called its upstream outlet.

Daffern explained that the Fraser River, which is used to supply drinking water to more than 500,000 people in the area, receives water from the Peace River, which flows from north to south.

Daffern said the river that is now polluted has "a history" of carrying polluted sediment upstream. "It's actually been deposited upstream over thousands of years, through the landscape, and this is a legacy of what's going on."

"It's just a matter of time before the contaminants really start coming back to us in the Peace River," he said.

Daffern said that when he was growing up as a child in North Vancouver, his family used to make a similar trek to the beach every day to avoid contamination.

He said some of the contaminants found in the river include arsenic, lead, and mercury.

Samples taken by the Peace River Conservation Authority, an organization affiliated with the University of British Columbia, tested some of the contamination detected at the top of the stream, including mercury, lead, and arsenic.

The B.C. and federal governments declared a state of emergency on June 26 because of contamination caused by the dam, and have been in contact with First Nations communities downstream.

Last week, the B.C. Energy Regulator informed the B.C. Utilities Commission [BCUC] that it has launched an investigation into possible public safety risks associated with the dam project.

The B.C. government announced in November that it had approved the site-council's request to proceed with the dam, but the project will now go through the public-affairs process.

A draft environmental assessment document obtained by the Straight lists two alternatives for the site of the dam that both involve a massive expansion of the dam site. The first option increases the dam by 1,080 feet and would cost about $531 million. The second expansion would increase the dam by 1,160 feet and would cost about $561 million.

I recall the sense of trepidation that came with learning about brain tumors, particularly those in the right parietal lobe. As a result, I sought insight from Dr. Jonathan Schwartz, a renowned neurosurgeon at the Neurosurgical Sciences Clinic in Boston. Our conversation delved into his experience treating patients with brain tumors and the potential long-term consequences.

I must admit that my curiosity was piqued when my mother was diagnosed with a brain tumor at the age of 12. I was astonished by the rarity of such tumors in the United States and felt compelled to understand the underlying causes. We spent the summer researching medical literature, seeking answers to our pressing questions.

On June 10, my mother began experiencing headaches while driving home from a soccer game. The next day, the headaches persisted, accompanied by seizures and difficulty walking. We were referred to Stanford University Medical Center, where a large, aggressive tumor was discovered in her right parietal lobe, as well as in her brainstem.

Given the urgency of the situation, we were advised to operate immediately. A surgical team was assembled to treat the tumor, which had spread to my mother's cerebellum. The procedure was complex, requiring the removal of the tumor and the growths within her brain. The surgery was delayed by several hours, leading to a harrowing experience in the waiting room.

When the medical team finally operated on my mother's brain, they employed a robotic arm to minimize blood loss and ensure safety. We were able to witness the procedure, which involved cutting techniques never before used on a brain of this size.

The surgery revealed that the tumor was too large to be removed entirely, leaving my mother with significant damage to her right parietal lobe. The surgical team knew that removing the entire hemisphere would be necessary, but it was a daunting task that took several hours to complete.

The blood loss and risk of hemorrhage during the procedure were significant, but fortunately, my mother survived. However, if she had not, the potential for brain damage and even death would have been dire.

As we reflect on my mother's experience, we are left wondering about the treatment she received. While the surgeons were able to remove a significant portion of the tumor, they did not address the critical brainstem structure. The long-term effects of this treatment are still uncertain.

A nostalgic treat. When I was younger, I used to make a lot of these sweet potato pies. You know how it is - the dry ingredients can be a real pain to mix together. But today, I'm going to share a different approach. First, you'll need a blender that can handle the job. My trusty KitchenAid is a bit too small, but any good blender should work just fine.

Now, the key is to not overdo it with the wet ingredients. You want to keep the dough from getting too runny. And, of course, you'll want to add your butter at the very end.

So, here's the basic process:

Start by mixing the dry ingredients together in a small bowl using your blender. It might not look like much at first, but trust me, it'll come together. Next, add your oil and water, and blend until it's smooth. Then, add your egg and whisk until you start to see bubbles forming. When it looks about right, the dough should be ready.

Now, it's time to shape the dough. Use your hands to scoop it into a container, and then roll it out to the desired size. Take a small amount of the dough and shape it into a ball, then roll it out again to smooth it out.

For the final step, take a small amount of the dough and roll it into a big ball. Place it on the blender's lid, and then put the lid on and blend for about a minute. You might need to shake the blender a bit as you go.

The result is amazing - the butter really brings out the flavor of the sweet potatoes. And the best part is that the dough keeps well in the fridge for a week.

Here are the ingredients you'll need:

* 3/4 cup unbleached flour
* 1/2 cup coconut oil
* 1/2 teaspoon salt
* 3/4 ounce maple syrup

And here's how you make it:

1. Mix all the ingredients together, then add them to your blender and blend until you get a smooth dough.
2. Cut out a circle and spread it out to the size of your pie tin.
3. Spread your butter over the dough, starting from one edge and working your way back along the middle.

npm install ng-app --save

You can now navigate and manage your project's configuration using the configuration page.

ng-app-template <file-name>.template.ts

The year was 2000. A pivotal moment in Canadian legal history. The Supreme Court of Canada delivered a series of judgments, collectively known as Kawa et al., Oakes et al., Re L'Est, St-Denis, and Kawa et al. These cases centered around the rights of individuals in relation to searches and seizures.

A crucial distinction exists between a search and a seizure. The majority decision in R. v. Smith revolved around a set of questions posed by the Canadian Bar Association. The inquiry focused on whether the fact of a search affects the rights of the accused.

In short, the answer is that only in rare circumstances would the court rule that a search infringes upon the rights of the accused.

The Smith case entailed two cases, specifically. R v. Smith concerned two brothers accused of shooting a police officer. The brothers pleaded guilty to various charges, including aggravated assault.

The case highlighted the importance of warrantless searches. The Ontario Court of Appeal Judge William Dickson and Ontario Court of Appeal Judge David Harris both found that the search warrant's probable cause justification infringed upon the defendants' Charter rights.

A fundamental principle of the Canadian Charter is that, except in exceptional circumstances, search and seizure are limited by the Constitution. The law requires justification at the time of the search and seizure to protect individual privacy.

The Supreme Court's finding of a right of entry stood out in Kawa. The Court held that a search is a seizure and can only be justified by a compelling state interest greater than the state interest involved when pursued by less intrusive means.

While a distinction exists between a search and seizure, it is a significant principle of Charter rights that warrantless searches never result in Charter violations, even if an actual intrusion upon a person's rights takes place.

Kawa has been applied in over 100 cases, with the police taking an unwarranted, unnecessary, and potentially unreasonable entry in many instances.

The Supreme Court's opinions may not always be consistent, but the Charter protects individual rights at all times, provided Charter protections are upheld in lower courts.

The Kawa decision is sometimes referred to as the first Charter case in Canada.
