A good night's sleep is essential for our well-being, but sometimes we struggle to get a restful night's sleep. Have you ever found yourself lying awake, wondering why you're not sleeping?

Sleepwalking is a state where your body is asleep, but your consciousness hasn't fully emerged yet. If you're experiencing this, it's essential to seek help. There are many reasons why you might be sleepwalking, including a lack of sleep, overstimulation, and psychological factors.

In this article, we'll explore some of the main factors that can cause sleep disturbances. You might not be able to identify the cause on your own, so it's essential to ask for help from a friend, family member, or healthcare professional.

We'll discuss insomnia, sleep staging, night waking, sleep debt, and problems at night. If you're struggling with sleep, feel free to reach out to us for support.

Here are some of the main factors that can cause sleep disturbances:

1. Insomnia

Insomnia can be caused by a variety of factors, including sleep time, illness, stress, tiredness, work or school stress, and medication. Many people are not sleeping for a number of reasons, and it's essential to address the underlying cause.

2. Night Waking

Night waking refers to waking up at a particular time, usually between 2 and 7 am. This can be triggered by medication, and it's essential to realize that some medications can prolong a sleep debt, leading to excessive night waking.

3. Sleep Debt

A recent study published by a team of researchers at the University of Virginia reveals that the US economy experienced a significant decline in manufacturing jobs between 1999 and 2014. In fact, the number of non-shipped manufacturing jobs was so high that manufacturing became the largest contributor to job creation during those 12 years, accounting for nearly half of all net "new entrants" into the labor market.

The study's authors, Mark Perry and David Autor, examined quarterly changes in industry employment as well as aggregate employment statistics between the third quarter of 1999 and the fourth quarter of 2014. Using a model to test whether changes in these industry employment numbers were caused by productivity increases or market forces, they found that the manufacturing sector's role as a job creator actually decreased during the period.

A common misconception about the relationship between manufacturing and economic growth is that manufacturing is a strong job creator. While it is true that between 1995 and 2013, manufacturing accounted for 6.4 million net new jobs, generating an additional $3.6 trillion in spending, this gain would have generated about 2.5 and 1.9 million jobs if it did not take away from manufacturing spending in the final three years of the period.

By the last quarter of 2013, when jobs were hardest hit by the Great Recession, manufacturing accounted for 3.1 million more jobs than it had in 1994, but it also created 1.9 million fewer jobs. Those net losses equaled the loss of 2.2 million jobs from the entire period and created the largest drop in jobs in manufacturing between the third and the fourth quarters since 1945.

The authors conclude that the manufacturing slowdown and its impact on a variety of industries can be attributed to changes in factors like productivity and globalization, but they also point out that the manufacturing industry's role as a job creator actually decreased during the period, which they blame on the shift away from manufacturing to service creation and globalization.

While the study does not prove that US manufacturing companies are not a job creator, it does suggest that the manufacturing sector is the largest cause of job losses during the period. The authors admit that their results do not provide conclusive evidence, but they do highlight the significance of the manufacturing sector's decline in job creation.

The study's findings have significant implications for the US economy, suggesting that the decline of manufacturing employment has contributed significantly to the national decline in employment.

Objective:

To explore the relationship between physical activity, carbohydrate and fat consumption, and the long-term success of a high-carbohydrate, medium-fat diet (HCE) in maintaining weight loss in adolescents.

Methodology:

A research study involving dietary and exercise interventions was conducted among obese teenagers.

Location:

The study took place within a university-affiliated obesity treatment program.

Participants:

Fifteen obese boys aged 12-15 were recruited from inpatient and outpatient services. They were randomly assigned to either a HCE diet (35% protein, 18% carbohydrates, 50% fat, and 12% fiber) or a control diet (30% carbohydrates, 20% fat, and 15% fiber).

Data Collection:

Energy, macronutrient, and fat intake, as well as physical activity levels, were measured at the beginning and at 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 16, and 21 months.

Findings:

Weight loss varied significantly over the study period, with an average loss of 12% (range 2% to 13%). No significant difference was observed between the trial arms in terms of percentage of body fat, percent change from baseline, or change between baseline and each 1-month point.

Conclusion:

Modifying dietary habits may not be an effective strategy for weight loss, although it could potentially reduce post-meal overeating and/or increase feelings of fullness, which is a crucial factor in maintaining weight. Physical activity is a valuable component of a weight-loss program for children and adolescents, but it does not appear to improve short-term outcomes when compared to a low-fat diet.

The Odyssey's latest discovery is a true treasure trove of history, says founder and expedition leader Peter Marzilli. The 18th-century shipwreck, which sank off the coast of North Carolina in 1816, is a remarkable find that will be added to the Odyssey's World Heritage Fleet.

Marzilli and archaeology professor Dr. David J. Williams of the University of South Carolina visited the wreck site in August. The ship, a frigate of the North Carolina Line, is a remarkable example of early American shipbuilding.

"The hull is mostly in the Atlantic, but it was the best built of any ship of its time," said Williams. "The mainmast is the only part of the hull that we know the extent of, but it's a fine example of an early American ship."

The wreck has yielded many artifacts, including a large "S" marking in the middle of the ship. Marzilli expects the original structure to surface sometime next year.

"This is a time capsule," said Marzilli. "It reveals information about the ship's structure and equipment, including its coal supply and the coal storage locker."

The ship's keel was cut, and the wooden hulls were torn to pieces. Marzilli hopes to exhibit the wreck in a museum in South Carolina, where it could be easily accessed by students and historians.

Marzilli has worked on many expeditions with Odyssey, finding over 30 wrecks before this one. "We all like to search for the most significant sites," he said. The search for this wreck is just beginning, and Marzilli promises that once it's fully explored, it will reveal a fascinating story about the people who built and sailed the ship.

"I'm not a fan of any particular book about the Civil War. I think it's much better to read about the actual war from the perspective of everyone who actually lived through it." – Andrew M. Seiler

A book's worth of facts, figures, and interpretations is bound to change over time, and each new generation of Civil War readers encounters a different book that they like or dislike. I have, personally, grown to like Andrew Seiler's history of the battle, and, I think, most everyone else has as well. In my opinion, History of the Union and Confederate Armies and the Civil War (published by Oxford University Press in 2000) is the best book of its kind.

Seiler is a Civil War scholar, historian, and military analyst at West Point who has written extensively on the military aspects of the Civil War. In addition to writing about the American Civil War and Civil War-related subjects in book form, he has written extensively about the Second Civil War, and his books have been translated into Spanish and French. I was lucky enough to be interviewed about History of the Union and Confederate Armies—even if we only talked about the book—so I asked Andrew (I will go ahead and abbreviate his first name and last initial because he doesn't like it when I do this):

I'm not a big fan of that specific war book—what one might call the second American Civil War. Is there a great military history book I don't already know about that I've missed by not getting this one?

As the first volume of Seiler's history of the Second Civil War I'm a fan of this book, but I would agree with you…it would do well to have a good survey on topics such as the "other" side, the Union and Confederate armies, the war-time military leadership, politics, finance, and war plans.

Another book you've written that is a good source, and a new book on the Second Civil War, is The Man in the Gray Flannel Suit: The Story of Robert E. Lee. What is special about your history? Do you find the Second War less difficult?

This is a great book, but again it is geared for the professional. The professional perspective can be found in my book, but I'm sure you can find it in more popular military histories in the market. My book is an account of the battle over the last hundred years of the Confederacy. It is not a biography of the individual soldiers; that's what the Lee-White accounts are. This book can be read by anyone who has ever read a newspaper, but it is a history of the battle. You are dealing with the people who participated, fought, and died, the politicians (both north and south), the generals, and the journalists.

I think that the second Civil War, in my opinion, is easier to write about than the first. During the war (and even after,) few people were killed, wounded, or missing, but the scope of the conflict was large. When we discuss the first war it is usually in terms of men killed, wounded, and missing, for example. In the second war the casualties came from the scope of the conflict. There were almost twice as many soldiers in the Union to oppose the Confederates. This means the average Union soldier was around eight to ten times more numerous.

And of course, the scale of combat was much greater, so one had, for example, hundreds more artillery pieces to deal with.

How did you go about writing this particular series of books? Did the publishers at Oxford University Press do an outstanding job with this series of books?

The publishers did an exemplary job. Oxford University Press was the original publisher of this book in the United States and in a number of other countries (including Japan and South Africa) as well. The editors at Oxford University Press did a superb job. They read many, many copies of my book, which they edited, translated, and corrected.

I think that the series of books on the war has the same kind of strengths, weaknesses, and strengths. The strengths of the first book—the research, the analysis, the writing, the editing, and the publishing—were excellent. The weaknesses for me were finding a voice, not having a voice, and not having the voice of a Southern writer. I have heard from people who said my writing sounded Southern. I don't agree. In fact, my writing has been described as "Northern." My writing was shaped by my research and history of the Civil War in the North and South.

I think my voice has been taken by many Americans. You hear that in our popular culture from the shows and movies made about the United States. The movies and TV shows that I remember were set after Lincoln and his successors assumed office. The Civil War was over by 1865, many Americans had died, and many more had been wounded and maimed.

A gentle breeze rustled the leaves outside as Harry's voice whispered secrets to the wind. "We'd rather you stay," he said, his words carrying a hint of longing. "But your presence could still be a double-edged sword." The silence that followed was heavy with unspoken emotions.

It was not the first time Professor McGonagall had cautioned Hermione about the risks of Harry's presence. Harry had often pondered seeking McGonagall's counsel on how to ask Hermione to stay, but now all options seemed closed to him. To avoid Hermione, Harry had no choice but to move forward.

"Do you truly believe a teacher would remain if their students threatened them?" Harry pressed. "That would be a rare occurrence, Professor. You have a remarkable record!"

McGonagall sighed, her expression a mask of sternness. "Mr. Potter, do not speak of your teachers. They do not wish to know about you. They only sought to protect you. Remember that."

Harry's words hung in the air, heavy with emotion.

McGonagall was right about one thing: even in the two weeks since Harry's departure from the castle, he had learned much about himself and forged a valuable bond. His sensitivity to his parents and Harry had also affected his relationships with his fellow students. While their reactions to Harry were less than favorable, Harry remained able to conceal his feelings from them.

"Thank you," Harry whispered, his smile genuine. "I'm glad you understand. I'm sorry I was so naive. You were right. I didn't know how much, but I knew."

McGonagall's eyes were suspicious, her intuition screaming at her that Harry was not telling the whole truth. Hermione, on the other hand, remained expressionless, and McGonagall appreciated her quiet composure.

The exchange left McGonagall with a newfound appreciation for her own wisdom, gained through years of watching Harry grow. She had been there for him during the darkest moments and the happiest times.

After a moment, McGonagall spoke again: "Mr. Potter, I know I said I'd rather you not stay, but I had no other choice. You've been an exceptional teacher, but there are things you've done that we cannot condone."

Harry nodded, a hint of a smile on his lips. "Thanks?"

"You are responsible for your actions, Harry. We've had to warn you several times; the first time was during the Transfiguration Tournament, when we told you not to use magic at any time."

Harry nodded. "Okay, I was wrong again. Sorry."

Hermione's expression remained unreadable. "Professor McGonagall, I said I've never trusted you, and I meant it."

For a moment, Harry was taken aback, then he realized she was right, and he agreed with her. "Don't worry, Hermione. I'm sorry. I know I would never be in a situation where I could do something like this."

Hermione's smile remained enigmatic. "You didn't need to be here, Harry. I'm sure everything will work out."

But McGonagall saw that Hermione was too optimistic. "You didn't come here for that, Mr. Potter."

Harry was surprised. "What do you mean?"

Hermione shook her head. "I want to apologize to everyone for letting them down. You were an incredible teacher who made it look easy. You took our best students and taught them things that even the most talented students in the school couldn't. You didn't cheat. I'm not even sure you've cheated once, but you've done more than that. What is the point of teaching if you don't help your students succeed?"

Professor McGonagall sat beside her head of house, watching the scene unfold. It was not a scene she was accustomed to seeing. Her best students had to be protected, and by McGonagall's own description, Harry had had to do the same for her students.

"You shouldn't have told them that," she finally said. "It was irresponsible of you. We had to take extra precautions because of it."

Hermione's eyes grew wide, heavy with emotion.

"Professor," Harry interrupted, "you don't have to be so angry. I thought you cared..."

The founder of the Open Society Justice Initiative, Sara Bhatt, was arrested at a New York City hotel and charged with a felony count of entering a foreign country under false pretenses. This occurred after an investigation into possible links between the Russian government and the Trump presidential campaign.

Ms. Bhatt's arrest has sparked a public outcry and is being held up as a warning to others who may consider going behind the backs of journalists and American diplomats.

Ms. Bhatt's legal journey began before President Trump took office in January. She was released on a $150,000 bond and charged with a misdemeanor. She was ordered to surrender her passport after failing to appear in court.

Ms. Bhatt then filed a lawsuit against the FBI, the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, and an individual identified as D.T.I. Her lawsuit was withdrawn last week.

The complaint against Ms. Bhatt was filed by the United States in the Southern District of New York. The government accused her of traveling to the United States on a false passport using a U.S. diplomatic passport she allegedly forged in 2013.

The complaint alleged that Ms. Bhatt had "intended to commit an offense" by entering the United States under false pretenses. The case is "based on her actions in attempting to commit the offense."

In a statement, the U.S. Attorney called the arrest "an unfortunate distraction" for the Trump Administration and its Justice Department.

The U.S. citizen has a right to challenge an arrest warrant, said the U.S. Attorney. "That right is the heart of the U.S. Constitution," he added.

Ms. Bhatt's attorney said his decision not to proceed with legal proceedings against his client reflected her "reluctance to compromise herself by engaging with the criminal justice system."

The arrest has drawn scrutiny to the Trump administration's handling of the investigation into Russian election meddling, including whether the Trump campaign colluded with the Kremlin to aid Mr. Trump.

The FBI began investigating Russia's interference in the U.S. presidential race in January, after U.S. spy agencies shared a dossier on allegations of corruption involving members of the Trump campaign with U.S. lawmakers.

The arrest has "caused a great stir" among members of the Committee on Foreign Affairs, said Rep. Adam B. Schiff, California Democrat, who is on the House Intelligence Committee.

Members expressed surprise and concern that a foreign official would be arrested while conducting official U.S. business, said Rep. Schiff.

The U.S. State Department expressed concern about the decision to arrest a U.S. citizen, noting that Ms. Bhatt was an employee of the Department's Foreign Educational Research Service on the New York City campus.

"We are deeply concerned that the decision to arrest a U.S. citizen could deter other U.S. consular employees around the world from cooperating fully with their government in their official duties," said the U.S. State Department.

A groundbreaking documentary utilizes the Google Glass camera, offering a unique perspective on the world's first Glass enthusiast.

"Those individuals are the ones that are getting Glass and they're the first ones out here doing stuff, so they're saying that they hate it. I don't think I'm the only one that's wearing a blindfold and placing a blindfold over their eyes. But it's not their first time," he said.

"A lot of people believe that [Google Glass is] for the elite," he says. "That's the way you look at it. In the end, the 'Glass enthusiast' remains standing – but not on the side of the roads this week. He says he is 'totally fine' but thinks he might be ready to move on.

"I think that was good for me to have this and I'm not saying that I wasn't trying and trying my best to enjoy it or anything but at the end of the day you realize that it could take away from what you're doing, it could take away from your social life or you can just become this person who only sees through glasses. "We all have our strengths and weaknesses and there's a really great side of you and there's a really great side of you that you can't see sometimes," he says.

The concept of commoning has become increasingly important in social movements, as it allows for the sharing and creation of resources in a way that is beneficial to all. This article will explore the idea of commoning in relation to the concept of a social space, and how it can be used to promote social solidarity and mutual interdependence.

The commons is a space that defines the social relationship between those who create, consume, and share goods and services. It is an inclusive concept that encompasses all people, regardless of social class, who participate in the creation and sharing of resources. The commons is in direct contrast to state or social ownership of property and resources, where a select group may control access to a resource for their own gain.

An exclusive social relation, on the other hand, is one where a select group controls access to a resource, often for their own benefit. This can be seen in companies where ownership is exclusive, or in state-owned enterprises where some individuals have a stake in maintaining the business.

There are many different types of exclusive social relations, including private, public, and economic relationships. Exclusive private relations are those where a select group has access to a resource, while exclusive public relations are those where a select group has control over a resource. Exclusive economic relations define the commons, where social users have access to a resource.

Commoning activities, such as creating a new commons, can be seen in initiatives like New Orleans' "crowd-sourced water" project. The city created a shared social space, where residents can access water tokens at various locations along the boulevard. This example illustrates how commoning can promote social solidarity and mutual interdependence.

In a commons society, social users would have a shared relationship with resources, rather than a exclusive relationship. This would promote a sense of community and shared ownership, rather than competition and exclusion.

The concept of electric showers has become increasingly popular in recent years, particularly among large families or individuals who are constantly on the move. In this article, we will delve into the world of electric showers, exploring the differences between traditional hot water showers and electric showers.

One of the primary distinctions between electric showers and traditional hot water showers is the voltage used. Electric showers operate on either direct current (DC) or alternating current (AC) electricity. The choice between the two ultimately depends on the power level required and the type of electrical system in place.

Direct Current (DC)

DC electric showers are often found in older homes with older water heaters and electrical controls. They are typically less efficient and may not be suitable for larger or more expensive homes. DC shower heads are usually smaller in diameter, ranging from 1/2 inch to 1 inch, and require a bucket or tub to collect water, as well as an outlet and faucet to connect to.

The components of a standard DC shower head include:

* Two 1/2-inch copper or stainless steel copper pipes
* A copper wire
* A 1/2-inch diameter heating element
* A 1/2-inch diameter cooling element
* A single wire connecting the two ends of the copper pipe

DC shower heads are typically rated to supply between 1/2 gallon and 3 inches of water, although some models can supply up to 2-2/3 or 4-2/3 gallons of water. A conventional water heater may require an additional 2-1/2 to 4 gallons of water to ensure a reliable shower experience.

Alternating Current (AC)

AC electric showers are more common in newer homes and are often preferred for their efficiency and larger capacity. They typically come with an AC adapter for use with an outlet and can be powered by a higher voltage than DC showers.

AC shower heads are generally larger in diameter, ranging from 1-1/1 inches, and may offer more space than standard DC heads. They can supply up to 14 amps of power, depending on the design and water delivery.

The AC Current

All electrical appliances, including shower heads, require a source of AC power to function properly. The current flowing into a home is generated naturally when appliances are plugged into outlets, and this current is distributed through wires connecting outlets to the home.

When a light is turned on, a small voltage is generated through the wire connecting the outlet and light. The voltage from the outlet carries this current through the wiring and enters the home, where it is used for lights and appliances.

In a standard electric shower head, the flow of water is so small that it does not require a significant amount of current to heat the water to a high temperature.

The DC Current

If an older standard DC shower head is used with a water heater that requires AC to reach the proper temperature, there is a solution. An AC adapter can be used to convert the DC current to AC, allowing the shower head to function properly.

The AC adapter is a conduit or cable that connects the DC shower head to the AC units plugged into the home's electrical circuit. This allows the hot water in the shower to maintain its ideal temperature.

In conclusion, electric showers offer a convenient and efficient way to enjoy a hot shower, particularly for large families or individuals who are constantly on the move. By understanding the differences between DC and AC electric showers, individuals can make an informed decision when selecting the right shower head for their needs.

The Czech Republic is a European nation situated between Slovakia and Moravia, both formerly part of Czechoslovakia.

During the communist era, the Czech Republic's population reached nearly a quarter million. In 1968, it gained independence from the Soviet Union.

Czech Culture

The Czech Republic boasts a rich cultural heritage, with four distinct regions: Bohemia, Moravia, and the Sudetenland.

Czech History

Czech history is marked by war, political struggle, and civil unrest.

The Czech people are Slavic, residing in the southern part of the world. Some believe that the Czech nation is the oldest in the world.

In 1795, the Kingdom of Bohemia was established by King Matthias. After two centuries of Russian rule, the nation gained independence in 1918. In 1991, Czechoslovakia gained independence.

Czech Politics

The Czech political system and government have their roots in medieval Bohemian times. The system is characterized by strong executive power and democratic institutions, with features of democracy.

The Czech government was founded in 1963, when the constitution written in the 18th century was finally accepted by the public. It was the first constitution in the region after the establishment of the sovereign state. The country has four political parties, with the two main groups being the Social Democratic Party and the Christian Democratic Party.

In recent decades, the Czech Republic has played a significant role in Eastern Europe.

During the 19th century, most people were farmers, and many cities consisted of villages.

Initially, the Czech language did not exist, but it was recognized as an official language in 1918.

In the 20th century, many major cities had populations over a million, causing issues for the Czech people and those living in Czech-speaking areas in former Czechoslovakia.

Czechoslovakia has its own flag and national anthem. The Czech Republic has its own national football team and national anthem, "The Star," written originally in German.

The country's flag features a circle with the Czech coat of arms in the center and the coat of arms of Bohemia on the perimeter. The coat of arms includes white letters, a white cross, a crowned shield, and a crown on each side.

The Czech language consists of two main languages: German and Czech.

In the summer of 2001, I had just turned 18, and my friends and I had already completed the first half of our college careers. We were now in our final year of high school, with some of us about to start freshman year at a state university. One of my friends went to a junior college nearby, while others lived home with their parents. All of us had a lot of time to kill. So I'd often sneak away before I got up and headed toward the library to do homework, to stay out of the way or to go out on dates. I wanted to be a doctor, not the kind of doctor who'd be on the phone calling in to the hospital with a sick kid; I wanted my career to be clinical. But I was a pretty good dancer, so I'd often go out with friends who were a bit hungrier and more energetic than I was.

In the parking lot in front of my high school, there were about 10-15 cars. There was this one guy in a pickup truck and he was driving right alongside me. He was a bit disoriented. His eyes were red. He was on a long line with two other guys, drinking and smoking. They were kind of talking about enjoying themselves, and one guy was saying, "This is going to be great," and the other guy was saying, "We should just relax and have some fun." I was just kind of looking back and not paying attention. Then he started saying, "Man, man! Let's just chill." We didn't really know each other. None of us did. I thought he was just trying to be friendly.

That's when I was struck by something. I didn't know whether I was surprised or not. So I did nothing other than just look back and see him drive closer and closer with each sentence so that he could finally get to me. He was very close to the car at that point. He had been enjoying himself for quite some time. I didn't really know him, either. So I just froze. I did nothing but just stare him down at that point.

He leaned in closer and said, "Man, let's just have some fun." He just gestured towards the car. Then he just drove through my body and slammed the entire windshield down onto my face. And my head went back, and my neck was bending.

I was kind of stunned at the time. Everyone around me was pretty surprised. Nobody did anything. I didn't know anything about gestures. Nobody had a problem with the gestures in our house, but I didn't know that we had two on our property. I wasn't exactly trying to protect myself. I don't know if I did that to get away, or if I was kind-of hoping that he would gesture to somebody else who was hanging out by my car. I don't know how I got away; I don't know if he thought I was a friend or something because I didn't start yelling, or if he just thought I was another kid on my way to the library that he gestured to.

It was the last day of school and we were out on a date somewhere. I was at a very small, dark, back porch, and he came around the corner from the house and said, "Hey, friend."

He was a lot closer than when I drove by him at the parking lot. We were just about as far apart as we could possibly get. And he said, "Let's just have some fun, friend, I'm in the middle of this driveway and I'm looking for you."

We got into a nice conversation. There was a lot of laughter. I wasn't scared at all. I was just kind-of enjoying the atmosphere. At one point, I just said, "Friend, do you know about gestures?"

"Uh huh," he said. "I know about them."

"Well, I want to learn more about them," I told him. He laughed and said, "Oh, that's all right, friend. You don't have to worry about it."

But I wasn't completely comforted in that. Because he said that to me like he thought I was a friend, and it kind of freaked me out. I didn't think he was joking or being coy. He said something that was really kind of friendly and I didn't know whether he meant it that way. I just felt really uncomfortable.

He just said, "Oh, friend, we don't really have any trouble here." I didn't know his brother or his friends.

"Oh, don't worry, friend," he said. "We don't get any problems."

That's when it got scary. I was thinking, "He's trying to talk to me like he thinks I'm here to be with him. Like, 'I'm sorry we have a little trouble, but you guys are good. We don't get any problems.'"

The concept of "sperm refinement" has been explored for several decades. It involves distinguishing "immature" sperm from "healthy" sperm.

The "healthy" sperm possess genetic characteristics linked to male fertility. To enable the creation, utilization, and subsequent removal of embryos without relying on human embryo donation, scientists have sought to develop techniques that allow the separation and blending of some "immature" sperm.

Initially, it was believed that such processes could only be achieved if the sperm contained mitochondria – a type of cellular organelle. However, researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem have demonstrated the existence of a process called "sperm refinement" and are currently evaluating it in Israel and the United States. This process involves the separation of "immature" sperm from "healthy" sperm, and in some cases, the "maternal transfer" of both types of sperm – the healthy sperm is then re-mixed with that of the immature sperm.

There is no indication from the Hebrew University that such a process (or a similar one in the U.S.) has been tested on human embryos. However, some studies have shown that the process can also be applied to human sperm that are fertilized in vitro, without the use of an embryo donation.

What does this mean for infertility patients? It could be a significant breakthrough if it were true.

Let's be realistic – it's still theoretical to say that this method would allow a woman to not only conceive a healthy child, but also a child with no inherited diseases and a normal healthy life. This means the child would possess the genetic characteristics of both the woman and the parents of the child – the parents would need to provide the "maternal" component of that child to avoid "contamination" of the embryo, and this would necessitate the use of an embryo donation process. In that case, the process could be used to help the woman conceive a healthy child without the risks associated with IVF.

Some researchers are exploring the potential of these "sperm refinement" techniques for children with genetic disorders caused by mutations in specific genes. In fact, the Hebrew University is conducting a study on how this technique may affect children with certain genetic disorders carried by older parents.

Those missions, along with future human missions to destinations beyond low Earth orbit, still are possible only with the more powerful upper stage, but that's now expected to be fully operational by 2022 with the maiden launch date moving down to 2022.

It is unlikely the space agency would approve an earlier date for the maiden launch, which now has been pushed back again.

"The program was developed with an ambitious launch schedule in mind, and our first launch in 2017 or 2018 represents a substantial advance over the program's original approach," said Bob Cabana, NASA's associate administrator for human spaceflight.

The new rocket was designed after SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket suffered a catastrophic rocket explosion in September 2015 at Cape Canaveral, Florida. An investigation into Falcon 9's collapse determined the explosion was triggered by a buildup of superpressure in the liquid-oxygen rocket's propellant tank, triggering a rapid expansion that destroyed the rocket.

SpaceX had not planned to fly SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket with the heavier, more powerful booster before the investigation showed the Falcon 9 explosion was to blame. NASA later selected SpaceX to build and fly both rockets.

SpaceX's next booster, dubbed the Falcon Heavy, will serve as a heavier-than-usual upper stage for the Falcon 9 rockets in its current configuration.

"It had been a long time coming for us, and we've been working hard to get the right rocket," said SpaceX Chief Executive Elon Musk, who in the lead-up to the booster's approval said SpaceX would likely begin Falcon Heavy flights first, then the Falcon 9.

Musk said there would be another rocket in SpaceX's fleet for low-Earth-orbit missions to destinations such as the ISS.

With the Falcon Heavy, the booster's upper stage will be bigger and lighter and will be powered by three main engines rather than seven as in the Falcon 9's current configuration.

The Falcon Heavy will also fly with four landing legs, two on its central structure and two on the payload fairing. SpaceX is also developing a version of the Falcon Heavy capable of landing at sea, though it is not ready for flight or to fly yet.

Once the Falcon Heavy is ready, the rocket will use a two-stage version of the Dragon crew capsule designed to carry astronauts to and from the ISS. The two stages are identical, with the Falcon Heavy design keeping only the second stage's solid-rocket-powered upper stage. However, the Falcon Heavy's second stage will use eight engines for a total of 12, for a total thrust of 1.3 million pounds.

Musk said later that SpaceX will not be allowed to name its future launcher after a member of the company's founding family. "There's no way we could do that," Musk said, because the booster's name would be too similar to the one flying on the Falcon 9 rocket.

The Falcon Heavy's first launch is slated for Nov. 21, 2018, with a liftoff target of 6:42 a.m. EST from Cape Canaveral's Complex 37 support tower, SpaceX officials said.

The Falcon Heavy will be capable of launching payloads of up to 8,380 kilograms (14,500 pounds), according to SpaceX.

Despite little progress in Congress to regulate the Internet as a public utility like phone services, there has been significant activity at the state level. In addition, there are now over 30 resolutions introduced in the Senate to support the FCC's position.

One of the more intriguing bills to emerge in Congress this session is the Internet Tax Freedom Act, which has the potential to fundamentally alter the Internet as we know it. This legislation aims to repeal all state and federal taxes on the Internet, effectively exempting Internet Service Providers from taxes imposed by states.

The main provision of the bill is that Internet Service Providers should not be subject to taxes imposed by states, including taxes on telecommunications, Internet access providers, tax-exempt charitable organizations, and Internet Service Providers. There are only a few other Internet taxes globally.

Net Neutrality, as defined by the FCC, prevents broadband providers from blocking or throttling traffic and allows Internet Service Providers to charge different fees for different types of content. Net Neutrality is often a point of contention among internet freedom and free market theorists who view it as a potential threat to freedom of expression and innovation.

The Internet Tax Freedom Act could benefit many Americans who currently do not receive the benefits of the Internet. The new net neutrality regulations have actually made it harder for smaller companies to grow their businesses online by imposing onerous regulations.

In a groundbreaking discovery, researchers have found that a specific class of medications used to treat HIV have a profound impact on the virus, potentially leading to a significant reduction in the transmission of HIV worldwide. A study published in Nature Medicine reveals that these medications, known as nucleoside analogues (RNAi), can effectively halt the replication of the virus in the human body.

According to Jonathan Liles, PhD, who led the study, the HIV-1 genome shares similarities with certain cellular proteins involved in HIV replication, which can have therapeutic effects in specific circumstances. The RNAi also demonstrates efficacy against viral nucleoprotein (nNP), a common byproduct of retrovirus infections.

HIV, a widespread and devastating epidemic, claims the lives of approximately 14,000 individuals daily. The virus, known as HIV, is highly adaptable and can replicate quickly within human cells, including macrophages, which play a crucial role in the immune system.

The researchers discovered that these medications do not require a lengthy or dangerous immune response and can target the virus directly for a brief period before clearance from the body. They also found that the drugs show promise in preventing HIV transmission in the adult brain, suggesting they could eventually function as HIV vaccines.

While HIV can replicate easily within human cells, the researchers are working to find a drug that can both block its ability to replicate and induce an immune response effectively. Their study focused on antiretroviral drugs and eventually led them to search for a way to inhibit HIV in the human body by targeting a viral protein rather than just a viral genome.

The researchers noticed that the HIV-1 protein contains repeating sequences of amino acids, which are important for its survival and growth in macropoiesis. They discovered that these repeating sequences are essential for the protein's expression in cells and macropoiesis, a process by which cells multiply to form more cells.

The team then developed a system that targeted a specific DNA region of the viral protein, which activated it in macropoiesis-grown cells. After two decades of research, there are only three medications that treat HIV, although experimental therapies are being developed.

The study's findings have significant implications for the development of new therapies to treat and prevent HIV infections. The researchers are continuing to explore the potential of these medications and other molecules to combat HIV.

A groundbreaking discovery has been made by scientists, revealing a novel gene that serves as a "key" to regulate the behavior of certain neurons, enabling them to retain memories. However, the researchers emphasized that the exact mechanisms by which these genetic "keys" are generated within neurons and the brain during the learning process remain unclear.

The findings were published in the April edition of a prominent scientific journal.

The research was led by David Sinclair, a renowned expert in the field, and his team compared DNA samples from cells that had undergone genetic modifications and those that had not. The genetic manipulation led to a modification that activated the gene responsible for memory in neurons. However, when the scientists removed the genetic modification, the memories were lost.

"These results demonstrate how genetic "keys" can control memory function, enabling us to understand how and why neurons retain their memory functions well into adulthood," said Sinclair. "The ability to alter gene activity during development is a crucial step toward the development of targeted therapeutic strategies for the treatment of certain neurological disorders."

The study of memory has been a long-standing area of interest in medical research. Scientists have found that memory retention may occur in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in learning, memory, and emotion. It may also be a potential target for treatments that target memory-related psychiatric disorders such as depression and schizophrenia.

Researchers have identified brain regions involved in the memory retrieval process, including the periaqueductal gray (PAG), an area located in the back of the brain. The PAG is crucial in learning and in learning new details about an old event, including recognizing it correctly.

The gene-mediated regulation discovered by Sinclair's team is unique because it is activated by RNA, a molecule that can pass from one cell type to another. RNA is produced by the cell's own DNA coding, and in addition to controlling gene expression, it can also carry out functions unrelated to the genes it codes for.

"This discovery shows how genetic information, in our case an RNA molecule, can be used to determine whether neurons can retain memories as we age, and thus potentially guide us toward effective therapies for neurological disorders," said Sinclair.

In the future, Sinclair and his team plan to characterize the genetic mechanism underlying cell memory and to discover how to manipulate RNA and therefore alter memory functions. They also aim to unravel in greater detail genetic mechanisms that activate or inhibit memory processing during a learning process.

This research was also funded by the Department of Veterans Affairs' Agency for Health Care Research and Quality (AHRQ), National Institutes of Health (NIH).

Medications that combat bacterial infections are a crucial tool in the fight against disease. These medications, known as antibiotics, are effective against a wide range of bacterial infections, including those that cause pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and skin infections.

In contrast, medications that target viral infections are a vital part of the treatment arsenal. These antiviral medications can be used to combat a range of viral infections, including the flu, common cold, and HIV.

There are several reasons why it is simpler to develop medications that target bacteria compared to viruses.

Firstly, bacteria and viruses exhibit distinct characteristics. Bacteria are relatively simple and small, with their own mechanisms for reproduction and repair. This allows for a more targeted approach to developing medications that can effectively kill bacteria.

Viruses, on the other hand, are more complex and smaller than bacteria. They rely on hijacking the cells of the host organism to replicate, making it more challenging to develop medications that can target specific viral components. This increased complexity can also result in more side effects for antiviral medications, as they may interact with host cells.

Another factor contributing to the relative ease of developing bacterial medications is the increased sensitivity of bacteria to medication. This allows for the use of lower doses, reducing the risk of adverse effects.

In summary, while both antibiotics and antivirals are essential tools in the treatment of infections, the development of bacterial medications is generally simpler due to the simpler nature and increased sensitivity of bacteria to medication.

However, the government argues that it can force individuals to purchase health insurance through the federal exchange if they do not qualify for any other source of insurance.

At first glance, these responses appear to be a natural extension of the "don't ask, don't tell" approach. However, upon closer examination, the results reveal a more complex and nuanced picture.

This may seem counterintuitive, given the party's reputation for being more progressive on drug policy. However, the support for legalization appears to stem from individuals who have not yet achieved political accountability or taken control of their government.

The survey suggests that Americans would benefit from less-stringent marijuana laws, as long as they are not punished for their actions after becoming voters or living in states that have legalized the substance. The reason for this may lie in the fact that Americans believe that voters would benefit from less-stringent policies when they become responsible adults. In the same way that a responsible parent may not always make good decisions, Americans may believe that legalizing an illegal substance is not as bad as others claim.

The result is that there would be few major consequences of legalization if it were made easier to use. The survey does not believe that legalization would create a crime wave, and if there were significant consequences of marijuana use, this would be an issue to address rather than ignore.

The surprise stems from the stigma surrounding marijuana. Once one acknowledges that people consume marijuana in small amounts on a regular basis without serious consequences, it becomes clear that most Americans support legalization.

A considerable portion of newly diagnosed cancer cases can be attributed to modifiable dietary habits [1]. The primary source of vitamin D is derived from both sunlight and dietary intake. This paper provides an overview of the current evidence from epidemiological studies examining the relationship between vitamin D and cancer risk, mortality, and incidence. The studies in question have investigated the association between vitamin D and risk of cancer of the upper aerodigestive tract, colon, breast, and prostate. The findings suggest that, for most cancer sites, the optimal intake of vitamin D corresponds to the lowest risk of disease. Furthermore, evidence indicates that vitamin D intake below 2000 IU per day is unlikely to be linked to an increased risk. Case-control studies of lung, colorectal, and ovarian cancer support increasing the recommended daily intake of vitamin D, which should be at least 1000 IU. Case-control studies of colon, prostate, and breast cancer also support increasing the recommended daily intake of vitamin D to 2000 IU, and, if appropriate supplementation is administered, vitamin D3 should be added. Overall, there appears to be no evidence that vitamin D supplementation reduces the risk of cancer deaths, cancer incidence, or cancers of the upper aerodigestive tract. The findings presented in this paper suggest that the optimal intake of vitamin D may be closer to 2000 IU daily per person rather than 2000 IU daily from sunlight and food. For cancers of the colon, prostate, and breast, a lower intake of vitamin D appears to be associated with a higher risk of disease incidence compared with a higher intake. However, for cancers of the upper aerodigestive tract and the lung, the evidence regarding increasing to a higher intake is less clear and appears to be the exception rather than the rule. These differences may depend on the exact circumstances of dietary analysis. The conclusions about which route of intake may be most protective for cancer are dependent on the exact exposure of the subject and the duration of time in the study. Furthermore, there are important methodological considerations when studying the association between intake of vitamin D and cancer. Some of these concerns include the lack of information on the frequency or duration of exposure; the absence of measures of intake without supplementation; the reliance on population-based data; and the use of different categories of intake, rather than the same categories, for each cancer site. Due to these limitations, this paper does not assess the association between dietary intake and cancer risk. Instead, it focuses on cancer incidence and mortality.

The sensation of the phone ringing, with the caller ID displaying on our screen. Or, the anxiety that arises when the new year arrives, and we're constantly reminded of our existence. What we don't fully grasp, though, is that those around us are more attuned to our emotions, even if we're not aware of it ourselves. And those we live with are more aware of our moods and experiences as well.

We've been taught that our world is filled with negativity, and that those who complain are seeking fame. Now, we understand that we feel this way because certain emotions are more common or important to us. We're less inclined to seek help for these more common issues and may instead put them off or ignore them.

It's essential to comprehend why we feel the way we do, but it's not as if we can force it. However, it appears that control is not as easy to achieve as we think. We know that our feelings and responses to them are entirely under our control, but how can that be the case?

We can attempt to make sense of this. Here are 10 possible reasons, although remember that no one can ever be certain of why we feel the way we do.

1. The world is just too much, and we can't change it.

2. Life is too stressful, and we have no control.

3. We have too much on our minds, and no control over anything.

4. We don't really care about other people's opinions.

5. We're just too tired to care.

6. We're just too busy to care.

7. We're just too overwhelmed to care.

8. We're just too anxious to care.

9. We're just too depressed to care.

10. We're just too confused to care.

It's possible that life can be a bit of a drag if we're not prepared, or our mental health is in any way less than optimal. This could be due to work pressures, lack of sleep, or other factors that may not be under our control.

As well as living in a stressful world, we're also often told the world is out to get us – we're just an unfortunate case, in need of protection or some kind of 'fix'.

The truth is that we can't control anything. Even the people around us can't.

We can try to make some sense of this.

The notion that the government's response to the recent Ebola outbreak has been ineffective cannot be sustained. The problem was genuine, but the treatment to date has not been as successful as the government claimed. The government responded with public health measures that are well-known, including prevention, isolation, care, treatment, and so forth. It's a straightforward concept. What the Ebola response does is prevent the disease from spreading by keeping individuals in contact with one another and healthcare officials involved. However, these measures have not been effective. The government is supposed to have compiled a list of contacts for the entire country, but in the Sierra Leonean town of Kenema, there are only seven. Many people are still dying due to lack of care or worse.

There are two types of individuals who believe the government's response will never work: those who do not have AIDS and those who think the Ebola virus is not infectious and will never mutate. Ebola might not be contagious, and that hasn't stopped a number of people from attempting to use it for other purposes. This does not mean that healthcare has been effective; it's simply a good rule of thumb to apply to outbreaks.

When an outbreak occurs, I always prefer to use the terminology "migrations" or "waves" to refer to the localized and varied sizes of the disease's spread. And when the government is unsure which individual at a particular hospital has Ebola, which individuals within the same ward have Ebola, or where the individual is in the ward, and there is no contact tracing that covers the entire country, public health measures will not be sufficient.

So the public health measure implemented to try and stop the flow of patients into hospitals was simply that healthcare personnel were not allowed to interact with the sick, even if they were. This will likely have the effect of stopping most Ebola cases. However, it's not effective. One can argue that the public health measures didn't go far enough, but that makes the lack of contact tracing all the more perplexing, since the lack of contact tracing would have at least provided information about the actual locations of contacts.

There are many areas where the government's response has been effective, such as on the streets and at airports. The government banned the public from taking food into Ebola-affected areas, which will prevent infected individuals from spreading their disease.

The government also must be held accountable for the failure to provide adequate medical care. It didn't take long for people to say that all these medical schools had been shut down, and some doctors were in hospitals having to beg their patients to die in order to avoid having them infect other people. And now we have a hospital that doesn't have blood bags anymore but uses saline. This isn't what we were led to believe when they said hospitals were fully functioning.

I don't think it's fair to blame doctors solely for the failure of the response to save and treat those who were dying. They had a choice: To stay at their posts or go home. Many refused, and the government's response wasn't effective. But doctors are not angels and made choices. To some, those choices seem less rational.

What about the idea that the government is going to close all schools, and thus kill all the students? It's an interesting idea—a plan to end education in one district. The government has been doing everything else it can with the virus, and now it is going to shut down schools, which means the students who aren't infected and aren't dying are going to get sick and die. If we're going to blame one person for the failure of the government's response (or one person for everyone), I'm going with everybody and especially the government.

There's some evidence to support this idea. A lot of people have gone into the countryside and told the rural people that they will be able to go somewhere for education if they allow the government to take their children. They've taken all kinds of measures, and they're still at the end of the trail. The government is still in charge in Sierra Leone; I can't imagine that the government will give the rural people the education for which they are dying.

I'm glad there's an Ebola "epidemic." It's a useful tool for the government, and it can still give people some hope that if government works, if it does something, they can get health care. But it's too soon to conclude that the Ebola epidemic has caused the government to have no idea how to control the disease.

The author who is often credited with writing The Godfather is Mario Puzo, the same person who adapted the novel into a blockbuster film.

It is possible that Puzo's influence was subtle. Puzo was born in Sicily, the son of a Sicilian immigrant and a mother who experienced five pregnancies in less than 10 years. Puzo's mother passed away in childbirth. Puzo's first written work is about his mother, and it is the first time he shares this story publicly.

Although Puzo himself passed away a few years after the book was published, his words live on through his biographer and literary executor, Michael J. Greenberg. Puzo was the sole survivor of eight siblings raised by their Sicilian immigrant mother, who struggled with addiction and alcoholism.

Puzo describes his childhood during the 1920s in an unpublished autobiography:

"My father, who was one of six children, was a self-made man. He built a small fortune in the steel manufacturing industry... but his father also made it a custom during his prosperous years to buy two new clothes each Christmas, the same one for me and a new suit the next year. I was twelve, not yet old enough to vote with my own two feet, but I knew my place in the universe."

Puzo and his brother shared their mother's money, and despite his younger brother's natural talent for swimming and other athletic abilities, young Mario was a hopeless swimmer, his only sport as a child being the swimming pool.

"One day I was sitting out in the pool when I swam to a nearby ledge... I jumped off the ledge, took a few steps back... and suddenly was face on with a giant. I was shocked. 'What are you doing, Mario?' I shouted. 'What are you doing out here in the pool?' And he said: 'You can see my house from here.'"

Puzo told the story for the first time in his 2011 biography Mario Puzo. He wrote much of it when he was an amateur wrestling champion at the age of 12. That's how much his parents believed sport and school would serve as a buffer between their lives.

Puzo also had a difficult time fitting in and struggled to gain acceptance on his block, where his siblings dominated the sports fields and their lives.

For his part, Puzo also had a long stint on the run before he was tracked down one night by the police. The family fled in a hurry. Puzo wrote:

"I was never able to forgive my father; though I loved him. A man I still admire to this day."

For the next five years in Sicily, the Puzo brothers battled poverty and a lack of money, ultimately ending up on the run from the Mafia in Sicily in 1934.

While most Italian immigrants were able to find work in Sicily's iron ore mines and shipyards, Puzo couldn't. His mother had already given up work, deciding to use her final years to raise her son and give him a good education.

The Puzo brothers' lives changed for the better once they landed safely at Ellis Island. While still living in Sicily, the Puzos were arrested by the military and sent back to New York, where they were separated, the younger brother eventually entering a Catholic school and the elder going upstate to join an army.

"When I graduated from the Catholic School in Schenectady, I was enrolled at the New York Military Academy—you got a three-inch tall steel helmet. And I liked it—I was the first boy to wear that at the Academy. I didn't want to leave—but my father was dying of lung cancer, and the school was a big step for him. We never got together. He died a year later."

When Puzo got to New Jersey, he went to school at Rutgers University. He was part of student body in the fall of 1936 during the worst of the Depression and, when he was 18, applied to the Marine Corp. His application was rejected.

However, the rejection came without a slap on the wrist or anything else, simply being sent back to Newark. He returned to school but never graduated from there. He then went on to Syracuse University and graduated from there in 1941.

When the war came, Puzo was drafted into the Army, where he served two years. He was stationed in Europe for a year and returned to the States in 1945 as a sergeant and sergeant major.

"I felt more American than any other American. My Americanization came from those three years in Europe and then my training at Marine Barracks and the training at Quantico. If it had been for all the training in Europe that would have been enough for me."

Puzo's experiences in Europe were pivotal in his life.

A fascinating week unfolded in South Carolina, with notable Congressional members facing challenging re-election battles in districts leaning towards the Republican Party. The Democratic Party's prospects of capturing the Republican-controlled House of Representatives in red states that have historically voted for Democratic presidential nominees began to fade as Republicans maintained more House seats and gained a majority of seats contested in the 2012 presidential election. However, just hours before the Democratic National Convention, the South Carolina Democratic Party elected its nominee, South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley. Haley, a Republican, has been mentioned as a potential vice presidential pick by both major parties. (It's worth noting that she seems like a decent governor, even if she's an establishment Republican, perhaps more moderate than Joe Biden could accept.)

I sought insight into the Republican Party's perspective on Haley's potential selection. I reached out to a South Carolina Democratic Party staffer by phone, as Haley was campaigning in North Charleston at the time, and asked about her relationship with the Republican Party and its leaders.

"There is no relationship," the staffer replied, stating that she had no idea why Haley would be considered for vice president or secretary of state, which the Republicans had selected Mitt Romney for.

I wanted to hear the party's stance on this matter, as many Republicans I spoke with expressed similar opinions. It took some effort; the official South Carolina Democratic Party Twitter account and Haley's campaign page did not mention her Republican Party affiliation, and it was challenging to find her biography on the official campaign website, which did not include any information on her party affiliation. (The link led to an article on the Republican National Committee's website, which does mention Haley.) The South Carolina Democratic Party also had a webpage with her biography, but I couldn't find it through a Google search.

One piece of information suggests that Haley is not a registered Republican. According to a report on The Hill, Haley was reelected by the South Carolina Republican Party in 2010, when she ran as an Independent. However, she was asked to take the party's oath by an officer of the party who told the candidate she would be a Republican nominee if she ran again. (Haley reportedly declined. In 2010, the South Carolina Democratic Party endorsed Republican Gov. Nikki Haley—but it seems unusual that this isn't mentioned.)

If Haley was indeed a registered Republican, I wondered, why would she support the party's nomination?

"She is a lifelong Republican," the South Carolina Democratic Party told me, but noted that Haley's support is not unconditional—she only endorsed Romney the first time she considered him.

When I asked Haley's spokeswoman, Rochita King, for her reaction to the South Carolina Democratic Party's claims about her party affiliation and party loyalty, she said, "No comment."

If Haley was indeed a registered Republican, I wondered, why would she support the party's nomination? It's not as if she was endorsed by Barack Obama or any other member of Congress, so it's not like she was an official endorsement of the party. I also asked if she'd be interested in running for president, which is perhaps the most obvious job for which Haley might be qualified.

"It doesn't matter, because I will always vote for Republicans," Haley said in the call I had with her office, when I pressed about a presidential run. She wouldn't "rule out" a presidential bid in the future, though.

However, the next day, when Haley was campaigning for Rep. Jim Clyburn, a key member of Congress from South Carolina's 2nd district, she said she'll definitely not be running for president. "People ask me the question all the time: will you ever run for president?" Haley said to a crowd at Clyburn's campaign headquarters in Georgetown, in an interview on CNN. "As a former governor, and a governor in terms of my party affiliation, I'm always open to the invitation to run for president; however, it is an honor to be a member of Congress."

She added that as a Republican elected official, she is the first to say she loves both parties. However, she said in the interview with CNN, "it was really interesting because, at the Democratic convention, there are many candidates that came and spoke, and we were the only ones who didn't speak."

After being pressed about her Republican Party affiliations in the call I had with her office, Haley didn't offer any explanations or rebuttals.

The concept of descent is a fascinating phenomenon. When an object descends, it is subject to a constant force that is uniformly distributed throughout its trajectory. This force, which is inherent to the object's mass, remains constant regardless of the object's distance from the point of origin. However, as the object continues to fall, it begins to accelerate at an increasingly rapid pace. This acceleration is a direct result of the unopposed force acting upon the object, with no external influences to impede its progress. As the object gains velocity, it eventually reaches a point of maximum velocity, often referred to as the terminal velocity. At this juncture, the force acting upon the object is balanced by an opposing force, namely the drag or air resistance it encounters. This equilibrium enables the object to cease its acceleration, allowing it to maintain a consistent velocity. To illustrate this concept, consider the scenario of a ball being released from one's hand. Initially, the ball will exhibit a slow and gradual descent due to its initial lack of velocity. As it continues to fall, it will gradually increase its speed, ultimately reaching a point where it can no longer accelerate further. This parallels the experience of a person falling, where the force of gravity is countered by air resistance, resulting in a cessation of acceleration.

I recall the first time I saw him emerge from the building after a concert, we hadn't seen each other in a while. I remember inquiring if he needed anything, and he replied he was happy to be there. My initial concern was whether I should leave him be. Was this an inopportune time to be alone? Would there be issues? A few days later, I spotted the same individual walking in, dressed in casual attire, and thought, "This doesn't quite seem like him." I didn't recall ever perceiving him as a stranger; I probably never recognized him. I simply thought, "That's someone I used to hang out with." He appeared friendly, seemed okay, just out there on the streets, looking for work. He was a friendly acquaintance, and for a few days, that was all that mattered to my life.

He wasn't a close friend, however. Instead, he was a roommate, an important one: someone who provided a home away from home for him and his partner. He would sleep in, occasionally wake up and play the blues in the backyard, then return at 7 p.m. to study the night's lessons, and by the time it was time to get up, it was time to leave the house.

I remember thinking at the time that this individual was a diligent student, an exceptional one on the LSAT, and even a student of literature. I didn't know much else, and I thought he was a good person. He would wake up when he got up, clean himself up, and head to work. I never knew why he came to school on Fridays, but then again, I never had to wonder why.

A few days later, he passed away.

That was seven years ago, and I remember how it felt to be able to move past such a difficult experience and begin the healing process. I've experienced this before with people I care about. Not as traumatic, but still challenging. This marks the end of a chapter in my life, but it has been a long journey, one filled with sadness and regret for the many times I did nothing as it happened.

I also think about myself now. The time is drawing to a close, and while I'm still grappling with the pain of the loss, I still hold onto a glimmer of hope that I'll soon find a way to move forward. I believe that as we age (and perhaps as we become ill), it's the last thing we need, and we need to let go for now. Sometimes a life ends suddenly and unexpectedly, like our own, but it doesn't have to, and it would be wrong to use it as an excuse to prolong mourning. I'm not going to let him take it away, not by a long shot.

One thing I think is crucial to know when we're grieving is who we're grieving for, and that's especially true in these times. I was mourning a friend at the time of his death; a friend who was an extremely strong, self-sufficient individual. But beyond that, I was mourning a piece of myself. I wasn't grieving for him; he wasn't grieving for me. He was grieving for himself.

I am now living. I've left behind all the darkness and pain that made the past seven years long and painful. The darkness has changed and gone, and I have a chance to do things differently. I have a chance to be a better version of myself. I have a chance to live.

But you know what?

Recently, I received a eulogy for this person and had the opportunity to reflect on how his choices affected me. I realized there are parallels between his choices and my own. It's no surprise that many people have shared their own insights on grieving. So now, when others ask me if I regret anything, I feel the urge to say, "No, not ever. You know how it is. You know all the right answers."

I know this sounds like a cliché statement, and I know what I'm saying is true. It's not a great answer, and I'm a poor writer. But the question is, why do we even answer the question?

I remember being afraid of the fact that this was the way things were, and that there were no other choices. I can remember how alone I felt; how I didn't fit in. I had never had the opportunity to figure out who I was to fit into a world that I didn't understand, and I didn't believe I could come up with new answers. My answers were simple: I was a kid, I got caught up in a bad situation. I went home, I tried again, I worked harder, I got better, I got a job. That's the norm.

A recent investigation conducted by the Harvard School of Public Health's Prevention Research Center has shed new light on the relationship between violent video games and aggressive behavior in children and adolescents.

Researchers compared the effects of playing the "Call of Duty" shooter game to playing nonviolent games such as "Madden NFL" and "Mario Kart."

Dr. Matthew Bush, a professor of health and exercise science, noted that this study is the first to replicate and extend previous findings on the association between exposure to violent media and aggressive cognitions.

The study, titled "Video Games and Adolescent Aggression: Evidence from the National Longitudinal Lesbian Family Study," will be published in the journal Child Development.

Bush highlighted several strengths of the study, including its longitudinal design and the fact that it followed adolescents from early childhood to young adulthood.

He also emphasized that the study examined the effects of violent video gaming on adolescents, rather than young adults, and that this allowed for a more precise examination of the relationship between exposure to violent content and aggressive cognitions.

A growing body of research suggests that exposure to violent video games can increase aggression, including behavior that results in serious injury and death.

However, Bush noted that many people still believe that there is no such thing as a safe place to play violent video games, despite research demonstrating that there is no link between violent video game exposure and increases in aggressive or criminal behavior.

"Our study shows that aggressive cognitions were at its strongest for those adolescents who were exposed to the game, but those adolescents did not report greater aggressive cognitions for having played the game," Bush said.

He added that the study's findings suggest that the effects of exposure to violent video games may depend on a variety of factors, including people's attitudes toward the game, the frequency of engagement in the game, and the extent to which the game is engaging.

Other research has found that exposure to violent video games could result in violent recurrence of aggressive cognitions in young adults, particularly in males who play such games very long term.

To better understand the relationship between playing violent video games and aggressive behavior, researchers analyzed data from a longitudinal study that followed young people between the ages of 10 and 12 from kindergarten through high school.

They found that early exposure to violent video games was associated with a greater likelihood of engaging in aggression at each follow-up interview.

However, when asked if they had experienced violent video games that they could still play to this day, most (85 percent) said they had not.

Researchers assessed the aggressive cognitions of a sample of 2,879 adolescents and found that early exposure to violent video games was associated with a heightened risk for aggressive cognitions.

Specifically, early play of the Call of Duty violent game was associated with several measures of aggressive cognitions.

Researchers have proposed an idea for black holes that could potentially survive in a universe with nearly no stars.

The scientists discovered the possible solution by utilizing information from an instrument known as the Galactic Legacy Infrastructures Survey (GLIS). The experts are still debating whether this is the most comprehensive explanation for black hole formation or not.

"Although it is plausible that other solutions exist, we believe this solution has the most compelling arguments for it," Harvard astrophysicist Frank Wilczek told CBS News in an email.

In order for black holes to form, enormous stars must be born in the galactic center, where gas and dust clouds are swirling around the newborn stars, much like a cosmic tornado. This is a picture of a galaxy in which a supernova explosion formed a black hole. Image released in December 2013 by NASA.

Eventually, these gas and dust clouds are heated and pushed into the galaxy's core by gravity from these stars and formed into a dense, central, hot body.

When stars are born too far out, they are surrounded by dust. The dust blocks most of the incoming starlight to create a night sky in which only bright stars and faint stars are visible. As the starlight does not reach the dark corners of the galaxy, stars lose their light over time, but their light is still bright enough to be seen.

This can happen repeatedly: Each star system will eventually form one or more black holes and then be surrounded by dust, leaving it permanently cloaked in darkness.

As the gas and dust in the centers of these galaxies dissipates, it may leave a remnant shell of material that is just big enough to have gravity. This shell is called a quasar, named after a star from the 1980s science fiction film Back to the Future.

As light is blocked from reaching the center of the quasar, more of the bright stars it contains are forced to merge their quasar to form more quasars. Eventually, the process will create a large black hole at the center of the quasar, which then swallows the newly-formed stars.

In the new proposal, Wilczek and his colleagues are proposing that at some point in the history of our universe, a very large black hole — the size of our Milky Way, with an observable "event horizon" — formed and swallowed a star.

"Our theory suggests that the very earliest galaxies started off with very small black holes and then developed into large, powerful supermassive black holes," Wilczek said.

When a galaxy was formed, it likely had many more stars than the current one that astronomers observe today. In a very young galaxy, black holes could have been forming stars as fast as they are forming galaxies, which would have led to the formation of a quasar within a few million years.

If the formation of black holes happens extremely quickly, these quasars may have already been eclipsed by quasar-black hole encounters due to gravitational interactions.

"Thus our observation of quasar (black hole) binaries, in which quasars are engulfed by black holes, is consistent with our scenario," Wilczek said. "This hypothesis is not as crazy as it may sound, because the earliest quasars probably had to merge with other quasars for evolution to continue."

It's not possible to confirm whether Wilczek's theory is correct by observing quasars today, however.

"It is possible that new observation techniques will point to a quasar-black hole interaction long before our current GLIS observations," study co-author Thomas Greiner, of the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan, said in a press release. "However, this must be confirmed in future observations if this paper's predictions are to hold up."
