In recent times, it has been reported that all American "extremists" have been purged from social media platforms. However, this claim is not entirely accurate. These individuals are still present, albeit hidden from public view. It's crucial to acknowledge that the most perilous types of extremists today are those who spread hate speech online, often without any factual basis. The notion of "extremists" portrayed in the media is vastly different from the reality. In reality, the majority of "extremist" leaders in the US and other developed countries are part of the mainstream political landscape. In fact, it is the mainstream party that has been accused of supporting extremist ideologies. The distinction between believing a government is extremist and engaging in violent acts against it is crucial.

The reason why so many "extremists" continue to operate online is due to the vast number of angry and frightened individuals who consume news daily. Building an online presence using anonymous or pseudonymous accounts is relatively simple. Fame and fortune can be achieved by logging onto social media platforms under a false identity. With over 60 million individuals online, a few of these accounts may gain notoriety.

It is essential to recognize that the notion of "extremists" involved in online attacks may be misattributed. It is possible that a few individuals using their real names may be responsible. In fact, it may be challenging to identify the actual perpetrators due to their online personas. This phenomenon has occurred in the past with political activists, journalists, academics, and others.

I do not intend to focus on these cases. I suspect that the true culprits may not be from this country. They could be from various nations, including Mexico, Russia, Brazil, or others. This is the reality we face.

In general, I do not trust law enforcement or the mainstream media as much as I used to. However, I am not an extremist myself. I would have been the first to protest against oppressive regimes if necessary. If you wish to label me as an extremist, I will defend my stance vigorously. What I desire is to contribute to the defense of liberty, democracy, and the opposition to those who seek to divide our nation. For many of my fellow citizens, particularly young people like myself, this divide is growing rapidly.

It may seem unusual or ironic to write a lengthy article about "extremists," but it is essential for those interested in free speech. Anti-extremist groups are not the only ones fighting against these forces. They are, in fact, our adversaries.

In the past decade, the cost of crude has decreased significantly, with a 50% drop in the past 10 years. This downward trend has had a substantial impact on various sectors, including autos, utilities, and natural gas, with prices falling to around $20 per barrel. Although economic uncertainty has undoubtedly played a role in reducing costs, the overall trend of lower prices is crucial for consumers.

The reduced prices have also led consumers to make more informed purchasing decisions, particularly when it comes to cars, appliances, and housing. As a result, median household income has risen.

Lower oil prices do come with a direct economic cost, which is borne by consumers. In 2012, the Consumer Price Index for all urban consumers dropped by 0.2 percentage points, with the decline being most pronounced for food and energy.

However, consumers also benefit from lower prices on other fronts. A 2014 study by the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service found that the price of home-heating oil, natural gas, diesel fuel, and propane is significantly lower in states with high dependence on natural gas. The price of fuel oils is now roughly 10% lower in energy-intensive states compared to energy-independent states.

Anecdotal evidence supports this difference. "The fall in consumer prices can be attributed in part to the increased use of natural gas and oil in heat," said Joe Schmelzer, chief financial officer of the U.S. Conference of Mayors. "We are also seeing a large impact from higher oil prices, which have affected retail gasoline prices for several months."

Some economists argue that oil is an "asset class" that can be traded between oil producers, importers, and consumers, thus reducing the "price" of oil. However, Schmelzer argues that energy prices are set in the context of global markets, where the value of a barrel is determined by various factors. The impact of lower oil prices should have no significant impact on the price of natural gas for consumers.

The impact on companies may vary. For example, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its member countries have a significant economic and political stake in maintaining oil prices at current or higher levels. Companies are unlikely to suffer as much as consumers of goods and services to the extent that they pay a premium for oil when there is a lower "markup" between supply and demand.

There may be some oil producers that are losing money on oil. However, in our view, the loss of revenue is very modest compared to the gains that consumers will have from lower prices.

The United Nations General Assembly is considering a proposal that would prohibit government-funded religious organizations from utilizing public funds to advocate for or against individual autonomy and self-expression within their membership.

The non-binding proposal was submitted by Australia as an amendment to the "Nordic Charter on Fundamental Rights and Freedoms" – a document currently being negotiated in the UN's Department of Political Affairs. The proposal would explicitly prohibit governments from funding any organization that promotes individual autonomy and self-expression, out of respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, according to a summary provided by the office of Australian Foreign Minister Julie Bishop.

The United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, and most Western countries currently involved in the charter negotiations have supported a proposal that would bar government organizations from funding a range of activities that contradict the fundamental principles of human dignity and respect for individual autonomy. However, some Western countries have threatened to veto the proposal due to concerns over its compatibility with their own constitutional frameworks.

The proposal has been widely anticipated to be unsuccessful after a draft calling for the same ban was leaked online.

Earlier this week, Bishop stated that the UN has had over 30 other issues put forward, but this one was the most crucial to the Australian delegation.

"I have spoken with numerous government diplomats in the last fortnight," the Australian foreign minister said. "It was essential to have the Australian Parliament and the Australian people on this matter."

Under a resolution adopted by the UN in the past, countries seeking membership on the human rights council must first ensure that their human rights records respect the principles of universal human dignity and respect and protect the right to free and permanent residence of all individuals. The United States currently serves as the only country to have failed to fulfill this requirement.

In the Australian draft proposal, any foreign funding provided to or by members of "organizations that are religious organizations, as defined for the purposes of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, from a body or institution within the United Nations or to or by a member of such an organization must not be used in any way to promote or support individual autonomy and self-expression."

A proposal is required to be adopted by the General Assembly if there is sufficient support throughout the General Assembly to pass. Currently, 38 Security Council members, including those that are current members of the Human Rights Council and non-members, as well as African and Caribbean countries in the Human Rights Council that have a seat on the General Assembly, support the proposal.

The United Kingdom, Japan, and other Western countries currently holding seats on the Human Rights Council could not support the proposal due to their lack of recognition of individual autonomy and self-expression.

A Gentle Reminder: The Art of Writing About Unfamiliar Topics

As writers, we often find ourselves stuck in our comfort zones, exploring topics that resonate with our passions and interests. However, there may be instances where we need to venture out of our comfort zones and write about subjects that don't necessarily spark our enthusiasm. This article aims to provide guidance on how to approach such tasks with ease and creativity.

The Challenge of Writing About Unfamiliar Topics

It's common to struggle with writing about subjects that don't align with our personal interests or expertise. This can be attributed to our natural tendency to focus on what we know and love, making it challenging to muster the motivation to write about something that doesn't capture our attention. As a result, we may find ourselves getting sidetracked or losing focus, making the writing process more arduous than it needs to be.

The Solution: A Mindful Approach

To overcome this hurdle, it's essential to adopt a mindful approach to writing. This involves taking a step back, acknowledging our thoughts and feelings, and focusing on the present moment. By doing so, we can tap into our inner creativity and channel our thoughts into a compelling narrative.

Here's a simple yet effective technique to help you stay focused:

1. Take a few deep breaths and acknowledge your thoughts and emotions.
2. Reflect on the topic you're about to write about and consider the people or experiences that are relevant to it.
3. Allow yourself to explore the topic without judgment, and let your thoughts flow onto the page.
4. As you write, pay attention to your inner dialogue and gently nudge yourself back to the present moment whenever your mind wanders.

By adopting this mindful approach, you'll be able to tap into your creative potential and produce engaging content that resonates with your audience. Remember, the key is to stay present and focused, allowing your thoughts and emotions to guide your writing.

There are no graphics or sound effects, just text from the anime. There's no voice acting either, unless you reach a certain point and then you'll likely have to start over.

You'll meet a girl at the beginning who serves as your guide, but as the story unfolds, she'll become just another character. I've been trying to find an English translation of the original Japanese novel for ages, so this is my way of remembering the characters' dialogue.

The text is mostly translated from Japanese, with some additional English words. It's a lot to take in, with so many pages to get through.

It's more like a game in the early chapters, where you play as the main character, Shikimichi. You live in a small town called Akihabara, and after hearing rumors about mysterious lights in the night sky, your mother takes you to Akihabara to see it for yourself.

One night, your grandmother visits and shows you mysterious writings on a tablet she found in a library bookshelf.

You have to go to Akihabara to uncover what's happening. You have this tablet with a pen, and if you write on it, it comes to life. If you don't use your pen, it will die and turn into paper.

The game gets more challenging later on, but the story remains the same. For me, it makes it a bit too easy. It feels too easy without much challenge, and when you're doing well, there's not much point to it.

The only annoying thing is the small issues that arise, like when you get in a car and the radio doesn't work. There's no music in the game, and if you lose your pen, it will turn into paper and you have to find it.

As you progress, you'll eventually meet the anime characters.

One thing I wanted to say is that I've been playing since the original release date of October 2013. I have to say that I liked it more than the other online version on Steam.

A new series of posts from the team at The Healthy Chef focuses on eating, cooking, and living with common autoimmune diseases. As I prepare for my new book, I'll be discussing gluten intolerance, autoimmunity, and more. To address these limitations, I created a special soup recipe a few years ago that I've been perfecting. I wanted to create something that anyone could prepare and enjoy without high energy, digestive issues, or digestive distress. My approach was to add ingredients that most people wouldn't typically eat, but love and want, to boost the immune system while taking on the world. This gluten-free vegetarian recipe is inspired by traditional French soups, but with a delicious and satisfying base.

My current vegan soup recipe uses a combination of sweet potatoes and sweet onions to add vitamin C, which is helpful for people with autoimmune disorders. The onions give the soup a sweet, oniony taste without being overpowering, and the sweet potatoes provide fiber, healthy sources of vitamin A and potassium. I recommend serving this recipe with brown rice or quinoa for added nutrition.

Grain-Free Vegetarian Soup

Serves four

Ingredients:

* 2 cups quinoa or brown rice
* 2 Tbsp olive oil
* 1 large onion, chopped
* 4 cups peeled and chopped sweet potato
* ½ cup sweet onion, chopped
* 8 oz frozen chopped carrots
* 1 cup frozen chopped celery
* ½ cup cooked white beans
* ½ cup diced corn
* 3 cloves garlic, minced
* ¼ cup fresh parsley leaves
* ¼ cup fresh thyme
* ½ teaspoon ground cinnamon
* ½ teaspoon cayenne pepper
* 1 cup water
* ½ cup brown rice or quinoa (soaked overnight)

Instructions:

1. Combine all ingredients except 1 cup of the ingredients in a 4-quart or larger pot and bring to a boil. Reduce heat to low and cover, cooking for 2-3 hours. Drain mixture well, rinse pot, and set aside.

2. Meanwhile, chop vegetables into small pieces and add to pot. Cook over medium heat until softened and almost done. Add potatoes to pot, stirring constantly to prevent burning. If potatoes get too dark, add extra water.

3. After potatoes have cooked, cook corn by microwaving or boiling until just absorbed steam (about 2 minutes). Drain and mash with hands until potato mixture will hold together.

4. Add quinoa, water, and cooked corn to soup mixture. Simmer over low heat for 45-65 minutes.

5. Stir soup regularly to prevent sticking to the bottom of the pot. Serve warm, with leftovers. Let cool before eating.

This recipe makes a lot more than enough for four people and could feed a lot of regulars. Be mindful when serving after it's been sitting out for longer than a few hours. It would also benefit from a little bit of water and food coloring.

The House Judiciary Committee recently passed the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act, also known as JASTA. The bill is now awaiting consideration by the full House. If JASTA becomes law, it could prevent countries like Iran and other nations deemed terrorist states from using an American statute or foreign criminal laws to take actions in the United States against their own citizens. This could potentially prevent the US from prosecuting individuals for terrorism-related offenses, such as the 9/11 attacks, if the US is unable to do so.

The Obama administration expressed concerns that JASTA would undermine ongoing counterterrorism efforts, claiming that it would severely hinder the ability of law enforcement agencies to protect the US from terrorists and other threats. However, the administration did not provide any evidence to support these claims.

JASTA would grant foreign courts the power to override a presidential determination that American law is applied in a certain country. Currently, Americans can be tried and punished in foreign courts if they are accused of committing a terrorist offense outside the US. JASTA would reverse this, making foreign convictions for terrorist offenses binding in the US. This change would be based on speculation rather than any actual reduction in the threat of terrorism.

The bill also allows federal prosecutors and court officials to bring their home countries' anti-terrorism laws into US criminal cases, even if those laws are not directly related to international terrorism or the financing of terrorism. This could allow foreign law enforcement authorities to prosecute those complicit in terrorism charges committed against the US, as well as crimes committed here with no connection to the US.

It seems that the Obama administration may have been looking for a way to limit its ability to prosecute domestic criminal acts, but its actions in the Senate to block JASTA are concerning. The bill passed in the Senate with a nearly identical vote as the House version, but Senate leaders have since reconsidered their position in light of the president's request. This is a welcome development for a bill that should be approved by Congress.

The most extreme forms of climate change and global warming are irreversible and the only way to avoid a catastrophic future for mankind is to do something — anything — to reduce the amount of greenhouse gases we release into the atmosphere.

There are only two ways to do it: to do something now or to wait until the problem becomes irreversible. This is the dilemma we began examining in 2010 when we established the X PRIZE Foundation — as the new X Prize Foundation, with X the prize code — to help solve the global warming problem.

Peter R. Diamandis – The X PRIZE Foundation is the sole non-profit vehicle that has been designated to conduct the X Prize. A curious misconception has arisen regarding the Federalist Papers, which were indeed authored by James Madison and Alexander Hamilton, along with another individual. However, this individual, often referred to as A. Hamilton, did not contribute to the Federalist Papers themselves. Instead, they wrote the introduction to a book titled A History of the Federal Convention of 1787.

The origin of the name A. Hamilton can be traced back to a letter from James Madison to Hamilton, where Madison refers to a letter he wrote to his brother Albert Hamilton, signing off as A. Hamilton. This letter highlights Madison's tendency to refer to himself in the third person, often addressing himself as Mr. Hamilton.

The Federalist Papers, published in 1788, do not provide any clear indication of A. Hamilton's contributions to the text. While A. Hamilton is frequently mentioned, their ideas cannot be traced back to their actual writings. It is likely that the person who wrote the introduction to A History of the Federal Convention was not the same individual who authored the Federalist Papers.

The first printed edition of the Federalist Papers was published in 1788, and at that time, most people referred to the author based on the text itself. Thus, Alexander Hamilton's words were often attributed to him. However, it is not accurate to claim that Madison wrote most of the Federalist Papers. He was likely involved in the drafting process, and his contributions can be seen in the Appendix I of the book, which includes excerpts from prefaces, notes, and letters. In Appendix II, Madison wrote a letter regarding the Virginia Delegates to the Federal Convention. It is possible that Madison held different opinions on the matter than A. Hamilton or Alexander Hamilton.

The original 1787 edition of the Federalist Papers does not require a historian to understand that James Madison did not write most of the text. Instead, all drafts of the Federalist Papers were first presented to the members of the Virginia Assembly. By 1788, Madison's draft of the American Constitution, known as The Federalist Papers, was widely accepted as the official text.

In A History of the Federal Convention of 1787, I list the names of the delegates who attended the Constitutional Convention of 1787. I have not included the names of all the authors, nor was I sure what to do when I discovered that A. Hamilton did not write most of the Federalist Papers. Appendix II lists only the name of A. In the recent past, there has been a significant rise in the number of reported sexually transmitted diseases in Australia. This increase is a concern, especially considering the previously declining rate of new HIV infections. The Australian Bureau of Statistics has compiled the statistics, which show that the rates of new infections have increased across the country. However, it is still too early to pinpoint the exact causes or reasons behind this increase.

Some of the possible factors contributing to this rise include an increase in people engaging in casual sexual activity and unprotected sex, which have previously been linked to an increased risk of infection. Additionally, some infections may be more easily reported and prevented.

To address this issue, the NSW government has initiated a program to distribute condoms to gay and bi men between the ages of 14 and 43 in Sydney. This program is an effort to promote safer sex practices and reduce the risk of infection.

Another key risk factor is unsafe sex due to STIs such as chlamydia, gonorrhoea, and syphilis. The statistics also show that the total population with HIV has increased by 13.8% between 2014-15 and 2015-16. This increase is largely attributed to people being diagnosed with the virus.

The numbers for each type of sexual contact, including kissing, intercourse, and having sex with a new partner, are also being compared with 2014-15. The report found that the rate of new infections rose in all age groups in Australia, except for the 25-29 age group.

This increase is mainly due to people living longer and a larger pool of newly infected men who have sex with men. For women, the age-standardized total number of new cases per 100,000 population decreased from 3.1 for women between 20-24 to 2.9 for women between 25-29.

The total number of new cases among men was 2.5 for men between 20-24, 2.3 for men between 25-29, and 2.3 for men between 30-34. The increase in infections seen among men between 30-34 is more likely related to HIV infection.

Although people with HIV are more prevalent in those aged 20-24 than in any other age group, the gap between these groups in 2015-16 compared with 2014-15 was only 8% higher for men. This suggests that there are underlying reasons behind the increase in HIV infections that were once seen in younger people and is not simply due to increased exposure to HIV.

There is a strong correlation between HIV infection and other types of STIs. One of the reasons for the difference is the increasing rates of gonorrhoea and HIV infection. Gonorrhoea is an infection of the mucous membranes that can cause inflammation, pain, and swelling of the genitals in men and pre-cancers in women.

It can also cause a change in the sex of the baby inside a woman and is linked to sexually transmitted diseases in men and women. In 2015-16, gonorrhoea was diagnosed in 10,100 people in Australia aged 10 years and older, and almost 4 in 100 had HIV in this age group.

HIV was detected in 3,400 men and women aged between 10 and 49 for the same purposes. It is particularly associated with sexual risk-taking and drug use. Gonorrhoea has also been linked to sexually transmitted infections, and therefore, other STIs are also increasing.

There was a time when people discussed the supposed demise of a character named Superman. It was said that this character had died in the 1990s, and later in the decade, another iteration of the character was criticized. Many people talked about this on the internet, but I'm not sure if there was ever a valid reason to say that the character had truly died. Recently, I had an opportunity to speak with someone who works on the Superman show, and they gave me a reason to believe that we haven't lost anything after all.

When asked about what's wrong with Superman, this person said that there's no problem with the character. However, they were referring to the character's place in popular culture, not the character itself. Superman is not a character that has died; it's a figure that has only been somewhat absent from the public eye. It's the same with another character, Batman, who has also always been present.

This is also true for the Superman from an animated series. The name Superman already implies that the character is still alive and active. The animated series even transitioned to a modern TV format. To say that there's no problem with the character is to say that there's no need for Superman. In my opinion, there's nothing wrong with the character as he was originally created, and we don't need to replace any part of him with something else.

Some people have always dreamed of a Superman who would bring science, space travel, and positive change to the world. The problem is that our heroes are often either old or too powerful to be effective without an evil villain to oppose them. With that said, Superman can still exist if we keep him out of the spotlight.

Some people might say that there's no need for Superman because other characters with similar origins exist, like Batman. What if, decades from now, we see a world without Superman? If Superman existed in a world where he was known for being the greatest hero on earth, who would protect all of humanity?

Maybe even Superman could start to think like Batman, giving Batman his own villains to fight. If I were a Superman fan old enough to read comics, a Superman who could act like Batman and help us fight evil might be acceptable.

I don't doubt that there's a place for an alternate timeline called "Superman Lives," but for now, it's back to the drawing board. But for those who are Superman fans, there's no need for a Superman reboot, because there's no Superman reboot.

The most significant aspect of the "Jupiter system" has been its four massive, icy satellites known as Ganymede and Europa. However, a new paper in Nature Geoscience reveals the presence of an additional, lesser-known entity lurking just beyond reach. A giant planet called Sedna may be the second-largest body in our solar system, even surpassing Jupiter, and one of the largest ever discovered.

Unlike its two most well-known siblings, Sedna is actually an ancient object orbiting the Sun far beyond the edge of the Kuiper belt—the unexplored region surrounding the giant Kuiper belt objects. "A substantial portion of our solar system lies beyond the outer planets, which is why we have many new Kuiper belt objects," says Paul Chodas, astronomer at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif. "Ganymede and Europa are situated within the solar system, while Sedna is situated outside."

The Kuiper belt consists of several objects captured by the gravitational attraction of Jupiter and Saturn when they were still far beyond the edge of the outer solar system—the Kuiper belt in our solar system is the icy debris ring that encircles Saturn and orbits at the outer edge of the system, in the asteroid belt. The inner Kuiper belt, including Sedna, is approximately 30 times further away, with no significant moon or planet, at about 2.4 billion miles from the Sun.

The researchers initially noticed Sedna as an anomaly during the first Kepler mission, launched in 2009. The two-year Kepler mission has scoured the sky in search of small, distant, and distant worlds beyond the solar system. If it detects an object like Sedna, it will alert scientists to its unique orbital mechanics, allowing them to attempt to determine its composition: its rock, ice, or water composition. The Kepler mission has not yet detected Sedna, but by comparing the orbits of the Earth and Sedna, Chodas expects it will likely be present within the next 10 years.

One of the significant questions astronomers have about Sedna, besides its size and age, is what caused it to leave its home and travel far beyond the orbit of Neptune. One possibility: Sedna's orbital path is unique and suggests it must have been born in a disk of gas and dust, and not a bubble—something the researchers also thought. There are hints such a disk may be the origin for many objects in the outer solar system, so its unique orbit may also make it the origin for Sedna. However, that's for a future visit by the next generation of instruments like the James Webb Space Telescope, the largest and most powerful space telescope ever built.

In the meantime, the research team has begun studying the objects they discover, hoping they can shed light not only on Sedna's origin but on the planet formation process in general. "This is a wonderful opportunity for astrobiology, because these are relatively young rocky bodies, and it's essential to understand the origin of these kinds of things," says Chodas.

In the past year, I've been asked frequently about developing a web service for extracting data from satellite imagery, which can be adapted for other applications. The primary use case is extracting and mapping roads on top of map tiles by street names. If you're interested in learning about the techniques behind this work, you can start with my GitHub repository or some free software I've written (see below).

As you can see, I began working on this project in 2010, and in June 2012, we introduced the GIS-Open project to the wider world, along with a Python client library called GeoFarms. The latter is still a work in progress, but we've already deployed GIS-Open in several commercial applications and received feedback from users.

Initially, the focus was on mapping and extracting data from satellite imagery. I started by using OpenStreetMap (OSM), a great open-source mapping community, but it was slow due to the amount of files and data sets involved. This slowed down the project, but I eventually set up a few servers (one in Germany and one in France, each with 1GB of storage) that process the data to a TIFF.

As I worked on the project, I explored the possibilities of using Python to develop web services. I was surprised to find that similar software already existed, as I hadn't been aware of it during my research.

Some quick pointers:

The main idea behind this software is simple: we use standard Python libraries for data extraction and web frameworks like Flask for server development and Jinja and HTML templating for HTML rendering.

The web services are created using Flask, which provides a HTTP server class (called app) for creating web applications.

When a user accesses a data set, the server takes care of all the data extraction as needed.

The Python client library is used for communication between the Python application and the server.

This article is part of a series about GIS-Open, aiming to provide an overview of the technology stack.

How does it work?

The project isn't about creating a web service, but rather extracting data from satellite images and creating a web service to provide it. The real idea was to create a web service that people could use to extract data using Python, then store and use it. This idea isn't innovative and is common in many GIS projects.

The Farmers' Alliance of the Maritimes - A recent study commissioned by the Maritime Agricultural Association reveals that nearly three-quarters of the farmers selected as priority for the Green Jobs Initiative have already ceased operations.

The research, conducted by the University of Prince Edward Island, found that more than half of the 16 priority farmers included in the Maritime Agricultural Compensation Scheme will cease operations within 24 months of the program's inception.

"It's an absolute shame that Maritime farmers are forced to continue working within a system that cannot provide them with benefits in the foreseeable future. When our farmers are forced to work and pay the price of the system's failure, it's only going to become easier to eliminate it altogether," says Pierre Roy, president of the Farmers' Alliance of the Maritimes.

For the first time, the Maritime Agricultural Association surveyed the Maritime farming community's economic needs and found that 80 per cent believe that the Green Jobs Initiative has failed. In reality, it is not only their economic needs that are not being met, but their most basic human rights-to health care, a secure retirement, good wages, benefits, and adequate housing.

Farmers have been told for decades that they are not receiving adequate benefits under the Maritime Agricultural Compensation Scheme. In fact, for several decades Maritime farmers have seen their farm equipment insurance skyrocket to record highs while the Green Jobs Initiative has grown stagnant and in many cases unfulfilled.

"All signs are pointing to the end of the Green Jobs Initiative," says Jacques Leblanc, vice president of communications for the Maritime Agricultural Association.

"It's the failure of the Maritime Agricultural Compensation Scheme that is preventing good producers – who rely on these programs to provide them with a level of income that will enable them to afford the cost of their business to keep farming – from receiving fair treatment. They are being forced to continue working under the same system that hasn't been working for them for decades. Many of the farmers being selected as priority are only picking their last day of work this season. When they quit, those who haven't left the industry won't have anyone to replace them for the next season."

Maritime Agricultural Association President Pierre Roy agrees. He calls for the Maritime Government to immediately halt Maritime Agricultural Compensation Scheme payments to farmers and to remove farmers from eligibility to receive these payments.

"Providing assistance like this to farmers is not just morally right, it is a necessity. It helps improve productivity and helps promote sustainability, but our farmers are not receiving equal treatment. If the Maritime Agricultural Association worked to ensure farmers weren't being forced to continue working for a dysfunctional program that they are not qualified for, we wouldn't have to reach this point," says Roy.

According to Maritime Agricultural Association research, 70 per cent of the farmers surveyed agree that the Maritime Agricultural Compensation Scheme is ineffective at preventing economic hardships such as loss of income, poor health and loss of farm equipment.

About the Farmers' Alliance of the Maritimes

The Farmers' Alliance of the Maritimes represents the interests and needs of farmers in the Maritime provinces throughout the agriculture sector. The alliance is the only organization representing farmers in the Maritime provinces.

One of the most popular Twitter accounts in the world has suddenly gone offline. At last count, the account had a nearly 24,000 follower count, but today its profile now features no tweets.

"The essence of a team's triumph lies in the collective alignment of its members towards a common objective," Gwynn opined. (Courtesy of Paul Gwynn)

Gwynn's name may evoke a sense of nostalgia, but the man himself was a paragon of excellence. He was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame not once, but twice, in 1994 and 1999, in a ceremony held in Cooperstown, New York.

And now, Gwynn has returned to the world of baseball.

Gwynn was honored by the San Diego Padres on Thursday evening as team captain during the inaugural meeting of the team that will compete in the San Diego Super Bowl this season.

"I'm delighted to see the organization flourishing, with a new generation of talented individuals joining the ranks," said Gwynn, 79, who joined the Padres in 1968. "The key to success lies in the unwavering commitment of each member to the team's mission. When the right people are on the same page, that's when true greatness is achieved."

The Padres have never had another captain before, although they did have a captain from 1970 to 1990. Gwynn was appointed team captain in 1998 and, after retiring in 2001, moved to a senior position as president of sales and marketing.

But even with Gwynn by his side, it was the team that stole the spotlight, exceeding expectations in both on-field performance and overall success.

The Padres won just one playoff game from 1997 to 1999, but then went on to win the NL West, defeating the Los Angeles Dodgers in six games. They had a record of 68-94, losing only nine games and clinching the NL West title.

After the 1997 season, Gwynn began taking on additional roles, including managing in the minor leagues and leading the Padres' spring training camp. When the season ended, he was given a raise to $2.5 million, becoming the highest-paid player in baseball for the second time.

Gwynn had just finished playing catch during a visit to his hometown of San Diego and was at a San Diego Padres game at Petco Park. When he spotted an empty seat next to him, he boarded a bus and drove to the stadium.

"I arrived at the park, informed the clubhouse staff, and [said], 'This is where we need to be,'" Gwynn recalled. "I had to wait in line behind Bobby Doerr and Dennis Eckersley, who were the top two starters in the American League, and we were getting off the plane.

"It was an early-morning flight, and we arrived at the stadium with all the other starters already there. Everyone was on time and ready to go, and I told the team: 'Here are my orders: I'm going out there as the starting pitcher as I have been all year, and I'm going to win the game.'"

He won, and his team won, defeating the Pittsburgh Pirates, 8-1. In fact, the Padres improved to 67-94, clinching the division against the Dodgers.

"That's one thing I remember about '97 – the Padres entered spring training with the expectation that we would contend for a playoff spot, and we came closer to a playoff spot than anyone had expected," Gwynn said. "Then we really got into a groove and had six, seven really solid weeks. We started winning, went into the second game of the season, with our pitching coach and a couple other guys, took the lead in the National League West, and started off with a lot of momentum."

Gwynn has two MVP awards, the only player to win two in the NL and one in the AL, and he was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1993. The Padres' payroll was close to $60 million when Gwynn joined, and Gwynn still spends part of his time coaching young players.

One of the reasons he is so active as a coach is because, as he puts it, "You are what you eat." And he likes to coach because he believes it is a passion, rather than just a job. He has no trouble giving his advice to players who come in for a visit or a meal, and he says it's always worth it to work in the organization.

"If I had a nickel for every time I said that, I'd be the richest man in the United States," Gwynn said. "I did that from '95 to '99. It was a fun ride."

The initial step in resolving a disagreement is to acknowledge its presence.

A practical approach to doing so is to consider the possibility that the world is comprised of similar elements to those we imagine.

If that were the case, I would no longer dispute the notion that the world is filled with these types of phenomena. Instead, I would tell my son, "The world can be a mysterious and complex place, and our experiences of it are shaped by our perceptions and interpretations. Perhaps the magic we experience is not actually magic, but rather a reflection of our own understanding of the world."

If the world is indeed full of magic, then I would be forced to confront the possibility that my perceptions of magic are not actually magical, but rather a product of my own biases and assumptions.

Therefore, if our experiences of magic seem to involve our own interpretations of a world filled with magic, I can no longer agree with such claims, as I do not truly understand what they mean.

The reality is that the vast majority of our observations of the world are accurate and describe reality with a high level of scientific precision. The world includes physical phenomena that we cannot accurately describe using our current understanding of the world.

Some of this seems obvious. Take the idea that reality is "incomplete." I do not believe in the notion that God created the universe to include only what seems intended. Why would creationism suggest such a thing? Why would someone who is willing to allow for supernatural events to occur claim that reality is somehow incomplete? There is a lot of room for variation in these opinions, but I find it difficult to believe it is that easy to hold.

Another example: what is "real," and how is it possible that I am "just a person" and the idea of real is subjective? What we mean by "real" is the truth of our own experiences. When we say that it is "real" that we see a red dot on the blackboard, it is true. We have just experienced that red dot that appeared on the blackboard.

Likewise, what we mean by "real" is that the experience I have right now, regarding the physical world and the world as it has appeared, is true. If it is not, it is false. Even if I do not agree with that idea (and I do not), the reality is that it is true.

One of the things that seems like magic is our ability to create our own reality in our minds. If we believe that that's all that reality is, then "fake reality" is what we're actually seeing.

My contention is that the reality behind these "mysteries" is something very different. It's something that we cannot fully explain using a mathematical or scientific definition. We may be able to explain what caused my perception to be exactly how I perceive it, but that does not answer what allowed that perception to exist in the first place.

If that were the case, the phenomenon we experience is not magic, but rather the reality we all experience. If that were true, then our understanding of reality seems to be at an inherent limit.

Perhaps some aspect of a higher power allows us to see reality for exactly what it is. Perhaps that is true; if so, it would only be reasonable to conclude that God does not need to create the universe itself.

I'm not saying that I know that this is the case, of course. It could just be a "mysterious" aspect of my own perception. However, I do not see how trying to explain it through a formal mathematical model for the world would be fruitful at all.

Instead of giving my son the lesson he might otherwise have gotten from watching my head explode, I would rather let him find out for himself through experience and research.

But as much as this point might be counterintuitive, a person's belief that the world is full of magical things is not actually a rational belief. It relies on a faulty view of the world.

A recent discovery by an international team of scientists may have uncovered a mysterious galaxy that could potentially harbor black holes. This galaxy, referred to as EGS, is roughly twice as massive as the Milky Way and approximately 10 times larger than its nearest neighbor, the Virgo galaxy. Researchers believe the black hole at the center of EGS could be at least five times more massive than the one found in the Milky Way.

EGS is one of many young galaxies located in a distant region of the early universe known as the Cosmic Microwave Background. Scientists at the Australian National University propose that this dark matter environment, characterized by cold, dense gas, has enabled the formation of black holes. The new research supports this theory and reveals that EGS is unique among the galaxies studied.

"This finding is truly remarkable, with many exciting features," said Australian National University research fellow Daniel Baker, a co-author of the paper.

"It's one of the most isolated and well-studied galaxies in this time period, with the highest fraction of black holes to mass ratios yet observed."

In the past three decades, astronomers have discovered thousands of galaxies featuring black holes at their centers. EGS is the first galaxy that may be home to black holes. The fact that it is surrounded by galaxies with similar gravity, yet at a great distance, suggests that the black holes must be extremely powerful.

The team analyzed approximately 250 hours of data from the Subaru Telescope, which operated in Hawaii. The team found that the galaxy is heavily populated with hot ionized gas containing a massive population of cold, dense ionized gas.

"As we gaze into the distant future, the number of young, cool galaxies with massive black holes should increase as the Universe expands," said co-author Stephen Webb from the University of Manchester in England.

In the paper, Webb and Baker used computer simulations to explore what would occur if the gas in EGS began feeding a black hole at its core. The researchers found that EGS likely forms a binary system with another Milky Way galaxy, but the black hole in EGS cannot get too close to the inner galaxy, as this would cause the black hole to explode.

"That's why our simulation shows that the black hole doesn't really get too close to the inner galaxy," Baker said. "This achievement gives us a better understanding of how our Universe will evolve."

Throughout the Middle Ages, a select group of skilled warriors and assassins operated within the legal system. They were an elite group, with a strong presence in the nobility. They were well-trained and had no trouble concealing their skills from the general population. The highest ranks of this group had the right to kill with a sword, or any other kind of rapier or dagger except knives, or, when using a longbow, a specific variety. They were considered among the most skilled martial artists in Western Europe and Europe itself.

This group was organized into small, secret societies, and at times they acted as royal guards for royal families or as bodyguards for royalty.

1.1 The Evolution of Elite Warrior Groups

The origin of this group is uncertain. The first documented record is in the chronicle of the early 11th century, the 'Acta de S. Ancula' ('An Alphabet of Mysteries'). In this, a young man named Claudio della Torre attempted to assassinate the Pope. After a battle in which Claudio stabbed Pope Alexander III, he was able to escape and recount how he did it. Claudio was then captured and sentenced to death by a mob. After some consideration, the inquisitors had Claudio's legs broken and then impaled him, in an attempt to kill him.

Claudio was the first successful assassination to take place. However, the group, which existed for several centuries, was no stranger to violence. They were warriors, artists, or even artists, with only a few exceptions: Claudio della Torre was no artist and had no artistic inclination. Another member of the group was Domenico di Girolamo da Mulano (1090-1155), who was an expert on human anatomy and poisons. He killed the Archbishop of Rome, a papal advisor, and later his brother-in-law, a prominent politician.

There were many more assassinations, a number of which we need to know about in order to understand what was happening in Europe at this time. In 1177, the Counts of the Rhine attacked and subdued a German force that had occupied their territory. The King of Germany, Frederick III, had called them into his own personal army to restore the territories they had lost. He and two of the leaders of the group, one of them Count William I, were slain. This event would lead to some of the most intense political and military battles in Europe, between the two sides for control of what was at the time a very unstable realm; a fact not lost on those who had to maintain the peace.

A recent study by the World Health Organization (WHO) has discovered that widespread use of condoms contributes to approximately 2.2 million unintended pregnancies among male-to-female partners and 1.1 million among female-to-male partners annually. This may be attributed to the failure or non-use of condoms in preventing sexually transmitted infections (STIs) during sexual encounters.

The study, published at a UN agency meeting in Geneva, was attended by nearly 600 researchers. The report highlights the importance of preventing the emergence and spread of STIs. WHO and its partners are working to increase condom usage among men during sexual encounters.

According to the report, to reduce unintended pregnancies due to condom use, "one needs to identify individuals at higher risk of STIs and offer appropriate interventions. Interventions that strengthen condom use must be tailored to individuals and social settings."

The report recommends that WHO create public health campaigns, educational programs, and health information and counseling that include information about the benefits of using condoms during sexual encounters.

The study also discusses the importance of male circumcision in preventing STIs. According to the report, "most evidence suggests that male circumcision is cost-effective in protecting the male and, if practiced properly, reduces genital ulcers associated with syphilis, herpes, and other infections in Africa."

The report also addresses the use of condoms during anal intercourse, concluding that it provides an additional barrier to HIV infection and prevents the spread of syphilis.

A few key findings in the report include:

* Men who have sex with men use condoms about twice as much as their heterosexual partners in almost half of all countries.
* Only about 15 percent of men in developing countries and Africa have had condomless anal intercourse during the last year.
* Among couples in which one partner is HIV positive, 75 percent of the time the HIV-infected partner is more likely to be using condoms during sex than the uninfected partner.

The report concludes by stating "This report is a contribution to the Global Strategy to Prevent and Control Unintended Pregnancy. We hope it gives a voice to young and future generations who want to lead a safer world with less unintended pregnancy and more effective birth control."

A New Era Unfolds at Syracuse's Renowned Art Institution

For a long time, the Syracuse University Art Museum was a hidden gem waiting to be discovered. Then, suddenly, it burst onto the scene.

I had the privilege of attending the opening weekend, surrounded by a diverse group of art enthusiasts and students eager to experience the museum's new chapter.

The atmosphere was electric, with a palpable sense of excitement and anticipation. I felt at home among the lively chatter and infectious energy.

But what struck me most was the transformation that took place over the next few days. The walls, once a dull gray, were now a rich, deep blue, and the ceiling glowed with a soft, ethereal light. It was as if the museum had been reborn.

I returned to the museum with my son, and we marveled at the stunning painting on the lobby wall, "The Sunken Garden" by Maurice Descoits. The scene depicted a man standing on a beach, a boat drifting into the distance, and a mysterious figure lurking in the shadows.

As we explored the museum, I stumbled upon a couple who had spent the night discussing art with a friend. We chatted briefly before heading to the Syracuse University gallery, only to find it closed – a surprise that added to the excitement.

But what I didn't know was that the museum had been quietly expanding its collection over the years, adding new pieces without fanfare. Today, the museum was buzzing with activity, and I couldn't help but feel a sense of wonder.

As we made our way to the front of the line, my son's eyes lit up with excitement. "Look at this," he said, his voice filled with awe. "It's my favorite painting ever!"

And as we gazed upon the breathtaking work, I couldn't help but smile. The painting, "Untitled" by Henri Cartier-Bresson, is a masterpiece that draws you in without revealing too much. Even as a fan of art, I felt a sense of reverence wash over me.

The museum's new home, located at 901 N. Hamilton Ave. Syracuse, NY 13206, will feature two permanent collections and over a dozen special exhibition galleries. Mark your calendars for the opening of "A Life Worth Living," featuring the stunning piece "I Want to Grow Up to Become a Great Artist" by Tadao Ando.

The notion that the stars of 'Star Trek: The Next Generation' share a connection with the British prime minister is an intriguing one. While I'm not sure I can grant the Prime Minister's Twitter account the level of fame it deserves, there's undoubtedly a certain level of renown that comes with working on the most popular science fiction show in television history at a time when its fandom is at an all-time high.

When I first watched "Star Trek: The Next Generation" in 1993, I thought it would be another space-bound adventure featuring a team of science fiction characters, similar to what I was used to seeing in films. The main difference, of course, was the replacement of "Star Wars" with "Star Trek," along with a few new actors, including William Shatner, John de Lancie, Wil Wheaton, and Patrick Stewart. As someone who was a huge fan of "Star Wars" before becoming a fan of "Star Trek," it's easy to see what they were missing.

The show wasn't as captivating as I had hoped. It wasn't as clever. It had the same issues I had with those "Harry Potter" movies. However, it was different. It wasn't about going to different planets to find a love interest to save your life, unlike what I was used to seeing in other shows. "Star Trek: The Next Generation" was the first show that didn't have a central story focused on the adventures of a starship crew in space, unlike most shows. You know the type. You don't even need to be a sci-fi fan. The fact that it didn't have a central theme didn't matter: You could find your own story there. It wasn't about a young man going off to seek adventure; it was about a young man going through things. The writers could tell a story, the actors could play that story, and everybody else was there to fill in the blanks. And if you went to the original series, you saw the cast playing with the writers' ideas.

In "The Next Generation," everyone is an expert on some subject and they have the ability to talk to each other in a way that's completely unique and unique as well as funny. It's a really good television series. The thing is, you wouldn't see it if you weren't a fan. Some of the "Trek" fans have said that they don't watch "Star Trek: The Next Generation" on DVD after having been fans since 1980. We may get a chance to see it a little later on in the show's life. It's so hard now to find a copy because it's so expensive on disc.

The original "Star Trek" had its flaws, but it always had great characters. What's happened over the last 30 years is that the characters of the cast became the story. You wouldn't find yourself rooting for anybody. If the show had a villain, I would expect the audience for the "Twilight Zone" to watch it a couple times before going for the villain. What they're doing is making the audience part of the main characters, which is an amazing thing. What better way to take away from the original series? What would "Star Trek: The Next Generation" be if it wasn't about the Enterprise? I can only hope that the show finds another outlet. If it goes on, it can't just be about the crew of the Starship Enterprise. I wish it did!

The federal government is searching for solutions to accommodate federal inmates in British Columbia as the current agreement with the province is set to expire in 2018. Documents obtained by The Globe and Mail reveal that the Canada Border Services Agency is exploring alternative housing options for the 578 federal inmates currently housed in a provincial prison. The agency is considering other jurisdictions to house inmates and is also looking into other facilities within British Columbia. 

According to the documents, the B.C. government is building a new prison to house over 4,000 inmates scheduled for release from provincial jails in February. There has been speculation that the province might consider housing federal inmates to make up for the lack of beds. 

A CBSA report highlights the Lamer Correctional Centre in Kelowna, B.C., as the only facility capable of housing federal inmates from the federal penitentiary in Burnaby. The report states that the Lamer facility can accommodate inmates for a total of five years, but does not provide the entire story. 

The report also mentions that the B.C. Corrections Branch is considering other options, including setting up another facility. The CBSA report suggests that if CBSA continues to accept federal inmates, the Lamer facility may require the transfer of eligible inmates after the current term is completed. 

The report has raised concerns in the local and national prison-rehabilitation industry. 

"It was clearly a poor analysis, and it suggests that some of those federal inmates are actually going to their death row," said Dan Kelly, executive director of the Vancouver-based Innocence Clinic. 

According to the CBSA report, when the current agreement expires, the province is expected to be able to take as many federal inmates as it can physically hold. 

The CBSA did indicate that the number of beds in B.C. is still under review. 

The CBSA report notes that when the current agreement expires, the government is supposed to cease its commitment to transfer offenders to the Ministry of Corrections, subject to the availability of necessary and appropriate beds. 

The federal government has said it intends to end the current transfer arrangement in March 2018. 

It has also said that the majority of the inmates it is keeping behind bars are convicted of non-violent offenses. 

"As Canada's largest and most efficient border agency, our mission is to ensure Canada's safe and secure border while protecting public safety," the CBSA said in a statement. 

"In the long term, when the current agreement expires, it is anticipated that the majority of federal inmates will be transferred to other prisons or community correctional centers as a means of dealing with the significant volumes of offenders our agencies are required to manage. 

"With no provincial option left, we will be looking closely at other facilities across B.C.," it added. "We will carefully assess all possibilities and consider those alternatives where possible."

The New England Patriots, led by quarterback Tom Brady, triumphed in Super Bowl XLIX. This is a gentle reminder of the Patriots' victory. As you may or may not be aware, prior to their championship game, Brady had a minor disagreement with Patriots guard Logan Mankins at the hotel. He was escorted by police, and later departed.

Now: It's a peculiar situation. It's not the first time it's happened, and it may not be the last. The Denver Broncos won Super Bowl 50 last year with Von Miller, and when asked about the incident, Miller said: "We won without him."

As you can imagine, the New York Jets were slightly inconvenienced.

"Our team lost tonight," Jets owner Woody Johnson said in a statement. "The NFL has lost respect for their players and the league office has lost respect for their business decision to ignore what actually happened that night.

"That is why we are working now on legislation that will make sure there is accountability both on the field and in the office. We expect the NFL to act quickly and make certain that nobody from my team will ever have another minor incident again."

It is true that Von Miller didn't receive a formal warning after the Patriots' AFC Championship game win. So let's just say it is unlikely the NFL will issue a formal warning to the Broncos' offensive lineman. (That could even include Von Miller or anybody else they want, so long as they aren't the Patriots themselves.)

I can't imagine the NFL would issue a formal warning to Von Miller for having a disagreement with a Patriots guard. (USATSI)

But I do expect the NFL to act. The league certainly seems likely, based on the reaction of the NFLPA, to issue a formal warning to Von Miller for having a disagreement with a Patriots guard. That's one way to go about the punishment for this incident.

But here's the thing that makes this scenario even more complex: Von Miller was never even charged with any crime. He was just issued a formal warning. That does not mean his actions did not constitute a minor infraction. It very well may not. But the fact of the matter is that he played for the Patriots when they won his Super Bowl and the NFL won't issue a formal warning to him.

Now there are only two ways a formal warning could happen: Either the NFLPA files a complaint for violating the collectively bargained domestic violence policy, because Brady did, in fact, have a disagreement with his teammate. If the NFLPA files a complaint, it probably won't take long for the NFLPA to determine what exactly "having a disagreement with another player" is in the NFL's collective bargaining agreement.

And then what? Well, Miller isn't the Patriots, he won't be issued a formal warning, and the NFLPA certainly will not lose respect with their fans even if they do file a complaint.

What does this all mean? There are no easy answers here. The NFL has its credibility as an employer at stake, the Denver Broncos might want to talk to the New England Patriots about re-accommodating Miller for 2015. We won't be seeing much of Miller again.

(Update: It appears the NFLPA did file a complaint for a minor infraction, citing the league's own domestic violence policy. The NFL filed a motion to dismiss that complaint, and Miller's lawyers asked a judge to put that ruling on the record to determine if the NFL, for good and for ill, violated the rules of its agreement with the union.)

New research by experts from the University of Wisconsin and the University of California, San Diego, reveals that approximately two-thirds of the world's mammal species are in danger of disappearing forever. The study analyzed over 3,100 mammal species and found that nearly 86% of those with more than two adults have vanished. Of these, 65% are considered endangered and 32% are at risk of extinction. The researchers identified 22 of the 24 vertebrate families threatened with extinction and also found five families considered "highly threatened" and 11 considered "near threatened."

"We also discovered that some of the mammal families listed as 'near threatened' have been increasing in numbers and range since we identified these families," said Professor William Ripple of the University of Wisconsin, a co-author of the study published in Nature Communications. "Although the loss of numbers of all endangered families would represent a serious threat to the future of the world's vertebrate fauna, our findings suggest that the loss of more than a few populations is also a serious threat. This shows that even a small shift in population size, or a population that is declining, can be catastrophic to many threatened families of mammals."

Due to the gravity of the situation, the researchers emphasized the importance of conserving the world's remaining mammal populations, especially those that have declined or are at risk of extinction. The conservation and restoration of mammal populations and ecosystems is one of the most effective forms of conservation. For example, the U S Forest Service protects nearly 5 million acres of land annually to prevent logging and wildfires. These "prescribed burns" have a profound positive impact on the survival of rare or endangered mammals and plants by clearing a path for regeneration of the forest and promoting the long-term health and growth of the forest.

The study also provides data on the status of all mammals with more than two adults for the first time. Of the species with more than two adults, 61% are threatened with extinction, 25% are likely to go extinct, and 3% are vulnerable to extinction. The report also found that, for some of the species, the extinction rate has increased significantly in the last century, and that some of the most threatened and endangered species may go extinct before the end of the century.

"We found that there are large ranges of species in almost every ecosystem that are threatened with extinction; even a few individuals in a family have a profound impact," said Ripple. "This is a sobering reality about the magnitude of the problem facing the world's mammals."

The researchers recommend prioritizing the management of remaining mammal populations to ensure that habitat and population dynamics are not disrupted by the loss of some individuals. "These findings support our idea that conservation and restoration efforts are essential if we are to ensure the survival of the world's many threatened and endangered mammal populations," said co-author Dr. Laura Sennelier of UC San Diego. "More than one part of the world's vertebrate fauna is at risk — mammals — which is particularly concerning as the world is still experiencing the sixth mass extinction in history. In order to ensure their long-term future, our hope is that this study motivates policymakers to take action for biodiversity conservation; it is critical that they take the same focus away from protecting individual species from extinction."

1. Citrusy Chicken Medley: In a large pan, heat two tablespoons of refined vegetable oil over moderate heat. Add four boneless chicken breasts and season with a pinch of salt and a few grinds of pepper. Cook the chicken for 6-8 minutes or until cooked through. Add 1/2 cup of white wine and 1/2 cup of freshly squeezed lemon juice, stirring the liquid around the chicken. Bring the mixture to a gentle simmer and cook for an additional 5 minutes. Add two tablespoons of unsalted butter, 1/2 cup of thinly sliced garlic, and 1/4 cup of chopped fresh parsley to the pan. Stir the ingredients and let them simmer for an additional 5 minutes. Spoon the creamy sauce over the cooked chicken and serve with your favorite accompaniment.

2. Southwestern Seafood Wrap: Preheat the oven to 400°F. Place a large salmon fillet on a baking sheet lined with parchment paper and season both sides with salt and pepper. Spread 1 tablespoon of refined vegetable oil on the fish and place in the oven for 18-22 minutes, or until the salmon is cooked through and flakes apart with a fork. To make the wrap, warm 8-10 small corn tortillas in a skillet on medium-high heat. I'm not exactly a culinary mastermind, which is why I often rely on recipes from this site. When my kids were younger, cooking wasn't a priority, but as they grew older, it became more important. In fact, I recently made a dish that my son prepared for us when we visited the doctor last summer. I think I'll call it "A Delicious Discovery."

This meal is the kind that's hard to stop eating, except for the pasta mixed in. It's also a great option to make for several days in a row. One evening, instead of just having it for dinner, I served it for the entire weekend. A key factor in making it a Sunday night recipe was that I had a large salad at the end of the workday. This salad is perfect for a weekend, and the pasta makes a great lunch. It's very filling.

I really enjoy eating it this way. You can serve it over spaghetti or another type of pasta, and it will still be a very satisfying meal. There are other options, such as a wrap, a pizza, or just a bowl. Here's the recipe:

**The Delicious Discovery**

Ingredients:

* 1-2 cups romaine lettuce
* 1/4 pound mozzarella cheese, shredded or grated
* 4-5 red onions, diced small
* 2 cups chopped tomatoes, including diced tomatoes, seeded if desired
* 2 Tablespoons olive oil
* 2-3 cloves garlic, minced small
* 1 teaspoon dried oregano
* 1 teaspoon dried basil
* 1 teaspoon dried thyme
* ½ teaspoon black pepper
* ½ teaspoon salt
* 2 cups cooked farfalle pasta
* 1/4 cup shredded parmesan cheese

Directions:

1. Combine all ingredients in a large bowl.
2. Mix well and toss to combine.
3. Let the salad sit at room temperature for at least 30 minutes or overnight.
4. Serve with cooked farfalle pasta (you can also use frozen) and/or a big slice of pizza.

The Supreme Court has established that it is permissible to redraw legislative districts using political considerations if they are not intended to discriminate against certain voters. If this is the case here, Republicans will likely lose. The party that lost the previous election, the GOP, faces a significant risk of losing elections in 2018.

The tale of the "Mellow Melodies of America". Their narrative could be a multitude of things - or a multitude of things could be "Mellow Melodies of America". "I'm like a 'Star Trek' enthusiast", says Mike Ritrovato, who resides in an old building on Third Street in the city's East Village. His favorite 'Star Trek' episode, he claims, is 1967's "The Trouble with Tribbles". "You know those, like, tribbles with their little furry coats? When they start multiplying and then they're just kind of gone. But if you don't stop, they come out like, 'Tribble! Tribble!'"

The individuals you've just met, and the ones who inhabit close proximity, are some of those "Mellow Melodies of America". They include Ritrovato, who works in maintenance at the city recreation department, and his acquaintances, a group of 10 or 15 men with the surname "Mellow". By night, they gather at their homes to watch films, imbibe, and play dice. "We're definitely like a family", Ritrovato says, "but most people just think it's a movie theater or a bar".

That's not what Ritrovato thinks at all. In fact, he has become convinced that the Mellow Melodies is a community. On the day we are meeting for our interview, they're hosting a "Star Trek"-themed party at a local eatery, known for the excellent taste of its cuisine.

In the years preceding the film's release, there were rumors that the government had initiated a secret "Project Mellow", a military effort to create a clandestine army composed entirely of Mellow Melodies, but there is no concrete evidence of that. What is known, though, is that the Mellow Melodies originated in the 1970s, and their connection to the production is a recent addition.

"George Lucas and I went to his house in Marin County one time and he had this little barbecue pit in the backyard", says Ray. "That was the beginning. We called it the Mellow Pit".

In 1982, Ray had the idea of establishing what would eventually become their group. The only thing that had been missing, he says, was the organization by which they called themselves. On the first night of the group's meetings, Ray says, "someone else said, 'Mellow, we're getting too big'. I remember him telling me he wouldn't like to be my leader any longer". Ray says it was a little later on, in 1986, that he told a group of Mellow Melodies that they should have a "company name". He chose "The Society for the Promotion of the First Rescuing Mellow and the Promotion of the Second Rescuing Mellow Organizations".

Ray still considers his creation the best thing to happen to his neighborhood since the construction of the subway.

"The whole neighborhood turned around around that one event", says Ray. "They just stopped doing cocaine and everything changed".

But as the 1980s went on, the Mellow Melodies continued to grow. "At some point, at least 10 guys were moving to the next apartment at 17th and Second", says Ray, who is now 67. When he started to get a bigger house, he was also getting more people. By the late 1980s, the neighborhood was starting to become "huge again".

"The first time it happened, the place was filled with people, all in one house", says Ray, who points to a large, black house at 24th and First. "At one point, we were talking to somebody about getting a new house", Ray says. "I turned and said to him, 'George Lucas wants to live here'. And I had no idea that I was going to wind up giving him the house that we now own!"

Christians, on the other hand, subscribe to the doctrine of the Trinity, with Jesus being the Son of God. Muslims, meanwhile, believe in a single, indivisible God, with Jesus being a revered prophet, but not the Son of God.

Another significant difference lies in their beliefs about Jesus. Jews do not recognize Jesus as the Messiah, while Christians believe he is the Son of God and the savior of humanity. Muslims also acknowledge Jesus as a prophet, but do not accept the notion of his divinity or messianic status.

Each of these religions has its own sacred text, considered the word of God. The Torah is the central scripture of Judaism, containing the first five books of the Hebrew Bible. The Christian Bible comprises the Old Testament, similar to the Torah, and the New Testament. The Muslim holy book, the Qur'an, is the final revelation from God to humanity.

Finally, the practices and rituals of each religion offer a unique window into their distinct cultures and traditions. Jews observe the laws and customs outlined in the Torah, celebrating holidays like Hanukkah and Passover. Christians follow the teachings of Jesus, commemorating holidays like Christmas and Easter. Muslims adhere to the Five Pillars of Islam, which include prayer, fasting, charity, and pilgrimage to Mecca.

A delightful treat that I always look forward to is a homemade vanilla cake from the freezer. This year, I decided to share this joy with friends at a party, so I made a batch of this vanilla cake from the freezer by preparing it in the morning or afternoon and freezing it for later. It's a perfect dessert!

I experimented with several recipes to find the perfect frozen vanilla cake that would freeze well and stay fresh for a party. I wanted a recipe that was low in added sugar and high in flavor, with fewer calories. This recipe comes from a talented blogger known as The Real Bakes.

To make this cake, you'll need:

* 2 egg whites
* 1 ½ tablespoon water (more if you prefer a sweeter cake)
* ½ tsp baking soda (I used sea salt, which is easy to mix with water)
* ¼ cup of granulated sugar (use more for a less sweet variation)
* ¼ cup of almond milk
* 1 tablespoon vanilla extract
* 2 Tablespoons of flour (or skip this step if your cake flour is already finely ground)

To prepare the cake, combine the ingredients in a stand mixer with the paddle attachments. Mix on low speed until smooth, then add ¼ cup of almond milk and continue mixing on medium speed until well blended. When the mixture becomes thin, it's ready to add water (or less) to thin it further. Stir in the baking soda and set the mixture aside for 10-15 minutes.

When you're ready to serve the cake, refrigerate it for a few hours to allow it to harden slightly. This will prevent it from sticking to food and make it ready for the ice cream frosting. You can also make the egg whites using your favorite whipping cream recipe or a pre-made egg whisk. I chose not to make it, but there are plenty of recipes you can use for this cake. You can also do this step a few hours later if you have time.

To pipe the frosting, you can heat it in the microwave or oven. I chose to use the microwave to soften the icing slowly.

This recipe is easy to make and requires only a stand mixer, an egg mixture, and an ice cream machine. The freezer version is a crowd-pleaser.

The court also found that a situation in which vehicles were not suitable for use on an urban road network would create a significant obstacle to the normal functioning of the internal market. A new home for documentation is now available on docs.microsoft.com. The latest information can be found at File Types, Text, and Formatting.

A file type is a container for a specific type of file, defined by a format attribute.

Text files store plain text.

Formatting is a file type specified by the format attribute.

File types

File types can be specified in several ways:

1. File type prefix
2. Path keyword without a file type

Examples:

*.vmdk
* psc
* xlsx

You can choose a file type prefix for a specific file by specifying the filetype option with a file type name. You can also specify the path with the path option.

Examples:

*.pst
* pst

Format modifiers can be used to create files with a specific naming convention:

*.ps
* ps
* xls
*.xml
*.md
*.vmdk

Examples:

*.ps.vmdk
* vmdk

Format modifiers can also be used to change file extensions for a specific file type:

*.vmdk -ext.txt
* vmdk -ext.txt

The -format option can be used with the file type suffix to specify a specific format for a specific subdirectory of the file type prefix or %.vmdk file type:

* %.vmdk:*.txt
* psc -format psc
* xls -format xlsx

File extensions

A file type can have one or more file extensions. For more information, see File Extension and Related Options.

Examples:

*.txt
* text
* text.txt
* text.txt.txt
* text.txt
*.xml -ext.xlsx -ext.xls
*.xls.xls -ext vbs
*.xlsx -ext.pst
* xls.xlsx -ext vb

There is no special formatting for these options; they are simply stored as a string and added to the file type suffix or %.vmdk variable.

Text files are created using a special text file type. For more information, see the following topics:

* File Attributes

A file can have its formatting and file attributes changed by a user through the Edit menu. For more information, see Windows: Formatting and Editing Files.

Visual C++ file types

Visual C++ and C++-supporting applications use a special type of file for files that are not text files. These files are created when a program runs on a computer that does not have the Visual C++ compiler installed. For more information, see Visual C++ File Types.

File extensions for Visual C++ file types
