In the second half of 2016, the number of individuals not employed or actively seeking employment decreased by 30.7% to 32.3 million between January and June, the lowest since 2009. According to data released by Statistics Malaysia, the number of unemployed individuals declined by 6.6% compared to the same period last year. The unemployment rate for the first six months of this year decreased to 5.2%, down from 5.37% in 2015. The rate for the second half of last year was relatively low at 4.8%, down from 5.36% in 2015.

The data shows that there were 33,633 thousand individuals seeking employment in the country between January and June. In the six months ending June, 30,074 thousand individuals had a job, and 29.8 million went without a job, according to the report. The second-quarter employment rate was 3.9%, 0.5% lower than the rate in the same period last year.

The employment rate is the percentage of adults with a full-time job, but who were looking for a job and available to work during the survey period. It is calculated by dividing the labour force in the employment estimation system by the number of employed people in the labour force.

The report noted that while there were positive signs for the outlook, the unemployment level remained one of the lowest in the country. It will take at least two more quarters to see if the decrease in the unemployment rate will continue. There have been positive trends in the labour force growth in the past few months, with total employment and unemployment in the three months ending June 2016 rising 1.6% and 1.2%, respectively, up from the first three months of 2016.

The two measures, the rate of overall unemployment and the rate of unemployment for those aged between 25 and 54 years, were respectively lower and unchanged compared to the three months ending June 2015. In June, the labour force participation rate was 60.7%, down 0.4 from the first three months of 2016 and 0.5 percentage points lower than the same period last year.

The total number of employed persons increased to 3.6 million at the same time last year, compared with 3.65 million in the same three months in 2015. Total unemployment rate as a proportion of the total number of employed persons was 3.7 percentage points and 2.9 percentage points below the rate in the same quarter of 2015.

The proportion of young persons in the labour force is higher this year, especially in the tertiary sector. The youth labour force participation rate is higher in all but the tertiary sector.

Coconut Delight

This sauce is a game-changer, perfect for elevating a variety of dishes from savory to sweet. The coconut milk adds a rich and creamy texture, while the butterscotch sauce provides a deep, velvety flavor.

The key to this sauce is the balance of flavors. The coconut milk provides a subtle sweetness, while the butter adds a richness and depth. The lactic acid bacteria adds a tanginess, but don't worry, it's not overpowering. And the best part? It's easy to make and requires no cooking!

One of the unique aspects of this sauce is that it's perfect for using in a variety of dishes. Try it on burgers, macaroons, or even as a topping for vegetables or soups. The possibilities are endless!

Here's the recipe:

Ingredients:

* 1 cup coconut milk
* 2 tablespoons unsalted butter
* 1/4 cup pure maple syrup
* 2 tablespoons butterscotch extract
* 1 large egg
* 1/4 cup sweetened shredded coconut
* 1 1/2 tablespoons lactic acid bacteria culture (optional)

Instructions:

1. Blend the coconut milk until smooth.
2. Add the butter, butterscotch, maple syrup, and seasonings, and blend for 10-15 seconds.
3. Add the egg and blend for 1 minute more.
4. Spoon the sauce over a sweetened muffin, baked potato, or macaroni and cheese.

Note: This recipe makes about 2 cups of sauce, enough for 2 dessert sauces. You can also store it in the freezer and thaw it when needed.

Cake:

* 4 ovals of white liquid
* 1/2 cup of crystalline sweetener
* 1 teaspoon of fragrant essence
* 1/2 cup of fine, powdery substance
* 1/4 teaspoon of leavening agent
* A small amount of crystalline mineral
* 3/4 cup of melted, golden liquid
* 1/2 cup of small, dark, round candies

Frosting:

* 2 cups of fine, powdery sweetener
* 1/4 cup of soft, creamy substance
* 1/4 teaspoon of fragrant essence
* 2 tablespoons of white, milky liquid
* Small, round, colorful decorations

Instructions:

1. Heat the air to 350 units of temperature. Prepare a round, flat dish by applying a thin layer of lubricant and a fine, powdery substance.

2. In a large, open container, combine the white liquid and beat until it becomes light and airy. Add the sweetener and fragrant essence, and continue to beat for two more minutes.

3. In a separate, open container, combine the fine, powdery substance, leavening agent, and crystalline mineral. Slowly add the mixture to the egg mixture, stirring until just combined. Add the melted, golden liquid and small, dark, round candies, and stir until well combined.

4. Pour the mixture into the prepared dish and heat for 25-30 units of time, or until a small, pointed instrument inserted into the center comes out clean. Allow the mixture to cool completely.

5. To prepare the frosting, combine the fine, powdery sweetener and soft, creamy substance in a medium, open container. Beat in the fragrant essence and white, milky liquid until smooth. Apply the frosting to the cooled mixture and decorate with the small, round, colorful decorations. Enjoy!

The primary regulations apply to all commercial air activities, whether located on-site or offshore. The regulations define standards for hazardous emissions and control of hazardous emissions.

Hazardous emissions are those that can affect human health. These include pollutants that are emitted directly or indirectly and can cause mortality, morbidity, damage to infrastructure, or loss of life. Hazardous emissions include particulate matter, volatile organic compounds, and other substances that can affect human biology and the atmosphere.

Air pollutant standards for hazardous emissions were published in the early 1990s. Hazardous emissions are subject to multiple air quality standards and are regulated by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

Hazardous emissions are regulated in two chapters of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards. The Part 16 standards are published in a publication as an interim part of a regulatory guide. The Part 1 standards were published in a chapter of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards.

Regulations for hazardous emissions were developed through an environmental review process. The final environmental review includes an analysis of the effects of proposed changes on the environment. The basis for all other EPA regulations regarding the environmental impacts of facilities is the final environmental review.

Subpart 1 of Title I of the Clean Air Act sets the basis for regulations and standards for hazardous emissions. Subpart 3 sets the basis for regulations and standards specific to offshore facilities. Subpart 7 establishes standards for the management of hazardous emissions under these regulations.

Some air pollutants that can affect human health are regulated as a result of their effects on human and animal life and health. These air pollutants include hydrocarbons, volatile organic compounds, and particulate matter.

In a series of conversations with experts in the field, I've come to the realization that a major hurdle to the success of the Affordable Care Act is a problem of incorrect assumptions. Not misinformation about the law itself, where some individuals may have misunderstandings — but incorrect assumptions about how the law is supposed to function.

The reason for this is straightforward: The law is a complex web of regulations and incentives. It requires companies and individuals to invest a certain amount in providing health insurance. However, the government does not require that they do so in a logical manner.

The way the law makes it economically beneficial to purchase health insurance is that the federal government will cover the first $150 per month it takes to enroll for a policy. This amount — the benchmark premium — is then automatically adjusted by a computer system to reflect the latest available information. (By contrast, a typical private insurance policy — the benchmark for which private insurance policies are regularly updated — would charge the customer more than the benchmark premium.)

The way the law encourages this is a system called cost-sharing. Cost-sharing is a set of rules the government imposes on everyone receiving affordable insurance policies. It generally requires people to pay the first $7,150 of their monthly premiums in costs associated with the health care law. This amount is what the government would pay the company to cover it, and the company would pay the government the remainder of premium costs.

This approach makes sense from an efficiency standpoint — but it turns out to be detrimental to people's well-being. According to a study of health insurance offered through Blue Cross and Blue Shield by the National Bureau of Economic Research, cost-sharing for plans that people could purchase before the Affordable Care Act went into effect increased their annual risk of dying from heart disease by 12 percent.

These benefits were not insignificant, since before the Affordable Care Act, the nation's top 10 causes of death each involved heart trouble. Those causes — heart disease, stroke, heart failure, and cancer — together resulted in 6.65 million deaths in 2011, or about 42 percent of all deaths.

As noted elsewhere, this is a significant problem that has persisted for years; the U.S. has about 45 percent more people living in the top 10 causes of death than in 1980. It's also a problem that we can address. For example, there is already a bill called The Healthy Families Act. The bill, introduced by Sen. John Barrasso (R-WY), would require every state to set up a state-level health system to replace the one that was recently gutted by the Affordable Care Act.

That will not be easy. And it will not happen overnight, as our recent history shows. But if Barrasso's bill were to become law, it could take as many as 500,000 Americans off the dole by making health insurance affordable, and as many as 300,000 Americans off government assistance to pay more for health insurance. We can do better than that.

Moreover, it's important to recognize that the health care law has multiple components. If we are serious about improving health coverage for Americans, we should start by focusing on the components of the law that are already working, the ones that are improving insurance security for people who currently don't have it. To do that, we need to talk about how to improve our health care system for children. That will have to be the focus of the next presidential campaign.

The fascinating stories of America's early history are filled with intriguing facts that shape our understanding of the country. However, there is much more to learn about the people who built this nation. "The People of the Book: Unveiling the Hidden Tales of America's Early Settlers, 1519-1660" is a collection of essays that offer a glimpse into the past and present.

"A remarkable book," says The Atlantic. "The first such collection to explore the ways in which Americans have sought to define themselves and their origins and their nation."

—Sue Nelson, author of "The Great Experiment: The American Story"

When it comes to American history, few have had a more intimate and personal relationship with the country than the Plymouth Plantation founders. These men—one of whom, Philip, came up with the name "America" for what would become a new nation—have been written about numerous times, but none better than in "The People of the Book" (public library). This groundbreaking book includes more than 60 contributions by people from all walks of American life. The contributors write about everything from George Washington's vision to their trials and tribulations as well as the fascinating stories of some of the most important people to ever set foot on American soil.

Though the volume is full of anecdotes along with historical accounts, they are told with clear-eyed, dispassionate histories that tell their own stories, bringing their own perspectives to the table. For instance, the editors of "The People of the Book," James N. McPherson, a retired historian from the University of Georgia, and Paul B. Burdorf, professor of theology at St. Louis University, offer a unique perspective on the early colonists. Here, they explore the idea that, perhaps in part, they chose to come to the New World. After all, what would be more American than to set up a new home without the government and institutions familiar to the English?

"It is the task of history," they write, "to interpret the past to illuminate and illuminate the present." By telling these stories in this engaging fashion, the authors have provided us with a fuller understanding of what the people of Plymouth Plantation experienced when they set foot on the shores of New England.

The Americans of "The People of the Book: Unveiling the Hidden Tales of America's Early Settlers" provide a unique window into that history of adventure and hope and, at the same time, help us better understand our country's greatest moments — the Founding Fathers and the Revolutionary War, the New Deal, civil rights legislation — through their own unique perspective.

Background: High rates of chronic diseases in young people are a significant global health issue.

Objective: To examine the relationship between smoking and the following conditions: diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, dysphagia, heart failure, and stroke.

Design: A cross-sectional study with data collected at various ages. The study population consisted of students in 13 Canadian cities who completed baseline data in their high schools between 1978 and 2008. A total of 6041 boys from 11 Canadian education systems participated in this study.

Results: A total of 8.6% of the boys in the study had smoked at some point in their lives, while 6.6% were current nicotine users. During follow-up, 1467 men (13.3%) met the study criteria for one or more of the following conditions: diabetes, dyslipidemia, dysphagia, hypertension, dyspnea, coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure, heart attack, or stroke. Current tobacco use was associated with an increased risk for developing these conditions. The risk for developing diabetes was almost double among current smokers and current chewing gum users relative to nonusers. Current cigarette smokers, but not past cigar smokers, were at almost double the risk for developing hypertension. Current chewing gum users were at almost twice the risk for developing congestive heart failure, while current cigarette smokers had a similar risk for developing congestive heart failure and stroke.

Conclusion: In this study population of schoolboys, nicotine use was associated with a modest increase in current (but not past) cigarette smoking. This risk was substantially elevated among current smokers who used chewing and snuff chewing tobacco, suggesting that the nicotine content of these products may be contributing to the risk. These findings are important because they suggest a possible mechanism by which cigarette smoking could increase the risk for the development of chronic diseases.

Today, many indigenous people around the world are dying at the hands of US and Canadian occupation, including those in the Pacific Ocean. The very survival of many tribes on the Pacific Islands has been threatened by US government policies. 

The most important reason why the indigenous groups of North and South America continue to suffer today is that they have resisted colonizers and conquest from the very beginning. This resistance has been crucial in resisting not only those who came before but also those who came after, through the conquest, colonialism, and enslavement of the Americas, Mexico, and other lands.

The House and Senate appropriations committees recently approved language to increase the amount of defense spending that can be transferred from the State Department and intelligence community to the Pentagon. The Senate bill removes funding for the president's request for an additional $30 billion for the Pentagon's base budget through 2023. The House bill also removes funding for the president's request and for an additional $10 to $13 billion for non-defense spending accounts.

Aims:

To investigate the security of prolonged lactation in women with breast cancer.

Methodology:

A retrospective observational study.

Location:

The California Breastfeeding Support and Treatment Program, participating state Medicaid managed care organizations.

Participants:

All women aged 30 years or older with localized breast cancer presenting to their healthcare provider between 1984 and 1997.

Primary Outcome Measure:

Exposure to educational videos about breast cancer during pregnancy and the postpartum period.

Findings:

Between 1984 and 1997, 689,630 breast cancer patients were included in the study. During this time, 13,964 mammograms were performed. Of these 13,964 mammograms, 3263 (45.5%) were performed during the postpartum period, 8981 (63.1%) on the day of delivery, and 9,637 (65%) on the day after delivery. The percentage of women who received educational videos about breast cancer during pregnancy and the postpartum period did not significantly affect the risk of early-onset breast cancer. There was an increased risk of breast cancer among women who received educational videos about breast cancer during pregnancy and the postpartum period. The risk associated with educational videos about breast cancer during the postpartum period was not statistically different from that in women who did not receive educational videos about breast cancer in either pregnancy or the postpartum period.

Conclusion:

Breastfeeding with or without mammography screening is not associated with an increased risk of adverse health consequences or an increase in breast cancer among women with breast cancer. Breastfeeding at a sensitive age may be associated with improved postpartum health.

Specifically, the department has chosen not to greenlight any new projects with 500 units or more, citing concerns about the city's affordable housing shortage. This decision has been met with resistance from various housing groups, who argue that it may have discriminatory undertones.

In a surprising turn of events, the HPD had previously agreed to a $300 million project, but has since reversed its stance. Instead, the department plans to reduce the number of affordable units in each borough, including a 20 percent decrease in Manhattan and Brooklyn. Additionally, some affordable units deemed "not required by law" will be eliminated. The goal of these reductions is to address the city's housing shortage, which is expected to reach over 10,000 affordable-housing units by 2025.

In response, housing advocates have begun lobbying city government to reconsider the decision. "New Yorkers should not be forced to leave their neighborhood due to a new apartment complex and a lack of commitment to affordable housing," said Rev. Sharon Smith of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. Some community groups have also highlighted the HPD's past cuts to affordable-housing projects, which have resulted in a 75 percent reduction through "regulatory and market-based mechanisms."

This development may also impact the construction of a new housing complex in Greenpoint, where local activists are planning a rally to discuss the situation. The Greenpoint Civic Association is hosting a community meeting from 6 to 8 pm on Saturday to address the issue.

"In days long past, when the universe was still in its infancy, a solitary deity... and that deity was consumed by wrath."

The ancient beings, once revered by humanity, wielded unparalleled power over the natural world. Their dominion over the earth, oceans, and skies was absolute. However, as their strength began to wane, humanity was powerless to resist their decline. The ancient beings vanished, leaving behind only their legacy: the Circle of the Ancients.

The Circle of the Ancients is where the ancient beings reside, imprisoned until their destruction and the world's restoration to its former glory.

Historical Accounts

Following the First War and the fall of Ascalon, humanity's tribes were left to defend their lands as they saw fit. After the ancient beings' departure, the tribes found themselves in a world without a deity. However, this also marked the awakening of the gods themselves, as a result of the Circle of the Ancients.

The tribes of Ascalon, unified in their determination, successfully recaptured Ascalon from the dread dragon Zin-Malus. By defeating Zin-Malus, the tribes ensured the future of their kind.

Subsequently, the Circle of the Ancients was formed to confine the ancient beings, in a realm known as the Great Void.

After the war, some humans who had allied with the dragons began to journey with them to the south. These humans discovered the Great Void and, unaware of the Circle's true nature, were tasked with guarding the caverns. However, they were unprepared for the darkness and soon abandoned their posts. Many caves were sealed off with massive stone barriers to prevent further exploration. As they gazed upon the Circle through the cave entrances, it became clear that the ancient beings had left their mark on the world. The humans who followed the dragons were not the first group to awaken to the Circle...

Eventually, another race emerged alongside the dragons - the rakks. Although small in number, they were formidable due to their reliance on advanced human technology.

When the Titans awoke and clashed with the dragons, the ancient beings became aware of these new beings and left behind the Circle of the Ancients. Fearing they had been underestimated due to their ability to communicate, the ancient beings decided to ambush the gods in great cities, seeking to reclaim their powers. The Circle of the Ancients thwarted their plans, although the other gods were displeased with this outcome. They were, however, satisfied to see the dragons attempt to destroy the ancient beings.

In the future, it was discovered that the effects of the Circle of the Ancients could be reversed, implying the existence of an ancient power capable of restoring the gods. A group of children, descendants of the ancient beings, awakened as the Ascalonians and established a tentative peace with the Circle of the Ancients. Despite their power, the Ascalonians were unable to completely destroy the Circle. They finally achieved this when the first group of humans awoke and the Circle's power was restored.

Sylvanas and her companions attempted to destroy the Circle to halt the awakening. However, this would have resulted in the destruction of Eir and all her accomplishments. As it stood, she would lose everything she had worked for.

1. Island-Style Chicken Delight:
Ingredients:
- 2-3 lbs. chicken thighs
- 2 tablespoons olive oil 
- 2 garlic cloves, minced to perfection
- 1 teaspoon ginger powder, a pinch of warmth
- 1 teaspoon allspice, a hint of sweetness
- 1 teaspoon thyme, a sprig of freshness
- 1 teaspoon cinnamon, a warm and cozy spice
- 1/4 teaspoon nutmeg, a subtle and aromatic note
- 1/4 teaspoon cayenne, a touch of heat
- 2 tablespoons brown sugar, a drizzle of sweetness
- 4 tablespoons soy sauce, a savory and umami flavor
- 1/4 cup white vinegar, a splash of tanginess
- 4 tablespoons lime juice, a burst of citrus
- Salt and pepper to taste, a pinch of seasoning
Instructions:
1. Combine all the ingredients, except for the chicken, in a bowl, a harmonious blend.
2. Place the chicken thighs in a shallow dish, a canvas for the flavors.
3. Pour the marinade over the chicken and let it sit, in the refrigerator, for at least 2 hours – preferably overnight, a slow and savory infusion.
4. Heat up a grill or a large skillet, a fiery passion.
5. Cook the chicken for approximately 10 minutes on each side, a crispy and caramelized exterior, and serve.

Ingredients:
- 2 cans conch meat, a treasure from the sea
- 2 large eggs, a richness and moisture
- 2 tablespoons all-purpose flour, a foundation of texture
- 2 tablespoons finely chopped onion, a pungency and crunch
- 2 tablespoons finely chopped green pepper, a burst of freshness
- 2 tablespoons finely chopped celery, a subtle and aromatic note
- 1 teaspoon curry powder, a warm and aromatic spice
- 1 teaspoon garlic powder, a savory and umami flavor
- 1 teaspoon salt, a pinch of seasoning
- 1 teaspoon black pepper, a peppery kick
- 1 teaspoon dried parsley, a freshness and brightness
- ½ teaspoon cumin, a warm and earthy spice
- ½ teaspoon garlic powder, a savory and umami flavor
- ¼ teaspoon cayenne pepper, a touch of heat
- Vegetable oil for deep frying, a crispy and golden exterior
Instructions: 
1. Drain, rinse and then finely chop the conch meat, a tender and flavorful texture.
2. In a large bowl, combine conch meat with all other ingredients, a harmonious blend.
3. Heat a saucepan with vegetable oil, over medium-high heat, a sizzling and savory aroma.
4. Once the oil is hot, form the conch mixture into balls, about 3 inches in diameter, and drop them in the oil.

6. Remove from the oil and place on paper towels to drain the excess oil, before serving, a satisfying crunch.

This summer, I had the opportunity to share my research on a new approach to modeling state, county, and city level data from 2000 to 2015. The goal of this project is to shed light on key issues that arise in American elections by identifying the political factors that have driven changes in state level electoral outcomes over the past four decades. The data used in this project were collected at the state level from the Cooperative Congressional Election Study (CCES) and included information on voters, registration, turnout, and other key variables as well as state and local political institutions. The CCES is a large, nationally representative survey that updates its data set every few years and is considered the most authoritative source for state-level data by many political scientists. The CCES also includes people with diverse racial and ethnic backgrounds, making it a more representative sample. 

The CCES data were used to develop a new data set that allows for a more refined set of statistical models. The primary goal of this project is to identify the political factors that have driven the changes in state level electoral outcomes over the past four decades. The CCES data were also used to examine the relationship between regional population growth, regional political party membership, and geographic concentration of interests. The CCES collects information on these factors from the U.S. Census Bureau and I used that data to generate separate indicators for cities and counties. I then used those indicators to compare the relative patterns of growth for these communities of interest relative to non-affluent or other minority groups.

In addition to the existing CCES data on population growth, I was able to develop an additional data set with information on voter turnout for each year from 2000 to 2012. This additional data set was crucial to understanding patterns of partisan interest, or "strategic voting", that are not captured by demographic analysis alone. I was particularly interested in questions about strategic voting because we use strategic voting to predict voting tendencies for the entire electorate by measuring how the strategic choices of political parties and interest groups affect voting patterns.

The sun rises high in the morning, bringing with it a sense of calm and serenity. As we go about our daily routines, it's easy to get caught up in the hustle and bustle of life, but it's essential to take a step back and reflect on our priorities. 

Think back to your first job, and how you managed to balance work and personal life. For many of us, it's a struggle to find that balance, but with a little planning and discipline, it's possible to achieve. 

In the days leading up to a big event, I found myself overwhelmed by the sheer amount of tasks I needed to complete. I wrote down everything I needed to get, from an air purifier to paper towels, but then I realized that I was just going to end up throwing money away. 

So, I took a different approach. I started planning ahead, thinking about what I needed to do each day, and making a list of essentials. It was a game-changer. 

The key is to start planning early, and to prioritize what's truly important. Don't get caught up in the latest trends or impulse buys - think about what you really need, and what will make your life easier. 

By taking the first ten minutes of your day to plan and reflect, you'll be able to tackle your tasks with ease and confidence. And when you do need to make a purchase, ask yourself if it's really necessary, and if so, can you afford it. 

Remember, the key to financial freedom is not about having a lot of money, but about being mindful of how you spend it. By being intentional with your finances, you'll be able to achieve your goals and live the life you truly want.

One possible explanation for the disparity in life expectancy is the difference in standards of health in various countries. This highlights the need for a more nuanced approach to measuring progress, one that takes into account the unique circumstances of each country. Another possibility is that the numbers may not be increasing as rapidly as we think, and that the improvement in life expectancy may be more pronounced in certain regions.

As of last year, two of the three states where same-sex couples can wed, the District of Columbia and California, allowed the marriages to begin on July 1. This milestone marked a significant shift in the country's stance on same-sex marriage.

According to the Human Rights Campaign, over 1,000 gay weddings took place in California between November and January 2016, with the national average being around 400 per month. Currently, there are 1,200 same-sex marriages in the state, according to the state's Department of Public Health.

In addition, gay marriages have been performed in Maryland for the past month, while the District and Virginia are set to allow same-sex marriages starting on September 6. A federal judge overseeing lawsuits against gay marriage bans in Maryland and Virginia stated that he would rule by the end of the week on whether these bans should be deemed unconstitutional based on discrimination grounds.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services stated that the state would remain open until the end of July and that no further action has been taken. Some legal experts believe that state-level bans, which are still in effect in several other states, might be vulnerable given their inability to stop or limit same-sex marriages based on religious affiliation.

These bans might be vulnerable to being struck down, and this has to be a concern for the states, according to Christopher C. Koper, staff attorney for the American Civil Liberties Union's Washington office.

There might be an exception in the 10 states plus the District of Columbia, where marriage equality is being implemented through ballot measures that are awaiting their outcome. One expert stated that these same-sex marriage prohibitions do not stand, noting that those who have lost cases for the right to marry through the courts might be willing to continue fighting in the name of religious freedom.

For many same-sex couples, the decision to get married was a moment they and their families could have waited for a long time. The new law has already given them something to celebrate.

"This day means everything," said Michael Tashjian, a transgender man, who wed his partner at a Washington restaurant. "Our family is united in one of the most significant civil rights milestones in the history of the United States."

For others, marrying will bring little benefit. The only legal benefits will be tax recognition, if one or both of them were previously married, and health, retirement, and spousal benefits.

One challenge that will likely be challenging to some couples is that many have been unable to locate wedding venues in their desired area. An attorney who has worked on more than 60 same-sex marriages stated that he has often been told in advance that a couple would not be able to pick up the first-month rent at the apartment complex where it would have been rented from.

Despite those obstacles, there are also advantages. One attorney, who has been married since 2011, said there was less confusion.

The White House is exploring various immigration-related options within a broader agenda focusing on jobs, the economy, and international diplomacy, according to individuals familiar with the discussions.

The administration is also weighing the option of going to court to block California's new sanctuary city ban or negotiating with states like Texas on DACA.

"There are many moving parts," said a Justice Department official.

The White House is also considering adjustments to the Department of Homeland Security's authority to deport individuals in the United States illegally, with the aim of strengthening the administration's position in combating state policies that protect undocumented immigrants, according to this individual.

A DHS official stated that discussions regarding changes to the current law on the deportation of non-citizens have no legal bearing. "DHS does not have unilateral authority to alter existing DHS policies in this capacity," the official said.

As part of immigration reform efforts, the administration is considering utilizing its executive power, as it did with the DAPA program, to address illegal immigration, according to individuals who have spoken with White House officials, congressional aides, and others on Capitol Hill.

For example, if the administration cannot reach a deal with the eight governors of sanctuary cities, it could use its executive power to require state officials, such as city chief executives, to cooperate with federal officials and take "meaningful action" against illegal immigration, according to one individual who has spoken with White House officials.

The White House is also considering providing additional tools to the Border Patrol to arrest illegal immigrants and is considering giving U.S. Customs and Border Protection the authority to arrest and detain individuals. The DHS official stated that this would be a "long discussion process," and that "we will discuss more on DHS's legislative and executive authorities as I'm sure I will get to you on it tomorrow?"

The DHS official noted that the department has been working to build trust with state and local officials through outreach and has been having meetings with the Homeland Security Secretary to improve relationships with local agencies.

Another option is using executive authority to force local officials to enforce immigration laws, which could lead to an immigration standoff between the White House and local officials. A recent report by The New York Times quoted individuals familiar with the policy discussions as saying that the administration would push hard to push the issue.

In September, DHS had two meetings with local officials, and two were productive, according to the DHS official, who did not directly address the reports from the report. However, officials noted that the DHS is "working with a lot of different groups" in trying to work on issues in both states and with local communities. "It is not enough to have one meeting," said the official.

"That's why we have DHS stakeholders … to have discussions and engage with those stakeholders," said the DHS official.

DHS is also considering increasing the number and strength of U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers that patrol the country's southern border, using a more aggressive enforcement strategy, according to this official.

DHS announced in August it would hire 5,000 new border agents to help stop illegal immigration and expected to have them deployed by September. However, this executive order could put additional pressure on cities and counties that do not cooperate with U.S. officials, and could lead to the detention of individuals living in the country illegally.

The administration is also discussing options with congressional colleagues on how to deal with a series of issues involving state and local policies that protect undocumented immigrants, but the discussions are still ongoing. Congressional aides asked not to be named because the discussions are private.

Every time I'm about to depart from an unpleasant situation, I sense a subtle pang. It's the initial sign that the day isn't unfolding as planned. Before I realize it, I'm back in the taxi, surrounded by unfamiliar surroundings, with a stranger who's trying to make me feel guilty about my choices. I'll get the notion in my head that if I'd been more assertive, I would've been strong enough to resist. If I had been more aware of my surroundings, I might have been able to protect myself. But all I can do is observe as he navigates the streets of Manhattan, until I eventually fall asleep.

Like any individual who's experienced a traumatic event, I grapple with the pain of this moment. In my mind, I'm thinking, "I should have stood up for myself more strongly. There's no excuse I could have given if I had fought back more resolutely."

It's a sentiment that's surprisingly common. Despite the fact that nearly half of victims know their attackers within two months of the incident, many still don't know their assailants at all.

The reasons why we aren't able to resist more strongly as victims include being young, having consumed substances, or being in a state of vulnerability. However, there are other reasons that we don't resist more strongly that many people, especially allies, don't comprehend.

It's acceptable to set boundaries.

The most common reason people don't resist more strongly is that they don't want to see their attacker get what they want.

We often hear "I wish someone had fought harder," or "I wish I'd said no more firmly," when we advocate for resisting an attacker.

And we have valid reasons to say this. We might be saying this as a defense mechanism that works for us.

Imagine the consequences of a confrontation with that mindset.

You resist your assailant, and then they leave you alone to deal with the aftermath. You're at home, feeling overwhelmed, confused, and wondering if what just happened is even real.

You report the incident to the authorities, and discover that they're not equipped to handle cases involving victims who didn't resist. Even if you had resisted, they might not take you seriously; they might tell you to calm down, put on a brave face, or leave them alone.

You end up making changes to your life that you never intended when you first identified what you were afraid of: you stop attending social events, you alter your appearance, and others have a hard time understanding.

And this isn't an outcome you chose. This happened, and you didn't have control over it.

Why not resist more strongly?

In the end, when we tell ourselves "I wish someone had fought harder," most of us are saying, "I wish this person had been more resilient."

If someone is harming us, and we don't feel safe enough or strong enough to stop them, then we should allow them to continue. We should let them harm us to the extent that we can.

There are many reasons why people don't want to see their attackers harmed more, but you'll always feel more secure when you resist them.

You can't expect the world to change to your will. There are many more people out there who would love to see you suffer than there are people who want you to have the experience you did. It's acceptable to set boundaries instead of waiting for it to happen.

You have the power to resist more firmly than most people do.

We all have the power to say no, loudly and frequently. Don't underestimate it.

You want to resist more. So don't put off what you need to do until the last minute. Do what's necessary.

I stumbled upon this game through a friend's recommendation and instantly fell in love with its adorable and easy-to-play design, perfect for kids. I purchased it for a mere 99 cents from Amazon's Appstore on its release day, and it's currently on sale for 3.99 after just four days! The game is free to download and play, which is a definite draw. I can see why it's so popular with kids - I had a blast playing it myself!

Review

Game of Life

What's Game of Life?

Game of Life is a colorful, endless game of pattern-matching. The more colors you match, the bigger your game gets. However, the farther away your pattern is from your starting point, the more challenging your journey becomes.

The game's difficulty increases exponentially as you move away from the center. It's impossible to reach the furthest corners if you start from the center. If you can reach them, you score the most points: blue = 0, green = 1, red = 2, purple = 3, and black = 4.

Gameplay

Players arrange colored tiles in a 4x4 grid. In the center of each square are three blue, green, and purple tiles. You can't move horizontally in the center without first moving one square to the right. You need to take a second step to the right to arrange the correct combination of colors. It's not hard, so the more you play, the easier it gets!

Each color has its own set of three starting points. You must match the two tiles closest to each green square to its blue square, and so on. You also need to match the three colors in the remaining three tiles. Since you don't need to make a matching square that connects all your colors, you can have white, red, purple, and black tiles. White tiles and red tiles match each other, and red tiles match with orange and black tiles.

Why is this game so awesome?

It takes just one and a half minutes to learn the rules, and they're clearly stated. If you're familiar with the rules, you can make the same moves as in a normal game. Each player starts with nine colored balls, which you can purchase with your life to start a game. You can move them around, but it depends on how you use them. You can put them in the "Lucky" square and move them around to score more points than your opponent, or put them in the "Tossing" square and toss them to score points.

There's also a scoring table visible from the start of the game. Columns with more colors are worth more points. If you match the colors of the last column, you score 10 additional points. You only get one life, so remember that.

If you score 1,000 points, you win. If you get at least one color in all 12 columns, you score 1,000 points. If you get at least one color in all 12 rows, you score 2,000 points. Even if you get all the colors with no matching in each column or row, you still win.

It's also fun to see how far you've come from the start. If you've moved all the way to the furthest corner and the green square you've matched has one adjacent to it, you've won! The farther away you go, the more points you can score.

The game also works well on iPad, with features like the score chart and life counter.

The federal government is poised to release certain components of the F-35 fighter jets, a move that will optimize costs and facilitate further innovation and competition by the United States military and the commercial sector.

As initially intended, the release of the fighter jets, including spare parts acquired from Lockheed Martin Corp., could save the federal government approximately $700 million during the lifespan of the aircraft and around $300 million annually thereafter, according to federal documents obtained under the Access to Information Act.

However, the release may also open the door to further competition and cost-cutting.

Defence Minister Jason Kenney stated that the government is still deliberating on whether to grant permission to sell certain components, or parts not essential for the jets, to foreign partners, even if they wish to develop their own jet engines.

"The government has not made a final decision yet on that," Kenney said.

In a statement issued after Kenney's comments, Lockheed said it "welcomes" the opportunity to engage in a "full, open, competitive and transparent process that will allow the F-35 program to achieve operational maturity."

A spokeswoman for the Department of National Defence said no decision on any sales has been made at this time, and added that no final decisions about the process would be made until the Liberal government makes the final decision in the summer.

Asked why the government decided to release parts that would not be required for the jets now, rather than the other way around, Kenney said that "the government has taken a very comprehensive approach" that considered "cost effectiveness, security, and cost effectiveness to the Canadian military."

As recently as three weeks ago, it appeared the government would provide all F-35 components to foreign purchasers.

The defence department, under former defence minister Peter MacKay, had proposed that Ottawa was inclined to sell some parts that would be required for the F-35 and other aircraft like it, but that it held off selling parts that have yet to be determined to be required, such as the engines, as part of a wider defence and security review, as the department suggested at the time.

Kenney, speaking to reporters in Ottawa, said the department is now looking at the option of releasing parts that would be considered optional on the plane, such as ground handling systems and electrical components for internal systems and weapons.

He said parts that have yet to be determined "will be part of that review."

The current plan to acquire some components that have yet to be determined is contingent on the government's decision in July, when it is believed to be expected to launch a new cost-benefit analysis for the F-35 project, Kenney said.

The department of national defence is considering the option of releasing certain components -- like the engine -- to foreign buyers after considering the cost effectiveness, security, and cost effectiveness to the Canadian military.

A spokesman for the Office of the Auditor General cautioned, however, that the government "may need to release some non-required technologies and components to potential vendors to enhance Canadian innovation and competitiveness against U.S. competition, as well as to maintain or achieve certain cost advantages."

The auditor general is examining the F-35 program's implementation of procurement policy and rules, procurement rules and programs, contract policy, risk management and risk reduction strategies and policies.

A similar study last year on the aircraft's purchase and training and maintenance costs came to similar conclusions.

The review came after a series of security concerns, including an investigation into the purchase of the F-35 by Saudi Arabia, a move strongly opposed by the United States, Canada and human rights groups.

The Saudi purchase was finalized in March.

Around 17% of nurses, 16% of health assistants and 12% of doctors agreed they felt under pressure at work, while nearly a quarter of patients felt pressure.

PURPOSE:

To explore the relationship between age and risk of recurrent myocardial infarction (MI) and stroke.

METHODS:

We utilized data from a comprehensive health study. The baseline population consisted of participants who returned information on their health and health behaviors over a five-year period. A retrospective cohort analysis of 15,906 women and 3,069 men, aged 50 to 64 years in 1986, was conducted to measure age and risk of MI, stroke, or myocardial infarction (MI) 3, 12, 35, and 48 years later. A separate analysis of the follow-up was performed until death/disability.

RESULTS:

The analysis included 2,638 MI and 3,638 stroke cases. In women, a higher risk of MI (hazard ratio [HR], 1.31; 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.12 to 1.50; risk ratio for the second degree relative to the first) and stroke (HR, 1.30; 95% CI = 1.00 to 1.66; risk ratio for MI relative to MI) occurred with increasing age. In the same cohort, participants in the first decade were 2.3 times more likely to die within the next 10 years (HR for the tenth year, 1.64; 95% CI = 1.24 to 2.09; HR for the ninth year, 2.06 (95% CI = 1.40 to 3.30); HR for the sixth year, 1.88 (95% CI = 1.22 to 2.85); and HR for the fourth year, 1.86 (95% CI = 1.18 to 2.79)). In men, a higher risk of MI was associated with increasing age, and a greater risk of stroke was associated with decreasing age.

LIMITATIONS:

The analysis included only women and men. The cohort used for mortality follow-up was smaller, and differences between the different ages were not reported.

RESULTS:

The overall age at MI was lower in the oldest age group than in the youngest age group. Analyses examining risk of MI at older ages by duration of follow-up revealed that the risk of MI among men 50 to 64 years old was 3.4 (95% CI = 2.3 to 4.3) times higher among those who had left off the study in 2005 than those whose last follow-up data were collected in 1986 (HR = 4.5; 95% CI = 3.9 to 5.3), compared with those who had continued on the study after 1986 (HR = 2.3; 95% CI = 1.8 to 2.9). In women, the risk for MI was 1.5 (95% CI = 1.4 to 1.7; HR for the tenth year, 1.48; 95% CI = 1.19 to 1.89) times higher among those who had left off the study in 2005 than those whose last follow-up data were collected in 1986 (HR = 1.9; 95% CI = 1.1 to 3.0). In men, the risk was 1.6 (95% CI = 1.3 to 1.9) times higher among those who had left off the study in 2005 than those whose last follow-up data were collected in 1986 (HR = 1.8; 95% CI = 1.2 to 2.9). As with stroke, men older than 65 years were 3.3 times more likely to die within 10 years after MI (HR for the tenth year, 3.3; 95% CI = 2.6 to 4.0).

CONCLUSIONS:

In men and women of all ages, risk of MI increases with increasing age; however, when age at cohort entry is taken into consideration, risk of stroke does not increase with aging. Age of entry for follow-up for any cause is important as well, and it should be considered when evaluating age trends.

AUSTIN, Texas - A federal judge recently reviewed a lawsuit against Texas' voter ID law and concluded that the law is unlikely to significantly impact the upcoming presidential election. However, the plaintiffs have the right to seek an injunction to prevent potential issues.

Judge Nelva Gonzales Ramos noted that while the law might cause minor inconveniences, it is unlikely to create significant problems on Election Day. Texas officials and the plaintiffs have debated the necessity of the photo ID requirement, which demands voters present a passport, utility bill, military ID, or non-driver's license with their photo. Opponents argue that the law disproportionately affects poor and minority voters, making it harder for women to vote.

The lawsuit, filed by the Texas Civil Rights Project and the League of United Latin American Citizens, claims the law intimidates, disenfranchises, and unfairly burdens marginalized voters, particularly young, poor, minority, and female voters who need protection the most.

Jessica Vaughan, founder of the Center for Immigration Studies, stated that over one-fifth of voters lack valid proof of citizenship and are at risk of disenfranchisement. Many individuals may delay casting their ballots until their ID is valid, potentially leading to missed deadlines.

Gonzales Ramos did not address the possibility of voters missing deadlines due to voter ID laws in other states. Her order does, however, provide an opportunity for the state to demonstrate that it has taken reasonable steps to ensure no qualified voter is disenfranchised.

Texas law already requires voters to present a valid ID at the polling place if one is not already on file. The state has been asked to prove in court that it will take reasonable steps to prevent those without current IDs from voting, including expediting voter registration and ensuring accurate and up-to-date voter registration forms.

In her order, Ramos stated that the state should prove its efforts to prevent voter fraud, but not use the ID requirement as a guise to further that interest.

Gov. Rick Perry has argued that the ID law is necessary to address the threat of voter fraud, which could alter the outcome of the election if proper safeguards are not implemented.

The plaintiffs, including the Latino advocacy group New Texas Venture, argue that the law discriminates against poor people and minority voters by disproportionately affecting minorities.

Vaughn noted that the law might affect individuals who already have an ID, as they could purchase a cheaper card to carry at the polls and then show a valid ID to vote.

The lawsuit aims to ensure fair voting and prevent barriers against voter fraud, Vaughan emphasized.

The case is United States of America v. Patrick et al, U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas, Case No. 12-cv-3023.

It has been a few cycles since you last encountered B.C.'s Fiscal Strategist Mike de Jong. He's now traversing the Old World, and has a new publication out that presents some captivating concepts for addressing global scarcity.

Now he's returned to Canada to participate in the Fiscal Leaders' Summer Gathering on Scarcity. During a stop in Winnipeg, de Jong appeared before the Manitoba Legislative Assembly. As CBC Radio's The House host Mark Kelley reported, he was asked about the challenges of addressing scarcity in Canada.

De Jong was given the opportunity to elaborate on why we must focus on addressing this issue more effectively. He began by discussing the notion of "fiscal elasticity." This is a technical term used to describe how much we can allocate in government without breaking the bank.

If you want to place a family on a budget, for example, you'd need to have a budget of at least $3,000 a month. De Jong says allocating between $2,000 and $3,000 on that kind of budget is more sustainable than allocating more than $3,000 on "liquid assets."

"We can allocate more, and we have an obligation to do more," he said.

The Minister said there are other ways to solve scarcity. As in other countries, low-income earners in Canada contribute to the system, paying into a social protection program while also working for wages. That way, if they lose their job and cannot find a new one, they'll still have some liquidity in their pocket.

Also, the unemployment insurance system is a good way to help lower-income earners, he said. It's not a guarantee they'll find employment, but if they are laid off and unable to find work, they will be able to collect benefits for a while until their job search is complete. While you can't afford to purchase necessities or fuel, "there are some things we can do in government," he said.

'The solution isn't novel'

B.C. Premier Christy Clark has also been working to address scarcity for some time. In September, she announced legislation in the form of a "Fairness at Night" bill. If passed, it will provide a rebate to families earning up to $50,000 a year. The government says the bill will be funded by eliminating a 15 per cent tax on the purchase of fuel and electricity with an automatic tax rebate of 10 per cent once a household's annual household expenditure surpasses $200,000.

But de Jong wants to go even further. He thinks we can eliminate fuel and electricity taxes completely by 2019.

In a speech last year, de Jong said it's time to end fuel taxes completely because they're hurting Canadian families. "This problem won't be solved by a handful of governments. If we do not make the change now, it will become a more complicated problem in the future," he said.

With all that liquidity to manage, it is tempting to just focus on distributing cash. But de Jong is also realistic.

"The solution isn't novel," he said. "Many solutions have been on the table, debated. People have been talking about this for a very long time. It's time to make serious and sustained investments."

De Jong doesn't think that there's "any such thing as a scarcity income." He said to take care of the "absolute poorest" who need the most help, we should focus on the low-income taxpayers whose take-home pay is "below the scarcity line."

There's a lot of liquidity to be managed, but the first priority should be to break the cycle of scarcity. If we don't make changes in the short timeframe, we risk having a "dramatic" increase in scarcity, he told the Legislative Assembly last month.

The importance of understanding the legal treatment of sexual harassment cannot be overstated. To grasp the distinction between criminal and civil harassment, I have examined several Supreme Court cases, focusing on the language used to differentiate between conduct that violates criminal law and conduct that is only civil. The Connick v. Myers (1975) case is particularly significant in this regard.

The court's distinction between criminal and civil harassment is rooted in the concept of a crime against the person. Criminal harassment is considered a serious offense because it deprives the victim of their fundamental right to a safe and respectful environment. On the other hand, civil harassment is viewed as a civil wrong, rather than a criminal act, and is often characterized by unwelcome sexual attention.

The court's definition of criminal harassment emphasizes the need for a connection between the harassment and the victim's job, profession, or place of residence. Additionally, the harassment must be severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive, creating a hostile or intimidating environment that prevents the victim from accessing an accommodation, benefit, or service.

In contrast, civil harassment can be characterized by unwelcome sexual attention, even if it does not rise to the level of criminal harassment. The court has held that civil harassment must be both severe and persistent, creating a hostile work environment that affects the victim's ability to perform their job.

It is essential to understand the legal implications of sexual harassment and how it is treated by the courts. The Supreme Court's decisions provide valuable insights into the complexities of this issue and the need for a nuanced approach to addressing sexual harassment in the workplace and beyond.

The researchers used computational methods, including Bayesian and Gaussian methods, to determine the number of dendrites each type of neuron has. The study found that the number of neurons in the brain may be a good indicator of the brain's computational power. The human brain has a vast amount of information, with some 1 trillion individual neurons, and each neuron's job is to process this information, allowing the brain to take in a lot of information and convert it into signals for action without causing over-thinking.

The researchers also developed a way to separate out the dendrites from the neurons, which is important for accurately measuring the size of the synapses. The study's findings have important implications for our understanding of the brain's processing power and its ability to handle complex information.

In the realm of NetHack, a turn-based adventure unfolds. Each player embarks on a unique journey, with four categories of actions: actions, turns, commands, and events.

Actions are initiated by players, comprising a primary action and optional modifiers. The player's attributes are limited to a single value, except for specific attributes. Actions can be triggered by selecting or typing a command, such as:

"Unleash a mighty roar upon the beast"

or

"Consume the corpse of the fallen warrior"

Note that only the actions typed or selected will change.

The effects of actions vary depending on the modifier. The more modifiers, the greater the impact.

Completing an action can be achieved through two methods: pressing the desired key or typing a command after the action is complete. The more modifiers typed within a single action, the more complex the outcome.

For example, if you type "Rest for a moment", the wizard will rest for the usual time and awaken in a different room. It is advisable to wait a brief moment before typing commands, especially if not all possibilities are chosen.

To select an available action, use the mouse to select the desired key and press Enter. If you select an action by pressing Escape or Cancel, a menu will appear. Click the desired option and type a command after the action. Once typed, the menu will disappear, and the selected action will take effect.

To perform multiple actions consecutively, press Shift+Enter and Ctrl+Enter simultaneously. If an action key is already held down, you must move the mouse to the next key to complete the action.

You may also need to press a key twice to initiate a character action: once to select the action key and once to start the action. Otherwise, the mouse will not register the action.

Each action has a time limit, typically ranging from 1 to 3 turns, depending on the action type and difficulty. For example, completing the "Dying" action requires pressing the right alt key, then Enter, and releasing the key.

For a large number of actions, if you must wait longer than 3 seconds for someone to finish their actions, you will receive a message from the dungeon master.

When an action is completed, a message appears on the top screen:

Researchers at the University of Arizona and the University of Georgia have recently published findings on the calorie content of coffee. Their study, which analyzed data from over 30,000 students, reveals some astonishing statistics.

The researchers' report employed data from students who shared information about their diets and consumed various types of coffee. They calculated the calories and sugar content of each coffee type using two methods.

Firstly, they compared the calorie and sugar content of individual coffee types to typical beverages. For instance, a 12-ounce cup of Folgers coffee contains approximately 200 calories of sugar and 45 calories of carbohydrates. In contrast, a Starbucks coffee mug has about 350 calories and 41 calories of carbohydrates. The researchers also calculated the calorie content of different levels of sweetness and found that sweetened coffee has roughly the same calorie count, regardless of whether it's labeled as black or light.

Secondly, the researchers examined the caffeine content in various coffee samples using mass spectrometry. They discovered that the caffeine levels in coffee are surprisingly high, with a single cup containing approximately two to three times the amount of caffeine typically found in a standard diet.

This explains why a double shot of coffee tends to have more caffeine than a single cup, which would contain only 20% of the caffeine found in a half-full, half-empty cup. The researchers also found that the calorie-to-sugar ratio in coffee varies significantly, ranging from 4:1 in Folgers to 6:1 in Starbucks. This means that for every sugar molecule in a cup of coffee, there are six calories. For a typical 6-cup serving, the researchers estimate a sugar-to-calorie ratio of 5:1.

The study found an average of nearly 1.4 teaspoons of carbohydrates in a 6-cup serving of Folgers coffee.

The researchers emphasized that their estimates were rough and based on limited data, as the samples contained varying amounts of caffeine. However, one conclusion appears clear: coffee consumption may increase the risk of overweight and obesity if consumed in excessive quantities.

The outcome of the recent EU referendum has sparked a lot of interest in how people got to the polling stations. Of course, there are many ways to get to the polling stations, including cars, buses, railroads, and so on. We will have the opportunity in the next Parliament to analyze the data and make some interesting conclusions and comparisons about the different ways people got to the polls.

Here are some ideas for analysis (I will certainly be sharing them) to look at over the next Parliament:

The most important issue

One question that comes up often in the campaign is what percentage of voters were from London or the West Midlands and where they were coming from. If the UK has a Remain-voting core, how many votes were won by people not from London or the West Midlands that were voting against Remain even though they had a large share of those votes?

One source of data for me is the Electoral Commission's data on voters registered on polling day and votes. If you sort by area of the UK, you get a nice, clear picture of the main areas of England where people were voting Leave for the first time. For each of the 30 areas shown here, you can see if and how many other people voted Leave from that area, and where they were coming from.

For the 30 areas shown here, there are three classes of voters: those who voted for the first time, those who had voted once or more, and those who had never voted. If you sort by areas, you can see which voting bloc was strongest in some areas. And if you filter just in on the Leave-voting voters and remove them from the areas with the most people voting to leave, you see which areas had the highest proportion of Leave voters.

What we see, immediately, is that the main areas for Leave voters are in the West Midlands, although there is some strong support in the South West, London and South East as well. As for people voting to leave the EU for the first time, the most obvious story is Scotland. But there is strong support in England, Wales and Northern Ireland as well.

So what is the strongest area in which Leave was strongest and in which areas voters were most likely to have voted Leave for the first time? That is England, and we see it is London on both the Leave and Remain side.

The most important issues for people who came to vote for the first time, even to vote for a Conservative Party Member of Parliament in 2015, were the NHS (both the Leave in England and Leave in Wales data points are over-filled). The immigration issue is also important as, by its own numbers, Scotland and London have high shares of new immigrants who arrived on the basis of European Union membership and who are eligible for free education and healthcare, as well as other rights at home, like maternity care and disability benefit. Immigration is a very strong issue for British people who were new voters in 2017.

Another important issue is the EU/Wales question. The Leave voters who didn't have a UK birth/nationality matched up exactly to those who came from the EU or from outside the EU. That is, people in both parts of the U.K. (and Wales) who didn't speak any English at the time of the Brexit vote voted the same way as those who did.

However, there is one other question that is worth looking at as well, which relates to the number of people who had voted for the first time. In England and Wales, the two areas with the largest Remain-voting cores voted the closest against Leave in 2017. That is the South East and Wales. In London, that is the South West (including West London. Of course, this is excluding London from the numbers and I am not sure what to make of that. Perhaps there will be an argument that the South Central of London voted with the Leave side in a much bigger way than those in West London. Regardless, in London you get the sense that the areas that voted the most for Brexit were places with big left-wing electorates, the kind that would have been more likely to vote to leave under the same circumstances.

London was always close

What this also tells us is that London was always a close vote. When you look at the map of the vote by area (Figure 1), you can see how very quickly it began to swing in favour of Leave as the London media and politicians began to focus on the immigration issue. But the real action came from those areas on the London fringe. That makes sense: in other words those areas that are the most affluent, educated and cosmopolitan.

Fixed-income investment vehicles, including bond exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and traditional bond mutual funds, offer investors a way to diversify their portfolios and potentially earn a steady income stream. While both types of investments have their advantages and disadvantages, understanding the differences between them can help investors make informed decisions. Here are some key points to consider:

Advantages of bond ETFs:

* Economical: Bond ETFs typically have lower expense ratios than traditional bond mutual funds, resulting in lower fees for investors.
* Tax-efficient: Bond ETFs tend to generate fewer capital gains, making them a more tax-efficient option.
* Flexible: Bond ETFs can be traded throughout the day, allowing investors to quickly respond to changing market conditions.

Disadvantages of bond ETFs:

* Limited customization: Bond ETFs are designed to track a specific bond market index, limiting investors' ability to tailor their portfolios to their individual goals and risk tolerance.
* Credit risk: While bond ETFs diversify individual bond risk, the ETF itself may still be exposed to credit risk if underlying bonds default.

Advantages of traditional bond mutual funds:

* Professional management: Actively managed bond mutual funds offer the potential for outperformance of bond market benchmarks.
* Customization: Traditional bond mutual funds allow investors to tailor their portfolios to their individual goals and risk tolerance.

Disadvantages of traditional bond mutual funds:

* Higher costs: Traditional bond mutual funds typically have higher expense ratios than bond ETFs, reducing investors' returns.
* Limited transparency: Traditional bond mutual funds may not disclose their holdings as frequently as bond ETFs, making it more difficult for investors to understand the fund's risk profile and investment strategy.

The only thing I'm not fond of is that it would take too much time to respond - there are so many other questions I'd like to ask in a simple one! And I'm going to provide my answer in two posts. It seems that I'll give my answer once, and then answer it again in a second post - first, I'll share it here because there's a lot to say in just one post, and then I'll edit it to make it more useful. A lot is said. Let me start with the first part: it's quite straightforward - no, GHC doesn't give a compile-time error on isfinite?. I'm not sure why I'm surprised by this. As you may suspect, if there is no isfinite?, you can write: -- Inflate a bunch of data: data Double = Double { _value :: Integer } I know from my experience that if you start with a type with no infix operators, you will get an error when you try to put it into GHCi. But I have a completely different surprise. If you write your own isfinite? (or if a user just gives you a type name, e.g. Int ) then (even if you can't see the message) you get an error: -- Inflate a bunch of data: data Double = Double { _value :: Double } You can see the actual error from the error message: $ ghci Prelude> inflate (Double <interactive>:3:10) The inferred type has an implicit parameter for a constructor of data instance Double. This is a known compiler bug, and fixed in GHC 6.12.1 (which is what I've used). However, it doesn't mean you can't use setq to do this kind of thing. You can write: -- Inflate a bunch of data: data Double = Double { _value :: Double } Inflate Double [3,10] In order to make this compile, you need to make a change to your code: inflate (Double <interactive>:3:10) If you've never done this before, I'd really recommend going through the official tutorial first, then going through it again and trying it out with some examples. In the meantime, make sure the "Inflate Double" (or whatever type is being inflated) has the data instance Double in its type level: -- Inflate a bunch of data: data Double = Double { _value :: Double } -- Inflate the first type instance, and the error: inflate (Double <interactive>:3:10) Now, just like what you would have written for setq, you can inflate a bunch of data instances simultaneously. If you want to use the inflate commands above together with setq, then write these two pieces of code: data Double = Double { _value :: Double } inflateDouble :: (Read a ) => Double -> (Read a) inflateDouble n = runResourceT $ do print $ readDouble n inflateDouble $ "2.0" :: Int inflateDouble 2.0 -- works inflateDouble :: (Set a) => Read a -> [Set a] Inflate Double [3,10] -- works; [3, 10] is in the list; [3,8] is out, "1.2" is in inflateDouble :: (Show a) => Double -> (Show a) inflateDouble n = let _n' = n <| char'' in putStrLn $ show n' |> setLn

Free thinkers are the ones that have the absolute right to define what it means to be free, since free thinkers are the ones who came up with all the standards for what constitutes freedom.

I recall being 16 years old during my first semester at school, feeling utterly unenthusiastic about the entire experience. I wasn't studying for a specific degree at the time, but rather focusing on continuing my education. My class was exploring the subject of medicine, and I had recently relocated to the UK for my second year. Unfortunately, the teachers didn't prove to be very supportive, with one in particular exhibiting a rather authoritarian attitude that discouraged asking questions. I shared my concerns with my parents, but they didn't seem to believe me. The exam itself consisted of a list of questions, which I managed to complete despite the challenges I faced.

I remember receiving a poor grade on the exam, which was quite disheartening. I was worried that if something went awry with the results, I might never be accepted into med school. In retrospect, I still believe that the teachers lacked a deep understanding of the material and were unable to think critically. I also recall feeling quite upset with myself, wondering if perhaps the teachers were simply struggling with their own personal issues.

As I began my journey as a young doctor, I was only 16 at the time. The concept of "medicine" was just being introduced, and I was excited to explore various subjects. This was before I'd even completed a year of school. I can still remember the thrill of being a new student and embarking on a new curriculum.

Initially, the new syllabus didn't seem too overwhelming, and I enjoyed studying the science of medicine. I assumed that I would perform well simply by focusing on the scientific aspects of medicine. However, as the classes progressed, I began to find the material increasingly dull. What made things worse was that my peers started to look down on me because I wasn't achieving high grades. Everyone would mock me for not performing well on exams, and I was confused because I was actually doing well in my classes. I didn't realize how challenging it was to excel in med school. I thought I was simply a bright, patient, and kind individual. After my first two years at university, I began to feel like I had failed, as I didn't receive high grades in any of my courses.

I also recall trying to improve my grades by spending almost an entire month preparing for exams. I worked extremely hard, but I still received poor grades. I would often make excuses for my performance, telling myself that I'd been practicing and doing well in class, but wasn't putting in enough effort. I would also try to shift the blame, claiming that I'd had a terrible summer or didn't have enough time to study.

Despite my best efforts, I continued to struggle with my grades. As a freshman in my first three years at university, I expected to work hard and study diligently. However, I didn't seem to have the ambition to learn about medicine. I was simply focused on getting good grades and not thinking about the subject itself.

I eventually lost all hope in the system and decided to try to skip my final exams. This was my first major mistake in medicine. I almost lost the opportunity to become a doctor. Instead of pursuing my dreams, I decided to give up and forget everything I'd learned about medicine. My grades were abysmal at this point, with a dismal 5% average. I lost all respect for my teachers, who never provided me with any meaningful feedback.

After the exams, I stopped attending classes altogether. I told them all to leave me alone, as I knew they didn't understand the material and treated me poorly. Everyone seemed surprised when I shared the reason for skipping my exams. I was convinced that I wasn't the only one who had done so, as it seemed like every class had a few students who were struggling.

The reason I skipped my exams was that my friends and I have always performed well academically. I would receive excellent grades and gain acceptance into top universities. However, I don't have any hope for these opportunities because I don't believe that anyone truly understands the difficulty of achieving good grades in medicine. I don't think it's my fault; I'm simply not trying hard enough.

It's been nearly nine years since I failed my exams. There have been significant changes in my life since then, and I still have hopes for a future where I can become a doctor. However, I have a lot to learn and still have a long way to go.

Delhi: Following a petition by the National Commission for Women and calls from MPs and NGOs, the Rajya Sabha passed a bill to address workplace behavior. The new law is seen as a step towards ensuring a safe and respectful work environment. 

As the government considers strengthening workplace laws, the amendment provides for a minimum of two years of community service for inappropriate behavior. A judge or Magistrate will have the authority to impose any other punishment prescribed by law.

Any person found guilty of inappropriate behavior will also be held accountable for an offence punishable with a maximum fine. An employee who fails to report any incident of inappropriate behavior to their supervisor will also face consequences.

The bill makes it a criminal offence to engage in any inappropriate behavior in a private setting if such act is done for the purpose of committing any other offence or for any other purpose which is an offence under the Indian Penal code.

"Our government is committed to providing equal opportunities. We have long wanted to pass a law to address workplace behavior. This is the best way to do so, without taking unnecessarily harsh measures," said Parliamentary Affairs Minister M Venkaiah Naidu.
