The facility, set to open in early June, will accommodate approximately 2,000 researchers, staff, and their families.

To make the facility an attractive option, the California Institute of Technology created the Integrated Science and Technology Program (ISTP). The ISPP is a prestigious partnership between the UC ICT and the California Institute of Technology to establish a cutting-edge facility for teaching students and postdocs to conduct research in fields like cancer, renewable energies, biofuels, and complex technologies. The center is designed to train high-caliber researchers on the forefront of research. UCI has established a unique partnership with the UCI ICT to provide students and postdocs access to the latest research at UC Irvine. It's also the first public-private partnership among top universities to support postdocs with a faculty mentor, peer advisor, and research funding.

In a recent announcement, Dr. Harshvardhan Anand, the director of the ISPP and a professor of electrical and computer engineering and mechanical engineering at UCI, emphasized the significance of the facility. "UCI and Caltech's combined engineering and technology programs already bring together top minds to generate breakthroughs in research by teaching them how to develop complex technology. By forming an innovative partnership that offers a generous support package, we'll enable our own students to become even more innovative and innovative in science and engineering research," Anand said.

The ISPP will consist of four separate facilities on campus. Students will have access to these laboratories and research centers under one umbrella: the Integrated Science and Technology Center (ISTC), to support undergraduate student research. The California Institute for Telecommunications and Information Technology (Cal-TIC) will provide support for graduate student research, and the Advanced Simulation Facility for Science and Engineering (ASFSE) will provide support for students conducting postdoctoral research. Anand said ASFSE will be home to the largest computer-aided design (CAD) lab in the state, with 30,000 square feet of computing labs and a 300 square foot state-of-the-art computer lab.

The ISPP will allow students to access the laboratory space and equipment of the Cal-TIC lab during the summer, and will serve as a training facility for faculty and postdocs. "The program at UC Irvine is unique not only with regard to the amount of money we're providing, but also the support we're providing," Anand said. "Many students and postdocs arrive at UC Irvine with a background in engineering and engineering technology that requires a great deal of professional training and work before they can graduate with the required credentials, which requires at least a bachelor's degree. The ISPP will help prepare students to take in this new world by providing expert scientific advice based on industry standards, which will have a lasting impact on their careers."

UCI ICT has developed a robust business plan for ISPP. The ISPP is expected to cost approximately $30 million, split between the five facilities. A key strategy to fund this initiative, Anand said, will be to leverage the UCI's vast network of alumni and donors, which "will ensure continued funding over an extended period of time."

The new facilities are expected to become operational on June 1, and will be open to the public starting the day after.

Recently, I stumbled upon an intriguing article on www.lifehacker.com, which piqued my interest in the concept of a "vitamin D flush."

Vitamin D is a hormone produced by the body, crucial for maintaining overall well-being by regulating genes that prevent cell damage.

Given the limited availability of vitamin D within our system, it is essential to balance its levels through various means.

Here are some examples that have been linked to reduced disease risk, particularly among the elderly:

1. Achieve a healthy weight

Research from the University of Alabama suggests that increased vitamin D intake (either through food or supplements) is associated with lower levels of metabolic syndrome, including high blood pressure, waist circumference, and blood glucose levels.

Vitamin D supplements may not only benefit your health but also enhance your overall sense of well-being.

2. Build muscle and lose weight

Many individuals struggle with weight loss, unaware of the key factors that contribute to weight gain.

Surprisingly, the primary cause of weight gain is not the quantity of calories consumed but rather the type of foods and beverages ingested.

It is the quality of food, not the quantity, that matters.

The study found that overweight women continued to consume two foods strongly linked to weight gain – bread and sugary sodas – without increasing their calorie intake.

They also consumed high fructose corn syrup (HFCS) in significant amounts.

The results showed that adults who reduced their processed food intake by at least 25% experienced greater weight loss and improved metabolic rates compared to those who did not.

3. Achieve weight loss quickly

The notion that a vitamin D flush is only suitable for younger adults stems from the fact that the body requires time to accumulate sufficient vitamin D levels.

Therefore, it is essential to take vitamin D regularly, either through food or supplements, to maintain optimal levels.

If your diet does not provide sufficient vitamin D, you can consider supplements or vitamin D-rich foods like leafy greens and fatty fish.

4. Consume vitamin D-rich foods

To obtain the necessary amounts of vitamin D, you will need to consume a variety of foods, including leafy greens and fatty fish like salmon and mackerel.

It is crucial to consume these foods in larger quantities than usual to ensure optimal vitamin D levels.

This will help your body function optimally and promote overall health.

5. Be mindful of your skin

If you have oily skin, it may be due to consuming foods rich in linoleic acid, a type of fatty acid. Linoleic acid can help maintain a healthy, radiant complexion.

Drinking vitamin D-rich foods can help maintain a healthy, radiant complexion.

Vitamin D is a hormone with numerous benefits, many of which can enhance the health of both you and your loved ones. Its importance in maintaining overall well-being is undeniable.

A few days ago, I stumbled upon an interesting factoid shared by a couple of blogs I follow. As someone who often finds themselves the only Asian in a room, I'm always eager to learn more about others. In this case, I discovered some fascinating statistics about Asian Americans.

According to recent data, Asian Americans make up 2.6% of the adult population, 1.5% of the workforce, and 1.8% of the total college student population. This is compared to 2.7% of the overall U.S. population, 3.5% of the workforce, and 6% of college students.

What's striking is that Asian Americans have a much higher rate of college education compared to other racial groups. On average, they earn 10% more than the general population, and in some cases, they even outpace whites. This is an impressive achievement, but it raises questions about how to explain this disparity to non-Asian colleagues.

For instance, a white male doctor earns 6.9 times the median wage for full-time white males. There are approximately 4.2 million Asians in the U.S., and given the time it takes to complete an undergraduate degree, it's likely that a significant number of Asian Americans will graduate and find employment.

For every Asian American woman who completes her undergraduate degree, 4.5 women become Asian American doctorate recipients. This is a remarkable statistic, especially when considering that white, working-class women earn 6.3 times what white working-class men earn during their adult work lives.

If an Asian American didn't have an Ivy League education, about 3,700 Asian Americans would have become doctors, scientists, engineers, lawyers, or other professionals by the time they were 40 years old, earning an average of $40,300 in today's dollars.

I also found interesting statistics on racial disparities in STEM fields on the Institute of International Education website. The data shows that Asian Americans are not overrepresented in STEM fields, with only 7% of all Asians enrolled in STEM courses compared to 28% for Hispanics, 15% for blacks, 8% for whites, and 3% for Americans.

Comparing the overall adult Asian population to the adult white population suggests the same story about Asian Americans. In 2010, only 2.5% of the Asian American adult population had an undergraduate degree in a STEM field compared to 3.8% of whites and 4.6% of Hispanics.

I'm not sure why white, working-class Americans don't tend to become scientists and engineers, but it's clear that this pattern is not unique to Asian Americans or any other racial group.

The art of self-preservation is a universal language, but it's not a one-size-fits-all approach. When it comes to sustenance, most of us have learned to be cautious and discerning. However, a recent study in the field of entomology reveals that orb-weaving spiders have a distinct perspective on defense.

Researchers have discovered that the aggressive behavior of these spiders is driven by their need to attract prey. The team found that spiders only engage in cannibalism when they are faced with a substantial and delectable meal.

It's well established that orb-weaving spiders have a voracious appetite, and this species is commonly found in many parts of the world. However, the researchers suggest that there is still much to be learned about why spiders choose to consume their prey.

Co-author Professor Andrew Barron, from the University of Cambridge, notes, "This study suggests that spiders have a unique sense of reward and reward potential compared to other insects. This finding has significant implications for future studies on brain function and animal behavior."

The researchers conducted their study using spiders from the family Pholcidae in the Philippines, Uganda, and Indonesia. They found that cannibalism was often triggered by the presence of a substantial meal. The spiders were placed in plastic containers where they could receive sugar water, fruit powder, or insects such as ants. They also placed the spiders in the same containers, but denied them access to food if they attempted to eat.

The study revealed that the spiders would often cannibalize any other spiders in the containers as soon as they realized a food source was nearby. However, the spiders were more likely to eat their prey if there was a strong, tasty meal present. The team also found that other animals were more reluctant to harm the spiders and were more likely to leave the room if the spiders attacked them.

In one experiment, spiders that attacked an ant species were repeatedly chased off by ants that did not harm them. The spiders, in turn, would sometimes attack any ants that tried to reach them. Professor Matthew Turner, from University College London, notes, "This work provides insight into why these spiders tend to kill each other. One of its findings is that the spiders are more likely to cannibalize when faced with an actual meal, rather than other sources of food. While this may seem shocking, it is in fact something these spiders have evolved to do."

The study's findings contribute to the growing trend of animals engaging in cannibalism. In 2010, scientists discovered that chimpanzees would kill and eat their own kind as part of "culture." In 2015, scientists found that ants engage in "co-operative killing" during battles, and that these killings are more common when the victim has a tasty reward.

The New York State Constitution contains a provision that ensures states have the power to regulate their own affairs without federal interference. This provision was intended to protect the rights of states and prevent the federal government from overstepping its bounds. In 1813 and 1816, the New York Constitution was amended to provide that the state legislature was under no obligation to pass additional capital punishment bills. These amendments were adopted to allow the legislature to focus on local issues and ensure that the state remained free from federal interference.

In 1824, a change in law by the Legislature allowed the legislature to enact death penalty bills without any constitutional sanction. Governor Nelson stated that the death penalty was used for the "crime of homicide" and a "small number of criminals." New York was not a "death penalty state," as some states in the South were, and therefore it is understandable how people came to think that New York should abolish the death penalty. Governor Nelson claimed that his decision to allow the death penalty bill was made based on the principle of the whole system of government and the duty imposed on the Governor of this State, to do what he should see the constitution prescribe.

When the new Death Penalty Act was enacted in 1824, New York was not a death penalty state. In 1851, the New York Supreme Court ruled in Aptheker v. Commonwealth that the 1821 amendment had been misinterpreted and that this amendment did not guarantee the abolition of capital punishment. The New York constitution, as construed in the Aptheker decision, did not prevent legislatures from enacting death penalty laws, but it did not require them to do so.

After Aptheker, however, it became increasingly common for legislatures to enact a law abolishing the death penalty without a constitutional amendment. In the years between 1851 and the late 1920's, nine states enacted death penalty laws without an amendment in 1854, 1858, 1872, 1882, 1891, 1910, 1913, and 1926. For some of these laws, the death penalty was repealed for certain offenses and the law was changed to include a provision to repeal it entirely for other offenses. Some states, such as Iowa and Minnesota, adopted a similar constitutional amendment that required death penalties for all crimes without specifying the specific crimes that are so prohibited.

In 1922, when the New York legislature considered the New York Death Penalty Act, a law to repeal the death penalty for all crimes, the New York Bar Association advised the State of New York to enact a constitutional amendment because repealing some crimes, but not others, "would defeat the great purpose of the adoption of the American constitution."

During the early 1920's, an argument arose in the New York legislature as to whether the death penalty, even capital punishment for murder, could be constitutional.

The World Health Organisation says that approximately one-third of the global population has access to genetically modified seeds.

The organisation has been monitoring the progress of genetically modified cultivation for 14 years and says that the practice is widespread, but the safety concerns are still being addressed.

The organisation, part of the International Agency for Research on Cancer, says that while GM crops are generally considered safe, there are still risks to health and the environment that need to be assessed.

Two groups of studies are examining the long-term effects of GM crops on human health, but the IARC group has concluded that GM crops are "probably safe" and that there is no strong evidence to suggest they cause harm.

The UN has been working on GM crops for about 20 years, and scientific research in favor of GM food has been gaining ground since the early 1990s.

A 1996 discovery linked GM rice to tumors in rats, which brought attention to the GM rice that had been growing since the 1950s and caused a panic among rice farmers.

However, this incident was not the start. Over the years, a number of scientific experiments have been conducted with GM foods.

In 1998, scientists at the University of California Berkeley found that rats fed on GM potatoes developed larger tumors than the control set.

This led to further studies to verify the findings and confirm that GM potatoes are a toxic food.

Around the same time, a study in South Africa found a significant link between GM potato production and the rise of GM herbicide-resistant weeds.

Independent studies in South Africa, Israel, and Argentina also verified that herbicide-resistant weeds had increased.

The International Year of Non-GM Crops began in 1999, and since then, studies have been investigating the risks that GM crops might pose.

Scientists have expressed support for GM crops, but are concerned that the growing body of scientific evidence may lead to a blanket ban.

Professor Michael Antoniou, of Sheffield University, believes that the scientific consensus is clear.

"I agree, the evidence is overwhelmingly that we can feed the world and feed it well with a mix of organic and conventional approaches," says Antoniou. "We would be far better off trying to increase the total number of crops on the planet, but try to increase diversity through organic breeding. That can make our crops more resistant."

Antoniou argues that it is not the responsibility of farmers to protect the environment, and does not mean they should have the rights over the natural ecosystem that gives a farmer their livelihood.

In a joint letter in February, over 100 scientists, including some from the IARC group, wrote in support of GM food.

"The research clearly establishes that GM crops have not damaged the environment in any way: GM methods have been shown to have fewer environmental impacts than their conventional counterparts.

"The evidence from research to date shows that GM crops do not present new risks, but are instead being developed to provide an important tool to protect the environment. This research further validates the scientific method that is being used to develop GMOs, helping farmers to protect the environment and ensure a sustainable food supply," the letter adds.

The UK has banned GM food, but the government has a positive approach to GM and has a policy of regulatory authorisation.

In November last year, the UK launched a consultation on whether to ban GM food from being grown here.

The government says the evidence shows there is no need for GM crops to be taken forward to the UK, and that this ban would only stop them that they would otherwise have been given approval to grow here.

At the very least, a ban on the commercial cultivation of GM foods in general is the obvious answer, if we want to ensure we can feed the world properly.

What is Spock? How does it work?

Spock is a lightweight and portable tool for writing tests in any language. It is ideal for integration testing.

One of Spock's most useful features is its ability to run on any platform that supports JUnit.

A typical example of a Spock test can look like this:

{ TestMethod test_method() should be_called with_items(..., "test_name") with_items(..., "test_item" ) with_items(..., "another_test_method", "test_item_item_test_method", "another_test_item_test_item_test_item" ) with_items(..., "test_id", "test_name", true) with_items(..., "test_method_name") }

In this example, we assume that item 2 of the list, or its test method test_method() will be called. With this information, we can use Spock (and JUnit) to execute our test.

Why does Spock work well with tests?

There are various reasons why Spock works well with automation tests, but I won't go into detail here.

In general, if you are writing automated tests using any scripting language (e.g. Python, Javascript, Ruby, Erlang, etc) using Spock is an excellent choice:

Spock's integration tests take advantage of the language's standard modules (e.g. exceptions, objects, interfaces, etc)

Spock's unit tests follow the same conventions as regular unit tests, and so are easier to reason about because you can use existing, well-tested tools

If you only pass one test, Spock will not complain because you are passing only one test, but it will stop at the first test failure.

How do we actually use Spock?

Spock uses Java 8 Language Specification for Test Specifications to help us write correct implementations. We can use this test type to build a set of tests in any language in the world with Spock.

Let's run Spock in a simple example:

java -cp./test/java8-spec-all.jar:./spock.jar main.java

We get the following results:

This shows that we have just four unit tests, one for each file. But how did Spock know that the unit tests are called main.java, and the other three unit tests will not be executed?

What happened here is the following diagram shows how the Spock runtime checks if we're going over the JUnit's "rule" of being executed tests.

The "rule" is a great tool for unit testing, with various extensions that make it easier and more robust, but Spock never looks to this rule and checks that our tests execute as expected.

The "rule" is used instead of trying to guess what the current test case should look like, because it is more accurate and more robust (to the JUnit).

But what if we made two tests?

java -cp./test/java8-spec-all.jar:./spock.jar main.java java -cp./test/java8-spec-all.jar:./spock.jar other.java

This gets you the following results:

Here, it's harder to tell what tests belong into the first test, and hence, Spock will only execute tests from the second test.

Spock makes the most likely thing possible: using a scripting language for writing unit tests in Java and the other parts of the Java platform.

We will not write our own tests with Spock, using this tool will only save time on manual debugging, as we should be writing Java code in tests instead of Spock's Java.

China is one of the few countries that emphasizes the importance of authenticity in its cultural products. Cultural workers face the challenge of verifying the accuracy of recreated historical works, as well as the potential for reinterpretation.

"Authenticity has been a pressing concern for a considerable period," said Wei Wang, chairman of the Chinese cultural watchdog Wen Wancheng, at a recent international conference marking the 30th anniversary of the publication of "Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution" in China.

He is also known for his candid opinions on Mao's legacy and Deng's policies. The fact that his statements are now being echoed by foreign critics is evidence that he is "undermining his own stance," Mr. Wen said in a later interview.

"It is only natural for the culture industry to evolve," Mr. Wang said. "We are just beginning this trend."

"The 'Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution,' in its essence, was a struggle for social justice," it added.

However, it is not accurate to describe the Cultural Revolution as a complete catastrophe: many of its most fervent supporters now argue it saved China and paved the way for Deng's reforms.

The first law of fluid dynamics, also known as Newton's First Law, states that a constant force acting on an object's center of mass causes the object to move in a straight line. However, when applied to liquids, this law becomes more complex, as the center of mass is no longer fixed at the center of the object.

In this scenario, there are two centers of mass, two moving objects, which can be at different locations. The center of mass is no longer the center of gravity, and a third center of mass is formed, which is described by the center of gravity. This concept is essential in understanding fluid simulation.

To illustrate this, let's consider a fluid object with a height (H) that depends on its density (D). The equation we will solve is:

H = f(D)

where H is the height of the object, D is the thickness of the object, and f is a function that describes the relationship between height and density.

By solving this equation, we can determine the density of the fluid object, which is a function of its volume and height. The bottom and top of the object can have the same density, but the top is an imaginary point that moves with the fluid.

The same concept applies to the center of mass, which can be below or above the surface of the bottom or top, depending on the density of the object.

Using Newton's Second Law, we can solve for the density of the fluid object, and we can also determine the speed of the fluid object, which is a function of the fluid density.

By plugging these equations together, we can analyze the behavior of the fluid object and understand how the center of mass moves in response to changes in density and speed.

For example, if the top of the object has a density of 0.1 and the bottom has a density of 0.75, and the top is moving at 3 m/s, then the center of mass of the bottom would be above the center of mass of the top. This is because the top has a higher density and is moving faster.

By understanding these principles, we can simulate the behavior of fluids in various scenarios, from simple flows to complex turbulence.

However, hemp's growth is being hindered by the United States, where demand has begun to outstrip supply, yet remains limited due to a lack of product development. This lack can be attributed to the absence of a unified regulatory framework and federal and state laws protecting growers in both legal and illegal industries. The results are encouraging and underscore the need for a shift in focus toward hemp's potential for sustainable agriculture.

"Now, we're returning to that tradition of making it legal again to grow and sell industrial hemp in this country. Abdullah, who is also an IT teacher, has created a petition on change.org titled "Google to Remove The image of 5 year-old Mohammed being burnt alive on their search results." The petition currently has over 2,500 supporters.

Although most of his students are male, Abdullah said that he would teach his female students to learn how to get organised, to be strong and to do what is right.

The most recent information about this topic can be found at Windows.Security.AccessControl.IsSystem.

Is System a System account or a user account?

A security feature known as IsSystem helps determine whether a requested resource or a system function result originates from a system process or a local process. For more information, see the article on Creating and Managing Resource Ownerships.

By default, IsSystem is set to the SYSTEM designation.

For instance, if the requested resource is an existing process, a user process, or the result of a system function, IsSystem sets the value to SYSTEM. The system function is typically accessed through the CreateThread function.

IsSystem does not always signify that a resource is not an output of a system process. Additional options are available, which are described below. For a comprehensive overview, see the Security Overview article.

If IsSystem indicates that a process requires privileges to access a local process or if no privilege is necessary, then IsSystem is set to the local system privilege.

If IsSystem indicates that a resource requires local privilege, then IsSystem is set to the resource's local privilege.

A significant milestone has been reached, marking the 30th anniversary of the signing of the Civil Rights Act, a landmark piece of legislation that has had a profound impact on our nation's trajectory. This historic achievement has been met with widespread acclaim and has significantly shaped the course of our economy and society.

However, some individuals see the potential for this legislation to extend beyond merely changing the way people live and think, but also to transform the way government operates and society is structured.

I understand both perspectives well.

For the first 30 years of our nation's existence, there were two dominant ideologies. One was Objectivism, which posits that humanity's ultimate goal is to self-actualize. The other was a school of thought aligned with Catholic social teaching, which emphasizes the importance of government in achieving a better life for all humanity.

I was raised in this school, with the teachings of Jesus and the Old Testament serving as guiding principles. My upbringing was marked by a strong sense of duty to guide and protect all individuals, regardless of their beliefs.

However, as I entered college, I began to question the mold of the ideal Catholic social teaching individual. I was more interested in learning and questioning than in conforming to traditional expectations.

I felt lost and confused, struggling with feelings of depression, loneliness, and fear. I saw the Church as an institution that could solve my problems, but I eventually realized that I needed to understand its true nature.

Through online research and reading articles in local newspapers, I discovered a growing movement of individuals who subscribe to Objectivism, a philosophy that emphasizes personal freedom and autonomy. They call themselves "anarcho-capitalists," and I was inspired by their message.

Today, there is ongoing debate about the morality of capitalism and its impact on humanity. However, there are more individuals identifying as "anarcho-capitalists" than ever before, and they have been invited to teach at some of the world's most prestigious universities.

I was struck by the number of students interested in learning about Objectivism, but I recognized that I was not the most logical person to initiate a conversation.

I had to overcome my fear of speaking with others and my desire to avoid being judged. I had to be humble and open to the possibility that I had made mistakes or that my actions may have harmed others.

In the end, I felt grateful for the opportunity to speak with students from my alma mater, as it allowed me to share my thoughts and experiences with others.

A notion in behavioral finance and choice-making posits that when individuals make decisions, their reasonableness is restricted by the mental and emotional constraints of their minds. This implies that people's decision-making is not always fully rational or systematic, but rather is influenced by their predispositions, emotions, and other mental limitations.

The concept of bounded reasonableness was developed by economist Herbert Simon in the 1950s and suggests that people's decision-making is not always fully consistent with the ideal of rationality as defined in traditional economics. Instead, people's decision-making is shaped by their limited cognitive capabilities and the data that is accessible to them.

Bounded reasonableness is a vital concept in understanding how people make decisions in real-world scenarios, as it acknowledges that people's decision-making is not always fully rational or based on complete information. It is also a crucial consideration in fields such as administration and public policy, where decision-making is often based on incomplete or uncertain data.

I've been meaning to write this post for a while now. Docker and Vagrant are great tools for running Linux machines on virtual machines (VM). While VMs give you the illusion of being able to run Linux natively in the guest operating system, they're fundamentally a very different thing. So when you want to take your Linux VM app out to the world, Vagrant or Docker can be a really useful tool.

But how do they do that? A few weeks ago we had our first discussion about how to run Linux apps on Vagrant. If you want the short version, check out that blog post.

I also want to make it clear that this post has nothing particularly new. There are a number of open source projects and Docker-based projects that implement the most basic features of running Linux on a VirtualMachine.

And for those who want to take it even deeper, there's the Docker Compose project that provides orchestration and configuration of Linux images via a build-tool. So if you're used to using Ansible, Chef, Salt, etc. for building Linux images out of a stack of dependencies, Docker Compose is about as close as you're going to come.

So in the meantime, here's how it can work:

Docker

First off, let's assume you've already got Vagrant installed on your system. So let's run the following command for building a Vagrant box.

$ vagrant up

This will pull down the necessary Docker image and then create a "primary" Docker machine, which you can SSH into, by typing vagrant ssh.

$ vagrant ssh ubuntu

Now that we have a virtual machine running on the Vagrant server, let's start up a project in it.

$ cd demo_vagrant/demo_dynamic_project $ docker-machine create -d docker_machine_host=$(vagrant_vm_id -m) -v $(pwd):/opt/vagrant ubuntu_ubuntu_vagrant $(docker-machine env debian ubuntu) -v $(pwd):/opt/vagrant debian -p 3306 -append "Vagrantfile" -c "Dockerfile" -e "Vagrant.toml:image 'd3:2.3.1'

Vagrant

Now that we have a virtual machine running on the Vagrant server, let's start up a project in it.

$ cd demo_vagrant/demo_dynamic_project $ vagrant up

This will pull down the necessary Docker image and then create a "primary" Docker machine, which you can SSH into, by typing vagrant ssh.

$ vagrant ssh ubuntu

And now let's run a simple shell application inside our virtual machine:

$ echo "hello world" |./example.sh

It should print:

hello world

If you don't get any output from it because your VM went down or something, you may need to run sudo docker-machine env debian ubuntu instead of vagrant bash ubuntu to set the IP address (or even use --help to find out where it says to do so).

Docker Compose

If you're familiar with Vagrant or the default Docker-based project creation script, I'm sure this will make a lot of sense. If Docker-based projects are your speed, here's the command that you can call to install a Docker Composefile in the demo_vagrant directory.

$ cd demo_vagrant/demo_dynamic_project $ docker-compose up

This will pull down the necessary Docker image and start a new Composefile in place. We can then run docker

The first two sections of the article by Mark A. Niedermayer seem to be without substance. In my opinion, a reliable report is one that is based on facts, not personal opinions. The evidence presented in the article is so flawed that it's surprising anyone took the researchers seriously.

The article relies heavily on the work of Dr. Nita Forgacs, a psychologist at McGill University and co-editor of the journal Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience. However, Niedermayer was not one of the authors of the paper. At the time of publication, Niedermayer was studying social cognition in dogs at the University of Florida.

The claim that children as young as six can process information about emotions, likes, and dislikes in others, but their ability declines sharply as they grow older, is quite astonishing. The study authors contend that their findings support a common sense view of children, that their cognitive capabilities are not developed past adolescence.

The issue is that Niedermayer is not questioning the quality, validity, or validity of the study, or the study of emotions in animals in general. He's asking a simple question about how children are typically presented: in a positive light. I can think of no reason why a study examining kids' reactions to other children, their families, or their surroundings would be less relevant than what the authors of this study did.

As for his claim that six-year-olds can learn about human emotions, that's completely fabricated, and I'll let Niedermayer answer for that one.

The idea that children can learn about other people's emotions at such a young age is counter-intuitive. However, the basic abilities of learning can develop at a young age, and children's social competencies are not only apparent later in life, but can be tested and proven at a very young age. The idea of child development based on socialization has also made important advances in our understanding of children's psychological, social, and biological origins.

One example of this approach is the research by Dr. Forgacs and colleagues showing that children's social knowledge at a young age and their ability to make inferences are important for learning about others. In other words, they can learn if another person thinks how they are, and it also appears that these abilities depend on social situations.

Niedermayer is making a straw man argument, namely that because he finds it's not obvious that children can learn to appreciate other people's emotions, it would be foolish to assume that children lack social skills like understanding the other person's point of view. He's wrong here, and he's wrong not just because "a" is wrong but because we know better, because we know that our brains and our emotions are wired differently, and because our brains are not all wired the same.

We only have a certain amount of time, and not just in the ways he mentioned, to use that understanding of our abilities. We are not all born with our brains in their original (and perfect) state, and we don't always have the opportunity to learn new skills with that knowledge. We need to learn through practice and repetition to get the best use of what we've got.

If the authors of the SCAN study had been asking a question about the best ways to present research on young children, they'd probably be asking, "Is it necessary to present children in positive, upbeat ways?" Rather than assuming that the study was intended to argue against the positive approach, which Niedermayer is actually doing, I'd rather assume that these authors were trying to figure out how the best way to present their work on youth development for the lay public might best inform educators.

When considering the narrative of human evolution, the account of the human-chimp divergence is a captivating tale. Both human and ape ancestors were bipedal (or "four-legged") for most of their evolutionary history. However, they evolved legs later in most primate lineages. There is evidence that bipedalism emerged early in human evolution. And then some.

There have been two primary types of researchers who have worked on the narrative of the human-chimp divergence. Anthropologist George Schaller of Boston University was a pioneer in both styles of research. Schaller was also a bit of a eccentric. Therefore, this week on The Sporkful, we're presenting a special three-part series exploring some of Schaller's most unconventional ideas in human evolutionary history.

Schaller once argued that the first bipedal hominins appeared around 1.2 million years ago, long before our own species emerged. There are numerous issues with that theory: We're only just now discovering fossils that clearly demonstrate Homo erectus — the earliest known human species — walking upright. Other hominins of that age (and even later) were bipedal, but there are no fossils that show them doing so.

We also know some animals don't just develop legs after they do. A few animals, like hippos and anteaters, never develop the legs required for walking or running. Instead, they develop arms later in life. And, sometimes, animals have legs and no arms in the same limb. Elephants are famous for this — they usually never have arms at all, only legs. This makes the trunk a very unusual shape.

Some researchers have also argued that humans evolved from an ape ancestor that existed alongside other human species. This kind of human-animal hybridization might have occurred, and maybe even occurred recently, but there are no clear signs of it.

When it comes to questions about human evolution, you can't really go wrong by thinking of anthropologists and palaeontologists as being on different sides of a divide. After all, while many palaeontologists study ancient animals — fossils of plants and animals, not just people — anthropologists are interested in living people, living human beings.

But they are not all on the same side of the divide: Many anthropologists think the human and chimp divergence was a one-time event; others think there were some changes in human anatomy, the way we're built now, that helped set humans and chimps apart. And they all think that there's been a lot of overlap among the species that lived on this tiny island in Africa some 20 million years ago. So while it's important to remember that anthropologists all think about the same questions, they don't always agree about the conclusions. So we thought, what better way to get the two sides talking, than to call them up on a field trip?

This week, we've got some anthropologists from the Harvard Museum of Natural History in Cambridge on Sporkful podcast:

For more information on anthropological theory, see the Museum of Anthropology's website.

For more discussion on Schaller's theories, check out this episode with John Hawks and William Kimbel. They are both scholars of evolutionary biology. You can also check out the University of Washington's website that has a collection of Schaller's papers. The U. of Wisconsin also has a collection of Schaller's papers; as we are using archival materials, we can't promise that it includes all of the papers.

In a recent conversation with Katie Couric, President Barack Obama shared his thoughts on the history of African Americans in America, particularly during the Civil Rights Movement. A pivotal figure in this movement was Martin Luther King Jr., who tragically passed away in 1968. The interview was published shortly before Obama's departure from office, leading to criticism from some quarters. They accused him of being uninformed about the Civil Rights Movement, and some even claimed that he and his administration had not made a genuine effort to combat racial discrimination in the country.

Despite facing criticism for his perceived inability to address racial discrimination, a new report has highlighted the significant impact of the Obama administration's policies in driving sweeping changes to the country's laws and social fabric. The report's findings include the fact that black Americans experienced less police violence than whites and that African American children attended school more frequently than their white peers.

"The policies of the Obama administration, particularly the Race to the Top program, have been a powerful factor in this," said William Darity, founder of the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights.

In his speech, King emphasized the importance of creating jobs, housing, and healthcare as part of a comprehensive plan to advance the rights of African Americans.

The report, titled "Race and Social Impact: The Obama Administration after Ferguson," was authored by the Black Youth Project 100, a coalition of over 250 organizations representing predominantly black ethnic groups. The report also presents statistics on systemic racism against minorities, gender, and gay rights.

Darity believes that the study demonstrates a significant shift away from racial discrimination in the country. "I think they really understand that this change has happened," Darity said.

For instance, the racial disparities in police violence between blacks and whites have decreased significantly since the 1970s. Between 1980 and 2000, black Americans reported being roughly nine times as likely to be killed by a police officer than whites. By 2010, this figure had fallen to 1.2 times, and in 2014, it dropped again, with a 4.9 times likelihood of being killed by police.

For African American students, the rate has declined even further, from 6 for every 10,000 to 2.5 for every 10,000, according to the report. The disparity between the unemployment rates of African American youth and their white peers has also decreased, falling from 15 to 12 percent over the past 30 years.

Darity sees progress despite the report's publication just weeks before Obama's departure from office. "The Obama administration has a long and impressive record of creating policy that's helping the African American community," Darity said.

However, critics are still concerned about the progress reported and some believe it is an attempt to change the narrative on what is happening in the country.

"Race-based policy changes have been a very good thing, but they do not erase the historical legacy of discrimination and unequal treatment of African Americans in this country," said Rep. John Lewis (D-Ga.).

In a statement sent to Yahoo News, the White House did not comment on the report's findings but said that "African American youth have made tremendous progress in overcoming racial disparities over the past four decades, but we know more needs to be done."

The report comes nearly a year after another report on the same subject was released by the Obama administration. That study claimed that racial disparities in educational attainment had fallen throughout Obama's presidency and that overall crime had declined to record lows. Those gains, however, were entirely or mainly due to increased incarceration and decreased police violence, the report found, rather than improving educational outcomes.

Rep. G.K. Butterfield, former chairman of the Congressional Black Caucus Institute, was more forgiving in his response to the report, saying that it suggests that the problem may be more complicated than the administration is letting on.

"I would suggest that it does indicate some progress to the extent that the racial disparities in incarceration and policing rates are declining," Butterfield said. "But what it does not demonstrate or suggest at all is that we have addressed these institutional conditions — and those institutional conditions do not disappear just because the numbers for them go down. These are still persistent problems that we have to work on for the remainder of President Obama's term."

Fresh data from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration suggests that intoxicated drivers cause nearly double the number of accidents compared to sober drivers, according to a report from a non-profit organization that has consistently questioned the federal government's alcohol policies.

Researchers at the non-profit Center for Media and Public Affairs analyzed national crash reports from 2005 to 2009 and found that the NHTSA reports approximately 8,000 fatal crashes involving drunk drivers annually. Of those crashes, the NHTSA estimated that 7,000 involved one driver who was intoxicated at the time of the crash, compared to 1,200 who were sober. However, they discovered that two-thirds of these drunk driving crashes likely involved sober drivers, whereas fewer than half of crashes involving drunk drivers who were sober had sober drivers.

The study's findings are presented in a report released on Thursday by the Center for Media and Public Affairs, a New York-based non-profit that has criticized the federal government's alcohol policies as being poorly enforced. The report also suggests that the NHTSA underestimates the number of drunk driving incidents involving alcohol-impaired drivers due to an omitted data point.

"This study raises questions about the reliability of federal crash data," said Christopher Hartwell, director of the Center for Media Studies at the University of Texas at Austin. "In fact, it raises more questions about the reliability of the data than it answers."

The data analyzed was gathered through the annual National Household Travel Survey, a series of surveys conducted by NHTSA that involves about 100,000 drivers on the road. The NHTS surveys are conducted by trained professionals and collect crash data.

Researchers analyzed over 150,000 crashes from the NHTS between 2005 and 2009. During this time period, the researchers found that approximately 50,000 accidents involving alcohol among motorists involved in the NHTS occurred, or about 21 fatalities per year.

Since these numbers did not include crashes that might have been avoided if the drivers had been legally sober, the researchers estimated the fatality rate among all drunk drivers involved in alcohol-impaired crashes is 20.2 per 100,000 drivers, or almost twice as high as the rate the NHTSA says is the safe maximum for alcohol use for adult drivers.

Voting rights are just one of the three factors that should be considered when a court challenges states' voting laws.

A celebrated hockey player, Mike Modano, received a prestigious honor last winter, joining a distinguished group of 11 individuals. Notably, four of these inductees did not participate in professional sports, while eight had never played in the National Hockey League.

Throughout his illustrious career, Modano accumulated an impressive array of accolades, including two Stanley Cup championships, six Olympic medals, and a gold medal at the 1998 Nagano Olympics.

As the first Minnesota-born player to be inducted into the United States Hockey Hall of Fame, Modano's achievements are a testament to his dedication and passion for the sport. He was drafted first round (12th overall) in the 1983 NHL draft and went on to score 17 goals and 51 points in 48 games.

Modano's induction into the Hall of Fame is a recognition of his outstanding contributions to the sport, as defined by the NHL as "outstanding contributors to the League and its fan base, who not only achieved great success but also set an example as role models for aspiring players."

In his junior and collegiate hockey days, Modano played for Minnesota State University, where he led the league in scoring with 24 goals in 1980-81. He was subsequently named the league's Rookie of the Year after registering 22 goals and 49 points in 48 games.

Over the course of his 11-season NHL career, Modano established himself as one of the league's top scorers, ranking 10th in career points and 20th in career goals. He also holds the distinction of being the third-highest scorer in league history, with a total of 1,059 points.

Modano's journey began with the San Jose Sharks, where he was drafted before signing with the Minnesota North Stars in 1984. His most successful season was 1991-92, during which he scored 30 goals and 60 points in 81 games. After a season-ending injury and a subsequent season with the Quebec Nordiques, Modano played a pivotal role in the team's Stanley Cup victory in 1994, scoring the only goal of the Cup Final and contributing five assists in six games.

In the playoffs, Modano was part of the NHL's "Legion of Doom," scoring nine goals and 25 points in 18 games. He eventually retired from professional hockey in 1999, following 10 seasons with the Dallas Stars, Anaheim Ducks, and San Jose Sharks. Modano was subsequently inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame in 2011.

In our current economic landscape, a crucial aspect stands out: the number of Americans who are neither employed nor actively seeking work has doubled since the mid-1970s. This phenomenon has a profound impact on the unemployment rate, which is often calculated for individuals who are considered "economically inactive." A more accurate term is "marginally attached workers," which encompasses those who are not employed but would like to work more hours if they could find a suitable job.

The unemployment rate is a gauge of the labor market's health, but there are two essential caveats to consider. Firstly, the unemployment rate has risen from 4.7% in the early 2000s to 5% today, indicating a decline in the number of working Americans among the employed and marginally attached workers. This is not a reflection of joblessness, as people who would like to work more hours struggle to find jobs that match their skills. Additionally, the percentage of Americans in the marginally attached worker rate is now comparable to the employment rate.

A smaller percentage of our population has been participating in the labor force for an extended period. This trend is evident in the labor force participation rate graph, which shows a decline since 2000.

These graphs convey a similar message. Individuals who are not in the labor force are not unemployed; they choose not to work. If we examine the number of people not in the labor force (represented by the black arrows), we notice that it remained steady during every recession since 1979, with the only difference being the duration of the period. If the labor force is growing, the black arrow will lengthen, and if it is shrinking, the arrow will shorten.

However, in 2010, there are no arrows indicating upward or downward trends, despite the overall labor force participation rate being slightly lower than in early 2008, when the Great Recession began.

It is essential to recognize that people are still working, albeit in different capacities. We can calculate the percentage of people with jobs by considering the employment rate and the number of part-time workers. If we assume an overall labor force participation rate of 66% and know that 56% are employed and 26% have part-time jobs, we can calculate the percentage of people with jobs as follows:

Work force = 56% + 26% = 71%

If people are not working, we have 72% of our population not working, as reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This rate measures the percentage of people in the labor force who have jobs, including those who would like to work more hours if they could find a job. It does not imply that people are not trying to find jobs; they simply choose not to work.

The fact that more people are not working than previously should not be surprising. If you were born between 1975 and 1999, you have been experiencing economic hardship since age 16. The median net worth, which is the amount by which your household is wealthier than you and your parents were at the time of your birth, has declined steadily, particularly for white households.

The graph above illustrates how these trends have affected the number of people who would like to work more hours if they could find a job. The number has consistently risen since the mid-2000s through 2009 and has become our economy's new normal.

What's the Difference Between the 2 Math Programs

We have two math departments at UT Austin in the department of mathematics and statistics (Mathematics): the basic mathematics math department and the statistics math department. Like with most departments in the U.S., the math departments have a major program, and a minor program. Both of these programs have two math degrees: an undergraduate degree or Bachelor of Fine Arts (BFA), and an upper division graduate degree, Master of Science (MS).

The math department in the mathematics and statistics department at University of Texas at Austin has a strong focus on statistics, and also allows students to complete a special curriculum in statistics and probability, which may be an option for students who are interested in a more specialized type of student. The graduate curriculum in statistics, on the other hand, includes a focus on Bayesian statistics, and offers students the opportunity to complete a specialization in statistics and probability. (The statistics department at the University of Illinois also offers a similar specialization)

For example, the bachelor's of science in statistics offers students the chance to choose a major that has a focus in statistics, while the math major offered to bachelor's degree students in Statistics offers a concentration in probability and statistics. (For more information on the differences between the majors programs, please see the page on Degrees at UT Austin)

It is important to note the two programs have very different degrees and degrees in similar topics at two different schools, so if you are planning to apply to either program or are undecided about which program you'd like to take, do more research into the different programs and make sure it is well suited to your unique personality and interests.

Why Can't I Take Math 1-11?

Mathematics 1-11 is a rigorous undergraduate mathematics degree with three or four courses that provide a broad and deep basis in basic mathematical techniques. Mathematics 11-12 is a rigorous upper-division math degree with two or three courses that provide a broad and deep foundation in advanced and applied mathematical techniques. These courses are similar to the advanced mathematics courses offered in the math major and the mathematics minors programs.

Students who take any mathematics courses other than Mathematics 1-11 are required to take and pass the same advanced mathematics courses in order to graduate. While a student has not taken and passed a calculus course in this program, they can take calculus in their second year or later. If a student takes calculus in their first year of their mathematics program, it is recommended that they start calculus from Math 12.

The difference is that while both of these programs allow students to take advanced courses, they are not required to do so. Students who do not have a mathematical background and whose only mathematical training comes from previous work in statistics can complete an advanced mathematics minor in one of the following fields, which is identical to the general minor programs for mathematics majors and minors at most universities:

Math/Applied Mathematics Math/Engineering Mathematics

This minor allows students to focus in one of three areas: Statistics, Economics, or Math/Applied Mathematics.

There are no restrictions for the other Math majors, or for mathematics majors taking the advanced calculus courses as their second or third year.

Several factors contribute to this conclusion: Firstly, the cost of developing such a system would be prohibitively expensive, making it inaccessible to the general public. Secondly, the vast majority of software is designed for 64-bit systems, and rewriting all of this software to accommodate 128-bit architecture would be a monumental task. Lastly, while 128-bit computers might potentially offer slight performance advantages in specific areas, the difference would likely be negligible, and the drawbacks would far outweigh any potential benefits. As a result, the practical realities of 128-bit computing render it a non-viable option, and we will likely continue to rely on 64-bit systems, which provide a suitable balance between performance and affordability.

The first line, read from left to right, refers to the "bread of immortality," which could sustain the dead forever. The next two lines describe the "bread of life" given to the faithful in churches. The third line distinguishes between two types of bread, one for the body and one for the spirit, with the former not made from wheat or gluten-containing grains. The final line specifies that the two types of bread for the body must be prepared by the priest and deacons.

The Eucharist can be described in various ways. It consists of three parts: the bread of the living with its "signet wine," the bread for the body, and the holy chalice. The Eucharist is comprised of numerous "signs and tokens" that are given to individuals, either voluntarily or by force. It has been referred to as the "cup of blessing" because the signs and tokens associated with it are blessed and used by the Eucharistic community in the celebration of sacraments.

It is noteworthy that, according to the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the body of Christ is not treated as a mere vessel to be blessed by the priest or minister. Christ is the head of the Church, and the sacrament of the Eucharist is His supreme priestly sacrament. Christ is the first sacrament that must be instituted, and it is necessary that He be born on the cross in the flesh. The Eucharist is the bread that has been "changed into the flesh of Christ," which Christ bears and has been received by faith (Col. 2:16): the sacrament of redemption.

The Blessed Sacrament is administered to individuals through a specific ritual. The priest first receives or prepares the "bread" by a blessing from the bishop. The bread is then placed upon a linen cloth, wrapped in new linen cloth, wrapped in white hyssop dipped in the blood of Christ, and sealed with the chalice dipped in the Holy Spirit. This is the form of consecration used by the priest.

When the priest combines the sacred vessels, the wine, referred to as the "holy chalice," may be poured into the chalice by the celebrant pouring it into a white cup. The wine is poured into the chalice with a procession involving the bread and chalice. The chalice is not filled all at once; it is first poured by one, then by two, then by three, and so on to the number of the faithful.

The priests then wash the chalice in white wine, and finally, they pour holy water upon it, from a chalice dipped in it. The water enters at the end of the chalice, where it meets the oil from the olive tree. The chalice is then brought to the place of prayer of the faithful. The faithful and the priest stand at the same location for a prayer. These symbols are repeated daily at the Mass.

The People

The priest is present in his vestments when he consecrates the bread and chalice to the people, just as they have been consecrated to him when presented to him by the bishop. However, as the priest performs his duties with reverence, so too does he present the bread and chalice to the people with reverence. Thus, the priest brings the bread and wine to the church, in obedience to the bishop, and the people, with reverence, bring them to the altar, in obedience to the priest. The priest carries the bread and wine in the hands of each person and in his own vestments when he leaves the church.

The Celebrant

In the celebration of the Eucharist, there are two celebrants. During the beginning of the service, after the priest has blessed the bread and chalice with the bishop, there is a singing of the liturgies (sometimes one is sung, and sometimes the other).

The subtle nuances of sonic fidelity. It appears that when a signal is not sufficiently resampled, it can lead to a curious phenomenon known as "distortion." This distortion can be quite vexing, as it can be challenging to identify and rectify.
